statement: In controlled-administration studies in adults, methamphetamine's plasma elimination half-life is about 10 to 12 hours and varies little by route: 10.7 hours (SD 2.4) after an intranasal and 10.7 hours (SD 2.1) after a smoked dose, with 11.0 to 11.8 hours for an intravenous reference dose given in the same sessions to the same 8 men (Harris et al., 2003); geometric means of 11.1 hours (smoked) and 12.2 hours (intravenous) in 6 men, with individual values from 8.3 to 18.2 hours (Cook et al., 1993); and 9.3 hours (SD 3.7) and 11.1 hours (SD 7.2) after single 10 mg and 20 mg sustained-release oral doses (Schepers et al., 2003). The figure applies to d-methamphetamine, the isomer given in those three studies: in a double-blind crossover, intravenous l-methamphetamine had a half-life of 13.3 to 15.0 hours against 10.2 to 10.7 hours for d-methamphetamine (Mendelson et al., 2006). Time to peak plasma concentration is a separate quantity that depends on route and formulation, and the active metabolite amphetamine has a longer half-life (about 15 to 17 hours) than the parent drug. Every study is small (6 to 12 participants), none randomized the order of routes except the enantiomer crossover, and the participants' own patterns of use were light or not reported.
plain: Meth leaves the blood slowly: after the level in the blood peaks, it takes about 10 to 12 hours to fall by half, and this is much the same whether it was snorted, smoked, injected or swallowed. People differ (about 8 to 18 hours in one study). The mirror-image form of the molecule, l-methamphetamine, stays longer. How long the drug can be measured in blood is not the same as how long its effects last.
population: Adults given single doses of methamphetamine in controlled-administration studies (6 to 12 participants per study; intranasal, smoked, intravenous or oral sustained-release)
exposure: Single methamphetamine dose (study conditions: 50 mg intranasal and 40 mg placed in the device for the smoked condition with a 10 mg intravenous reference; about 30 mg placed in the device with a 15.4–15.5 mg intravenous dose; 10 or 20 mg oral sustained-release; 0.25 and 0.5 mg/kg intravenous in the enantiomer study)
outcome: Plasma elimination half-life (with clearance, volume of distribution and the metabolite's half-life)
magnitude: t½ about 10–12 h: intranasal 10.7 h (SD 2.39) and smoked 10.7 h (SD 2.11), with the intravenous reference 11.8 h (SD 3.59) and 11.0 h (SD 2.68) in the same men (n=8; Harris et al., 2003); smoked 11.1 h and intravenous 12.2 h as geometric means, individual range 8.3–18.2 h (n=6; Cook et al., 1993); oral sustained-release 9.3 h (SD 3.7) and 11.1 h (SD 7.2) (n=7 and n=5; Schepers et al., 2003). By enantiomer, intravenous: d 10.2–10.7 h against l 13.3–15.0 h (P<.0001; n=12; Mendelson et al., 2006). Clearance about 0.19–0.27 L·h⁻¹·kg⁻¹ and volume of distribution about 3.2–4.3 L/kg across these studies; the metabolite amphetamine 15.2–16.9 h.

grade.reasoning: Controlled-administration studies with a within-person intravenous reference start high (METHODS §6.3). Risk of bias −1: three of the four studies were unblinded and did not randomize the order of conditions, two had no placebo, and the samples are 6 to 12 people (card judgments: high for Harris et al., Cook et al. and Schepers et al.; some concerns for Mendelson et al.). Indirectness is no longer downgraded: the parameter is now measured directly in four primary studies rather than taken from a narrative review that cited another review. Inconsistency 0: four studies in three independent laboratories (Research Triangle Institute with North Carolina, the NIDA intramural programme, and San Francisco) agree within about two hours across four routes. Imprecision 0 for the central estimate, while the statement carries the individual range of about 8 to 18 hours. The enantiomer difference rests on a single study and is reported as such. The second-hand anchor to Kish (2008) is kept only as the trail from the earlier draft and may be dropped by the editor.

statement: In two double-blind laboratory studies of single intranasal doses given to adults who used methamphetamine regularly and were not seeking treatment, plasma methamphetamine was highest at the 3–4-hour samples (the last sample taken in one study and the last before 6 hours in the other, so the true peak may be later; in an independent laboratory, where plasma was sampled to 72 hours after a single intranasal dose in 8 men, the peak came at 2.66 hours on average, SD 1.16, which bounds it), whereas heart rate and blood pressure peaked within about 15 minutes in both studies, and subjective ratings at 15 minutes in the one study that reported their timing. Both studies come from one laboratory, so they are not independent replications. In one of them, heart rate at the start of the next day's session was 9–11 beats per minute higher (editors' calculation from the printed means) after the two methamphetamine conditions than after placebo, but outside use of amphetamines was not excluded by the urine screens and some next-day values exceeded the acute peaks, so this may not be a residual drug effect.
plain: In lab studies, adults who use meth regularly were given single snorted doses. Heart rate and blood pressure peaked within about 15 minutes, and so did the felt effects in the study that timed them, while the amount of drug in the blood was still rising 3–4 hours later. In one study, heart rate the next morning was about 9–11 beats a minute higher than after a dummy dose, but this may have come from drug use outside the lab. Both studies came from one lab.
population: Adults who used methamphetamine regularly and were not seeking treatment (11 participants in one study, 13 men in the other)
exposure: Single intranasal doses of methamphetamine (study conditions 12–50 mg/70 kg)
comparator: Placebo, same participants (within-subject, double-blind)
outcome: Time to peak plasma concentration; time to peak cardiovascular and subjective effects; heart rate about 24 hours later
magnitude: Plasma peak about 3–4 h after dosing (values shown only in figures); cardiovascular and subjective peaks within about 15 min. Next-day heart rate 86.1 and 87.8 beats/min after the two methamphetamine conditions and 90.5 after the larger d-amphetamine condition, vs 76.8 after placebo (p<0.01); interpretation uncertain (see statement).

statement: Methamphetamine raises extracellular dopamine, noradrenaline and serotonin by promoting their release from nerve endings, apparently by moving them from storage vesicles into the cytoplasm (through the vesicular transporter VMAT2) and reversing transport through the membrane transporters; the mechanism is not completely understood. This is cited from a narrative review (Kish, 2008); the primary pharmacology, including the drug's relative potency at the three transporters, has not yet been read.
plain: Meth makes nerve endings release three chemical messengers: dopamine, noradrenaline and serotonin. It seems to do this by pushing them out of their storage sacs inside the nerve ending and running their recycling pumps in reverse, but the details are not fully understood. This description comes from a review; the original laboratory studies have not yet been read here.

statement: In adults with a history of heavy methamphetamine use, scanned after days to years of abstinence, striatal dopamine transporter availability is lower on average than in people who do not use: about 13–28% lower in individual PET studies (a further study reports DAT and VMAT2 together as 10–16% lower), and a pooled standardized difference of g = −1.47 (95% CI −1.83 to −1.10) across 9 studies of people who used amphetamine-type stimulants (108 people who used them, including people who used dexamphetamine recreationally, and 126 controls); the meta-analysis is rated critically low confidence and includes two studies each from two research groups whose samples may overlap, so its interval is probably too narrow. The direction is consistent across research groups (certainty low); the size of the difference is very uncertain (certainty very low), because every primary study is an unadjusted comparison and the pooled estimate comes from a critically low-confidence meta-analysis. Individual values overlap with the control range. Where reported, the methamphetamine groups smoked tobacco and used other drugs more than controls, though a Japanese study of 11 men who had used only methamphetamine, now read in full, found dopamine transporter binding potential 20.2% lower in the caudate/putamen and 29.6% lower in the nucleus accumbens than in 9 men who had not used it, with that methamphetamine group referred from psychiatric services and 8 of the 11 having previously had methamphetamine psychosis (Sekine et al., 2001). These designs cannot show whether the difference reflects lost nerve terminals, reduced transporter expression or differences that predate use.
plain: On brain scans, people who used meth heavily and then stopped have on average about 13–28% less of the dopamine transporter (the protein that clears dopamine after it is released) in the striatum than people who don't use. Some of their values fall within the range of people who don't use. Many research groups have found this difference, but how big it is remains very uncertain. People who used meth in these studies also smoked tobacco and used other drugs more often, though one study of people who had not used other illegal drugs found a similar difference. The scans can't tell whether the difference means damaged nerve endings, the brain making less of the protein, or a difference that was there before use.
population: Adults with a history of heavy methamphetamine use, abstinent for days to years
exposure: History of heavy methamphetamine use
comparator: Adults who do not use methamphetamine
outcome: Striatal dopamine transporter (DAT) availability on PET or SPECT

(2012). Pooled: g −1.47 (95% CI −1.83 to −1.10), 9 studies of people who used amphetamine-type stimulants. Group distributions overlap.

grade.reasoning: Observational comparisons start low. Rated for the direction of the difference, which is consistent across independent research groups, tracers and post-mortem tissue, so it is not downgraded for inconsistency; the study-level risks of bias (people with heavy use selected from treatment programmes compared with advertisement-recruited controls, unmatched tobacco and other drug use, overlapping samples) bear mainly on its cause, which this claim does not assert. The size of the difference is very low certainty: every primary study is an unadjusted comparison with imbalances in smoking and sex where these were reported and unmeasured other drug use, and the pooled estimate comes from a critically low-confidence meta-analysis with reporting errors and probable sample overlap. The displayed certainty applies to the direction only; for the size, a strict reading gives very low.

statement: In five adults from a court-supervised treatment programme who were scanned after about 3 months of abstinence and again after about 14 months, striatal dopamine transporter availability rose by 19% in the caudate and 16% in the putamen; in the same programme, a protracted-abstinence group of 10 (five of them the same people at their second scan) did not differ significantly from controls, whereas those in short abstinence (n=12) were about 25% (caudate) and 21% (putamen) lower. The five who stayed abstinent started with higher transporter levels than those who dropped out, and no control group was rescanned. Four cross-sectional analyses, including this programme's own baseline study, found no relation between time since last use and transporter levels (Volkow, Chang, Wang, Fowler, Leonido-Yee, et al., 2001; Sekine et al., 2001, read in full, in 11 men abstinent from 7 days to 1.5 years; Johanson et al., 2006, and McCann et al., 2008, as described by Hart et al., 2012); all are small, so they bound recovery rather than exclude it. A DAT follow-up with retested controls (5 people who used methamphetamine, 7 controls, SPECT) reported a mean 20% rise over 2 weeks, but its first scan was taken while urine tests were still positive (Chou et al., 2007, as described by Dean et al., 2013). The same review judges the PET rise unlikely to be simply an artefact of repeat testing (Dean et al., 2013), and a later follow-up from the first group (Volkow et al., 2015), which another review cites as supporting recovery, has not yet been read.
plain: Five people from a court-supervised treatment programme were scanned twice. After a year or more without meth, their dopamine transporter levels had risen by about a sixth to a fifth. No one who doesn't use meth was scanned twice for comparison, so normal differences between scans can't be ruled out, though one review thinks they are unlikely to explain the rise. A group scanned after many months without meth, which included these five, was not clearly different from people who don't use. But the groups were too small to rule out a large difference. Four studies found no link between how long people had gone without meth and their transporter levels. In another small study, levels rose over two weeks, but the first scan was taken while meth still showed up in urine tests. A later follow-up by the same research group has not yet been read. Five people is too few to know how typical this is, and those who stayed abstinent had higher levels to begin with.
population: Adults with DSM-IV methamphetamine dependence in a court-supervised treatment programme (relapse meant a return to jail)
exposure: Protracted abstinence (about 14 months; range 12–17)
comparator: The same people after about 3 months of abstinence; non-using controls (not rescanned)
outcome: Striatal dopamine transporter availability on PET
magnitude: Within-person: +19% caudate, +16% putamen (n=5). Cross-sectional: protracted abstinence 5% (caudate) and 9% (putamen) below controls, not significant (n=10 vs 11; editors' calculation: g −0.31, 95% CI −1.17 to 0.55, and −0.57, −1.45 to 0.30, so a remaining difference of more than 1 SD is not excluded in either region, although one as large as in short abstinence, about −1.5 SD, lies outside both intervals); short abstinence 25% (caudate; 26% in the text) and 21% (putamen) below.

statement: In people who had last used methamphetamine a mean of 2.6 days earlier, striatal binding of a vesicular monoamine transporter (VMAT2) tracer was 28% higher than in controls (28 people who used methamphetamine, 22 controls) and tracked how recently and how often methamphetamine had been used (the amount variable is internally inconsistent); in the 17 who stayed abstinent, who had been less elevated at the first scan, binding no longer differed significantly from 9 rescanned controls after a mean of about 10 days, an imprecise comparison. The authors attribute the early rise to depleted vesicular dopamine competing less with the tracer, which the study could not test directly. Raised binding in early abstinence has been reported by one laboratory only (two studies with partly shared controls). A review reports post-mortem VMAT2 as normal in one binding study, whose subjects had all used methamphetamine within about 5 days of death, and, in a second study by immunohistochemistry, not significantly different, with a trend lower in the nucleus accumbens and putamen. One PET study of people who had used methamphetamine, abstinent a mean of 3.4 years (minimum 3 months) found binding about 10% lower, which a meta-analysis expresses as a large standardized difference (g 1.68).
plain: Another dopamine marker, VMAT2 (the protein that packs dopamine into storage vesicles), gave a higher scan signal on average in people scanned a few days after last using meth. In those who then stayed off meth for about 10 days, who had been less raised to begin with, it no longer differed clearly from a small comparison group. The researchers think the raised signal reflects low stored dopamine rather than more of the protein, which the study could not test. In the one scan study of people who had stopped for more than 3 years on average, it was about 10% lower. In brain tissue examined after death, it was normal in one study, whose subjects had used meth in the days before dying, and not clearly lower in another.
population: Adults who used methamphetamine regularly, scanned in early abstinence
exposure: Recent methamphetamine use (mean 2.6 days since last use at the first scan)
comparator: Controls who do not use methamphetamine; the same participants after about 10 days of abstinence
outcome: Striatal VMAT2 binding ((+)[11C]DTBZ PET)
magnitude: Scan 1: whole striatum BPND 3.09 (SD 0.71) vs 2.41 (SD 0.34), +28%, p<0.0001 (editors' Hedges' g 1.16, 95% CI 0.56 to 1.76; a meta-analysis prints the same g and interval for 'two early-abstinence studies', so whether two studies were pooled is unclear). Scan 2 (mean 9.9 days): 2.54 (0.39) in 17 abstainers vs 2.46 (0.34) in 9 controls, not significantly different (editors' g 0.21, −0.60 to 1.02). Long abstinence (mean 3.4 years): about 10% lower (g 1.68).

evidence.locator: Results › MA users have greater binding during early abstinence; Table 3
evidence.extracted: At a mean of 2.6 days after last use, whole-striatum binding was 28% higher in 28 people who used methamphetamine than in 22 controls (BPND 3.09, SD 0.71, vs 2.41, SD 0.34; p<0.0001); 9 people who used cocaine did not differ from controls.

evidence.locator: Results › Rapid recovery paragraph; Table 3
evidence.extracted: At the second scan (mean 9.9 days) the 17 who stayed abstinent did not differ from 9 rescanned controls (2.54 vs 2.46); within them binding fell about 11% (p=0.055), with individual changes from −34% to +29%. The 7 who did not stay abstinent had higher first-scan binding (full striatum 3.38 vs 2.85 in the 17).

evidence.extracted: Binding correlated with frequency of recent use (r=0.68), amount used in the past month (r=0.48), days abstinent (r=−0.49) and plasma methamphetamine (r=0.50).

evidence.extracted: The 7 who did not stay abstinent had 17% higher first-scan binding than the 17 who did and were not rescanned, so the recovery estimate comes from a subgroup that started closer to controls.

(2016) alone. VMAT2 is described as lower after 'three months of abstinence' (g 1.68, 95% CI 0.86–2.5) in Johanson et al. (2006) (ref 28), which Hart et al. statement: In one PET study, 15 people abstinent from methamphetamine had 14% higher whole-brain glucose metabolism than 21 controls (p<0.05, while the study set p<0.01 as its threshold). Significant decreases appeared only after each region was normalized to that higher whole-brain value (thalamus 17%, striatum 6–12% lower); in absolute terms (editors' reading of a figure) thalamic metabolism was about 4% lower, caudate about equal and putamen about 8% higher. Another research group, studying people 4–7 days after last use, found no difference in global metabolism. The same research group, comparing 12 of the same participants with a different control group, found a similar 14% excess that was not significant (Wang et al., 2004). In a study that retested controls, global metabolism rose more in people who had used methamphetamine than in controls over the first month of abstinence (Berman et al., 2007, as described by Dean et al., 2013), so timing may explain part of the disagreement. The two groups also differed in smoking (73% vs 24%) and in the share of women (60% vs 28%); in separate analyses by sex (9 vs 6 women, 6 vs 15 men; t tests only, means not shown), the lower relative thalamic and caudate values were reported in both sexes, while a higher whole-brain value was reported for the women (p<0.05) and none was given for the men. Cognition was tested only in the methamphetamine group.
plain: One brain-energy study found more activity overall in people who had stopped meth, but the difference did not meet the study's own standard for significance, and when men and women were looked at separately the study gave this result for the women but not for the men. Deep brain structures looked clearly lower only when compared with that higher overall level; in absolute terms, only one of them was slightly lower. That relative difference was reported in both men and women. Another group, studying people who had stopped more recently, did not find the overall difference. The groups also differed in smoking and in the share of women, so these scans can't show what meth did.
population: Adults with DSM-IV methamphetamine dependence, abstinent 2 weeks to 35 months (12 of 15 within 5 months); the same 15 people as in the first transporter study (Volkow, Chang, Wang, Fowler, Franceschi, Sedler, Gatley, Hitzemann, et al., 2001)

statement: In five people from a court-supervised treatment programme, rescanned after 12–17 months of abstinence (apparently the same five whose dopamine transporter levels were followed in the transporter-recovery study described in section 4: the sample descriptions match, but neither paper says so), thalamic glucose metabolism relative to the whole brain rose by 12% (SD 9%), while relative striatal metabolism (+2.7%), absolute regional metabolism and global metabolism (about −4%, editors' calculation) did not change significantly. Relative striatal metabolism remained lower than in controls, although in absolute values no group difference was found and the authors note that a higher whole-brain value in the methamphetamine group could contribute to the lower relative values. No control group was rescanned, and the reported test statistics contain errors.
plain: In five people re-scanned after a year without meth, activity in one deep brain region (the thalamus) went up relative to the rest of the brain, while the striatum stayed lower than in people who don't use, but only relative to the whole brain, not in absolute terms. They appear to be the same five people as in the dopamine transporter follow-up, though the papers do not say so. This rests on five people, with no comparison group scanned twice, and the paper's statistics contain errors.

statement: Whether methamphetamine use, as people use it, causes lasting loss of or damage to dopamine neurons in humans has not been established. Lower dopamine transporter levels in people who used methamphetamine heavily are consistently found, but other markers of dopamine terminals are not consistently lower (post-mortem dopamine metabolites and synthesizing enzymes were normal; binding of a VMAT2 probe was raised in early abstinence, which its authors read as low stored dopamine rather than more VMAT2; VMAT2 was normal post-mortem in one study of people who had used shortly before death and not significantly lower in another, and about 10% lower in one study of long abstinence), and low post-mortem dopamine comes from one laboratory's series of people who used shortly before death. The measures available cannot distinguish loss of nerve terminals from reversible down-regulation; in two small follow-ups of five people the transporter rose with abstinence (one rescanned after about 14 months; the other over 2 weeks, from a first scan taken while urine tests were still positive), while cross-sectional studies found no relation with time since last use; and the pattern differs from that of Parkinson's disease. Two record-linkage studies found more Parkinson's disease diagnoses in people with methamphetamine- or amphetamine-related diagnoses (in one, 0.30% vs 0.11% over about 7 years, a count that includes diagnoses made on the same date as the first stimulant code), though misclassified diagnoses are a plausible explanation (see the Parkinson's disease claim in section 9).
plain: Does meth damage dopamine nerve cells? Not shown either way. People who used meth heavily have less of one dopamine protein (the transporter), but this protein can drop without any nerve cells being lost, other markers of dopamine nerve endings are not consistently lower, and in two small follow-ups the transporter rose again after people stopped, though other studies found no link between how long people had stopped and their transporter levels. The pattern also differs from Parkinson's disease. On the other side, two health-record studies found Parkinson's diagnoses more often in people with meth-related diagnoses (about 3 versus 1 in 1,000 over 7 years in one), though some of those diagnoses may be other conditions. See the contested question.

exposure: Methamphetamine use
comparator: No use
outcome: Loss of, or structural damage to, dopamine neurons or their terminals
magnitude: Not estimable: no study has counted dopamine neurons or terminals quantitatively in people who used methamphetamine.

grade.reasoning: Observational and post-mortem evidence, starts low. Risk of bias: the people studied post-mortem died soon after use, so acute depletion and lasting damage are confounded; imaging samples are small and selected. Indirectness: the markers are surrogates for neuron or terminal loss, and the animal evidence uses regimens unlike human use.

debate.question: Does methamphetamine use damage dopamine neurons in the human brain?
debate.evidence_yes: People who used methamphetamine heavily, scanned after days to years of abstinence, have lower striatal dopamine transporter availability than people who do not use it: about 13–28% lower in individual PET studies and g −1.47 pooled over 9 studies (Volkow, Chang, Wang, Fowler, Leonido-Yee, et al., 2001; McCann et al., 1998; Ashok et al., 2017). The difference was found in groups abstinent for years on average (about 34 months in McCann et al., 1998; about 6 years in McCann et al., 2008, as described by Hart et al., 2012), and three cross-sectional analyses found no relation with time since last use. Post-mortem, striatal dopamine was 50–61% lower in 20 people who had used methamphetamine within about 5 days of death, in one laboratory's series not yet independently replicated; two of the 20 had near-total caudate loss (95% and 97%), which the authors place in the Parkinsonian range (Kish et al., 2017). The first imaging group reports transporter levels within the range of mild Parkinson's disease in three people, without giving their values (Volkow, Chang, Wang, Fowler, Leonido-Yee, et al., 2001). The authors of the follow-up argue that a recovery taking longer than 6–9 months is slower than down-regulation would produce (Volkow, Chang, Wang, Fowler, Franceschi, Sedler, Gatley, Miller, et al., 2001); in five people retested after protracted abstinence (apparently the same five) striatal metabolism did not recover, which the group reads as adaptation of surviving terminals rather than reversal of damage (Wang et al., 2004); and the group likens the equal caudate and putamen transporter loss to atypical parkinsonism rather than Parkinson's disease (Volkow, Chang, Wang, Fowler, Franceschi, Sedler, Gatley, Hitzemann, et al., 2001). In animals, high doses damage striatal dopamine terminals (Kish, 2008), and in vervet monkeys given an escalating regimen that the reviewers describe as resembling a common pattern of human use, transporter and D2-type receptor availability were reduced (London et al., 2015; magnitudes not reported). Two record-linkage cohorts found more Parkinson's disease diagnoses in people with methamphetamine- or amphetamine-related diagnoses: in Utah HR 2.8 (95% CI 1.6–4.8; 0.30% vs 0.11% over a mean of about 7 years; HR 2.2, 1.2–4.0, without diagnoses coded on the same date as the first stimulant code) and in California HR 1.76 (1.12–2.75), with no clear increase after cocaine-related diagnoses (Curtin et al., 2015; Kish et al., 2017).
debate.evidence_no: In five people rescanned after about 14 months of abstinence the transporter rose 16–19% toward control values (Volkow, Chang, Wang, Fowler, Franceschi, Sedler, Gatley, Miller, et al., 2001). A SPECT follow-up of five people found a mean 20% rise over 2 weeks, though the first scan was taken while urine tests were still positive (Chou et al., 2007, as described by Dean et al., 2013). Post-mortem, the metabolites and synthetic enzymes that fall with neuron loss in Parkinson's disease were normal in people who had used methamphetamine, and no obvious nigral cell loss was seen (Kish et al., 2017). Binding to the vesicular transporter, a marker used for terminal integrity, was raised rather than lowered in the first days after use, and in the 17 people who stayed abstinent for about 10 days it no longer differed clearly from 9 rescanned controls (Boileau et al., 2016). Post-mortem dopamine loss was greater in the caudate than the putamen, and transporter loss on PET was similar in both, unlike Parkinson's disease, in which the putamen is most affected; people with Parkinson's disease had far lower putamen transporter binding than people who had used methamphetamine (Kish et al., 2017; McCann et al., 1998). Animal neurotoxicity comes mainly from large doses given to drug-naive animals, and in a few rat studies escalating pre-exposure prevented or attenuated the neurobiological and behavioural effects of a later binge (Hart et al., 2012; Dean et al., 2013). In a vervet-monkey study of an escalating regimen, cognitive deficits improved with abstinence (Groman et al., 2012, as described by Dean et al., 2013), and a review cites the same study as some evidence that D2-type receptor availability recovers with protracted abstinence (London et al., 2015).
debate.neither_can_show: No study has scanned people before they started using. Dopamine, its transporter and VMAT2 binding can all change without any change in the number of nerve terminals, and post-mortem samples come from people who used shortly before death, so acute depletion and lasting damage cannot be separated. People who used methamphetamine in these studies also smoked tobacco and used other drugs more often than controls. Registry studies record diagnosis codes, not use or disease: in the Utah cohort the broader movement-disorder diagnoses came young and were rarely treated with levodopa in both the exposed and the control groups, and antipsychotic-induced parkinsonism, tremor and differences in medical contact were not addressed (Curtin et al., 2015).
debate.editors_reading: Editors' reading (certainty: very low). Lower striatal dopamine transporter levels in people who used methamphetamine heavily are well replicated (Ashok et al., 2017; McCann et al., 1998; Sekine et al., 2001; Volkow, Chang, Wang, Fowler, Leonido-Yee, et al., 2001); other markers of dopamine terminals are not consistently lower (Boileau et al., 2016; Kish et al., 2017), and loss of dopamine neurons in humans has not been demonstrated (Kish et al., 2017). Whether the transporter difference reverses with abstinence is uncertain: two small follow-ups found a rise: five people selected by staying abstinent, rescanned after about 14 months (Volkow, Chang, Wang, Fowler, Franceschi, Sedler, Gatley, Miller, et al., 2001), and five people over 2 weeks, first scanned while urine tests were still positive (Chou et al., 2007, as described by Dean et al., 2013), while lower levels were found in groups abstinent for years on average (McCann et al., 1998; McCann et al., 2008, as described by Hart et al., 2012). The Parkinson's-disease registry signal (Curtin et al., 2015; Kish et al., 2017), which may partly reflect diagnoses that differ between groups in what they capture, is the main reason the question cannot be closed in either direction.
debate.what_would_settle_it: Quantitative post-mortem counts of nigral dopamine neurons and structural markers of striatal terminals in people with long use and long abstinence before death; imaging cohorts that scan people before and after regular use begins; long-term rescans of people who have stopped using, alongside rescanned controls; and Parkinson's-disease registry studies with better control of smoking, other drug use and access to diagnosis.

statement: Structural MRI studies report less grey matter in some frontal, cingulate, insular, temporal and parietal (precuneus) regions and in the left caudate in people with methamphetamine dependence than in non-smoking controls, but larger striatal volumes in two studies of people abstinent for an average of 3–4 months (parietal volumes too, in one of them) and, for the putamen, in people still using (as described in a review; those studies have not yet been read), so in the striatum and parietal cortex the direction differs between studies. Abstinence before scanning was short: 4–7 days, verified by urine tests, in one study; in the other, a mean of 6.6 days (SD 5.2) at the time of the mood assessment, with no verification described and the timing of the scan not stated; in one, grey matter increased in several regions over the following month (at an uncorrected statistical threshold), so some differences may be temporary. In the study that separated tobacco smoking, smokers who did not use methamphetamine also had less orbitofrontal grey matter than non-smokers (and less caudate grey matter, as a review describes the study), and people who used methamphetamine differed from smoking controls in only 4 clusters, mostly in places other than the 10 found against non-smoking controls; with education added to the model, the results held only at a more lenient uncorrected threshold. An earlier report of 7.8% smaller hippocampi (in groups that also differed in education, depression scores and smoking) was not reproduced by the same laboratory, and memory scores were never compared between groups in that report.
plain: Brain scans taken soon after stopping (4 to 7 days in one study; not stated exactly in the other) showed some regions with less grey matter (differences of up to about 11% in one study) in people dependent on meth. Other studies, of people who had stopped for 3–4 months on average or were still using, found some regions larger, including parts of the same deep brain structures. Most people who use meth also smoke tobacco, and in the study that checked, smokers who don't use meth showed some of the same differences. People who used meth also had less schooling and more symptoms of depression. In one study, grey matter grew in several regions over the first month without meth, though only by a lenient statistical standard. An early finding of a smaller memory region (the hippocampus) was not repeated by the same lab.

comparator: Non-smoking and smoking non-using controls
outcome: Regional grey-matter volume or density (MRI)
magnitude: Thompson et al. (2004; 22 vs 21): right cingulate grey-matter density −11.3% (left −0.7%, not significant), hippocampal volume −7.8%, white matter +7.0%, total grey matter not different. Morales et al. (2012): 10 clusters smaller vs non-smoking controls; 4 vs smoking controls, at mostly different locations; orbitofrontal smaller in smoking controls too; no dose–response.

statement: In double-blind, placebo-controlled laboratory studies of adults who used methamphetamine regularly and were not seeking treatment, single intranasal doses raised heart rate, blood pressure and positive subjective ratings in a dose-related way (peak 'good drug effect' 4, 46, 58 and 79 on a 0–100 scale after placebo and three increasing doses in one study), and also raised ratings of jitteriness, a racing heart and sweating, most at the largest dose. Both studies come from one laboratory, and both tabulated only items that changed significantly: ratings such as anxious, paranoid or bad drug effect were collected but not reported, so their absence is not shown. How these single doses compare with use outside the laboratory is uncertain: a review by the same group states, without data, that most laboratory doses were in the range people take for euphoria, while another review reports blood concentrations in police investigations (median 190 ng/mL, range 15–1600) well above the roughly 50 ng/mL after a single 30 mg smoked laboratory dose.
plain: In controlled lab studies, a single snorted dose raised heart rate and blood pressure and made people feel good, high and stimulated, more so at larger doses. Ratings of feeling jittery, sweaty and of a racing heart also rose, most at the largest dose (to about 25–43 on a 0–100 scale, against 2–11 after a dummy dose). These were single doses given to people experienced with meth, not binges, and both studies came from one lab. Blood levels measured in police cases were often much higher than after one lab dose.
population: Adults who used methamphetamine regularly (in one study 11 people, 9 with DSM-IV dependence, all mainly using it intranasally, each given the largest dose once before the study), not seeking treatment
exposure: Single intranasal doses (study conditions: 12, 25 and 50 mg/70 kg in one study; 12 and 50 mg/70 kg in the other)
comparator: Placebo, same participants
outcome: Heart rate, blood pressure and subjective ratings
magnitude: Heart rate, systolic and diastolic pressure raised at all three doses vs placebo in one study and at the larger dose in the other (magnitudes in figures only). Peak 'good drug effect' 4.36 / 46.46 / 58.27 / 78.64 and 'high' 7.00 / 42.18 / 55.82 / 73.18 (0–100; placebo / 12 / 25 / 50 mg/70 kg); at 50 mg/70 kg vs placebo, jittery 24.82 vs 7.36, sweating 25.09 vs 2.09, heart beating faster 43.18 vs 11.27.

grade.reasoning: Placebo-controlled within-subject studies (dose order randomized in one, counterbalanced in the other) start high. Risk of bias (−1): RoB 2 some concerns (Hart et al., 2008) and high (Kirkpatrick, Gunderson, Johanson, et al., 2012), mainly because every participant in the first study had received the largest dose openly before the study and blinding was not checked (subjective ratings), carryover was possible (24-hour residual effects), and only significant rating items were tabulated. The cardiovascular and plasma measures are automated or assayed and the effects are large, so one level. Not downgraded for indirectness because the claim is restricted to single intranasal doses in people experienced with methamphetamine. Both studies come from one laboratory.

statement: In two double-blind, placebo-controlled laboratory studies from one research group (11 and 13 adults who used methamphetamine regularly and were not seeking treatment), single intranasal doses improved some measures of attention and psychomotor speed (divided-attention tracking at all doses in both studies; digit-symbol substitution at the two smaller of three doses in one study and not at all in the other) and did not significantly worsen any measured task. A review by the same group of 16 controlled dosing studies reported no worsening on any domain, but its table has codes only for improvement and no effect: in one reviewed study d-methamphetamine was worse than placebo on a visuospatial task in the first session and better in the second, which the review scored as no effect. By the editors' count from that table, 14 of the 16 studies did not investigate repeated dosing, 10 gave oral doses, 11 were in people without a methamphetamine-use disorder (or with histories not reported), and 7 came from the reviewers' own laboratory; the studies from other laboratories are known here only from that review, so whether they independently replicate these results has not been checked in their own reports. The studies were too small to exclude small or moderate impairments, and larger doses given repeatedly, as in binges, were not tested.
plain: In controlled lab studies, mostly of single doses, meth did not measurably worsen attention, memory or reaction-time tasks, and on some tasks people did better. The two main studies gave snorted doses to people who use meth regularly; they, and the review that summed up the other studies, came from one research group. That review could score a task only as improved or unchanged, not as worse. The studies were small, so small or moderate harmful effects can't be ruled out, and binges or long-term use were not tested.
population: Adults who used methamphetamine regularly and were not seeking treatment (the two studies read); the reviewed studies also include people with little or no stimulant experience
exposure: Single doses (intranasal in the studies read; up to 50 mg/70 kg intranasal, 30 mg intravenous or 40 mg oral in the reviewed studies; study conditions)
comparator: Placebo, same participants
outcome: Performance on attention, psychomotor, learning and memory tasks
magnitude: Improvement on divided-attention measures at all active doses and on digit-symbol substitution at 12 and 25 but not 50 mg/70 kg; no significant change on repeated acquisition, rapid information processing or digit recall; no residual performance effects at 24 h in the one study that measured them. Effect sizes not reported (values in figures only).

statement: In emergency-department, psychiatric-emergency and trauma-centre series and in case reports, seen only through two reviews (figures second-hand; the primary studies have not been read), acute methamphetamine toxicity presents with sympathomimetic and psychiatric features whose reported frequency varies several-fold between studies and settings. A narrative review describes the common features, from case reports, as agitation, dilated pupils, tachycardia, hypertension and rapid respiration; other features include shivering, dyspnoea, chest pain, hyperpyrexia and cardiac, hepatic or renal failure, with coma and seizures less frequent, and deaths in case reports are attributed most often to pulmonary oedema or congestion, cerebrovascular haemorrhage, ventricular fibrillation, acute cardiac failure or hyperpyrexia. For non-fatal presentations it gives agitation in about 20%, suicidal ideation in 6–12%, acute psychosis in 7–12%, rhabdomyolysis in up to 14% and seizures in 3–4%, from a few series, some of them of amphetamine, without denominators. A systematic review of 23 studies (searches 1990–2017; 17 from the USA, 7 of them from one centre) could not pool any clinical feature, because the studies measured them inconsistently; study by study it lists tachycardia in 42% and 85% and hypertension in 6.4% and 69% of presentations (two studies), acute coronary syndrome in 9 of 36 methamphetamine-positive patients with chest pain (the review's table gives this study 171 patients), psychosis in 12% (two studies) to 80% (60 people at a psychiatric emergency service), agitation in 13% to 48%, aggression in 18% to 50% and suicidal thoughts or behaviour in 6% to 50%, mostly without stated denominators. Neither review gives a case fatality among presentations or compares fatal with non-fatal cases, so whether higher body temperature predicts death among people who present is not established; the narrative review cites forensic studies suggesting that a significant and possibly greater proportion of methamphetamine-related deaths arise from accidents, suicide and homicide. One series of amphetamine-related presentations (Perth, 2005) is a source for both reviews, so they are not independent.
plain: Meth poisoning can look like a body in overdrive: agitation, wide pupils, a racing heart, high blood pressure and fast breathing. Other signs include very high body temperature, chest pain, muscle breakdown, and heart, liver or kidney failure; seizures and coma are less common, and some people die. This picture comes from two reviews of hospital emergency studies and case reports; we have not yet checked the original studies, and some of them concern amphetamine rather than meth. How often each sign appears differs a lot between studies and settings: a racing heart was found in 42 of 100 patients in one study and in 85 of 100 in another, and psychosis in 12 to 80 of 100. Neither review says how many patients die. One review cites studies suggesting that many meth-related deaths come from accidents, suicide and homicide. Whether high body temperature predicts death has not been studied in the sources we have read.
population: people presenting to emergency departments, psychiatric emergency services or trauma centres with acute methamphetamine toxicity (in some series, amphetamine)
exposure: acute methamphetamine exposure (in some series, amphetamine or other stimulants)
outcome: clinical toxicity syndrome and mortality
magnitude: Second-hand, mostly without denominators. Narrative review, non-fatal presentations: agitation about 20%, suicidal ideation 6–12%, acute psychosis 7–12%, rhabdomyolysis up to 14%, seizures 3–4%. Systematic review, study-level and not pooled: tachycardia 42% and 85%, hypertension 6.4% and 69% (two studies); acute coronary syndrome in 9 of 36 methamphetamine-positive patients with chest pain (171 patients in the review's table); psychosis 12% to 80%; agitation 13% to 48%; aggression 18% to 50%; suicidal thoughts or behaviour 6% to 50%. Not given by either review: case fatality among presentations, the proportion of deaths with other drugs detected, or any comparison of fatal with non-fatal cases.

evidence.extracted: Based on case reports (references 29 and 44–51, several of amphetamine poisoning), the common features of overdose are agitation, dilated pupils, tachycardia, hypertension and rapid respiration; other features include shivering, dyspnoea, chest pain, hyperpyrexia and cardiac, hepatic or renal failure, and coma or seizures occur less frequently. Non-fatal toxicity presents typically with tachycardia, hypertension and altered mental status: agitation in about 20% of cases, suicidal ideation in 6–12%, acute psychosis in 7–12%, rhabdomyolysis in up to 14% and seizures in 3–4% (references 52–55: emergency-department series and a treatment trial, partly of amphetamine; no sample sizes or denominators given). Case reports attribute deaths most often to pulmonary oedema or congestion, cerebrovascular haemorrhage, ventricular fibrillation, acute cardiac failure or hyperpyrexia; forensic series (references 58–60) suggest that a significant and possibly greater proportion of methamphetamine-related deaths arise from accidents, suicide and homicide. Proposed toxic and fatal blood concentrations are guides only, because deaths and survival have been reported across overlapping ranges. No case fatality among presentations and no comparison of fatal with non-fatal cases is given. About 94 000 US emergency-department visits in 2005 were associated with recent methamphetamine use.

evidence.extracted: The review could not pool any clinical feature: the studies had no consistent measures of clinical characteristics, so its meta-analyses were limited to sex, age and the share of methamphetamine-positive attendees. The authors list problems with the chart reviews in identifying use, its pattern and frequency, the type of methamphetamine and other drug use, and with self-report; three included studies counted cocaine or other stimulant use; positive urine toxicology likely includes other amphetamine-like compounds and stays positive for 72 hours, which makes it difficult to link use to the presentation; time of last use was not accurately assessed. Two sets of included studies are linked to the same data, and Table 1 lists the acute coronary syndrome study with 171 subjects, against 36 in the text. risk_of_bias.note: The primary case reports and series cannot be appraised through either review: the narrative review's sources are unappraised (editors' narrative-review checklist on its study card: high), and the systematic review, itself of critically low confidence on AMSTAR 2, rated 22 of its 23 mostly retrospective chart reviews at low risk without showing the ratings.

inconsistency.note: Study-level frequencies differ several-fold (tachycardia 42% against 85%, hypertension 6.4% against 69%, psychosis 12% to 80%), without stated denominators or common case definitions, and the differences are not explained.

indirectness.note: Second-hand through two reviews (METHODS §6.3); some cited series concern amphetamine rather than methamphetamine, and three studies in the systematic review counted cocaine or other stimulants.

grade.reasoning: Descriptive features from case reports and emergency chart reviews start low (relation 'describes', METHODS §6.1). The claim now rests on two reviews: a narrative review (Cruickshank & Dyer, 2009), used as a pointer, and a systematic review (Sibanda et al., 2019) that searched four databases but pooled no clinical feature and reports no deaths (AMSTAR 2 critically low on its study card). Risk of bias, one level: the primary studies cannot be appraised through either review. Inconsistency, one level: study-level frequencies differ several-fold without explanation. Indirectness, one level: second-hand, and partly about amphetamine or other stimulants. Certainty very low (the floor). The two reviews share at least one primary series (Gray et al., 2007, amphetamine-related presentations in Perth), so they are not independent. Status replicated: independent series in different countries report the same features (tachycardia and hypertension in Perth and Taipei; psychosis or paranoia in Perth, Oregon, Seattle and Honolulu), and none reports their absence; the several-fold variation in how often they occur is part of the claim and is rated under inconsistency, not in the status label. The series shared by the two reviews (Gray et al., 2007) and the linked Perth and Oregon sets are counted once. Any statement about how often a feature occurs, about case fatality or about what predicts death needs the primary series read and, for prognosis, studies that compare fatal with non-fatal cases.

statement: Head-to-head randomized evidence on antipsychotics for methamphetamine psychosis, as identified by a systematic review and network meta-analysis with searches to June 2020 and by two other systematic reviews that contain the same trials (searches to November 2018: five of the six; to March 2026: all six), consists of six small, short (21 to 42 days), single-site trials with 395 participants in Thailand, Iran and China, mostly inpatients and mostly men, each comparing two of six antipsychotics (aripiprazole, haloperidol, olanzapine, paliperidone extended-release, quetiapine, risperidone); none had a placebo or no-medication arm, and two are titled as trials in amphetamine psychosis. The network meta-analysis reports that each trial found no significant difference between its two drugs on the main psychotic symptoms (the 2026 review instead gives one aripiprazole–risperidone trial a between-group p < 0.001 on positive symptoms, and the 2019 review describes that trial in both directions), and the trials were too small to show that the drugs work equally well. Chaining the trials through their shared drugs, the network meta-analysis estimated lower symptom scores at the end of treatment on olanzapine (standardized mean difference −1.09, 95% CI −1.89 to −0.28) and quetiapine (−0.86, −1.61 to −0.11) than on risperidone, and higher scores on aripiprazole than on four of the other drugs (the review compared end-of-treatment scores, not changes from baseline); these are indirect estimates only, rated low certainty by the authors because data came partly from open-label trials and the trials differ in participants and design, and both advantages over risperidone rest on one open-label trial of haloperidol against risperidone with 44 participants. Dropout did not differ, but its intervals were too wide to be informative. Because none of these trials had a placebo arm, they cannot show whether antipsychotics speed recovery beyond what abstinence alone achieves; symptoms fell steeply in every arm, but the large effect sizes the 2026 review reports (d = 3.4 to 5.5 in the 4-week trials, the two largest from one trial computed with an end-point SD of zero) are changes from baseline within each arm, which cannot separate a drug effect from recovery with abstinence and time, and the 2019 review's per-trial effect sizes do not state what they compare. Two small placebo-controlled trials, which the network meta-analysis did not include, enrolled people whose symptoms had already largely settled: aripiprazole for 8 weeks in 37 outpatients, a trial the network meta-analysis excluded because its participants had recovered from psychotic symptoms (symptoms fell more than on placebo, between-group p = 0.032 in the 2026 review, p < 0.005 or < 0.05 in the 2019 review), and paliperidone extended-release for 12 weeks in 80 people stabilized on drug-treatment wards before discharge (reported as favouring paliperidone, p = 0.006; 28% against 55% lost to follow-up); they bear on continued treatment after the acute episode rather than on its treatment. The only trial against usual care (Hong Kong, 2026; 165 people with stimulant-induced psychosis, about nine in ten of whom had used methamphetamine, mostly mildly ill) randomized them to aripiprazole, paliperidone or usual care, in which 55% were antipsychotic-free at randomization and 24% at 24 months. On clinicians' global severity ratings (CGI-S), aripiprazole improved more than usual care at 12 months (−0.55 points, 95% CI −1.03 to −0.07; d −0.31) and at 24 months, when ratings were no longer blind; paliperidone did not differ; and symptom ratings (BPRS-24) showed no consistent difference. That trial's registered primary outcome, relapse over 36 months, was changed after the trial ended, first to the BPRS-24, in the same registry update that shortened every registered time frame from 36 to 24 months, and then to the global ratings it reports; 17% of its participants had an earlier diagnosis of schizophrenia or schizoaffective disorder (the registry excludes people diagnosed with schizophrenia), and without them the 12-month CGI-S difference was not significant (p = 0.12); only 54% were assessed at 24 months. No trial has followed people after the antipsychotic was stopped, so how long to treat and the risk of relapse after stopping are unstudied. Side effects were not pooled; as the 2026 review tabulates them, extrapyramidal symptoms occurred in 15 of 29 participants on haloperidol and none of 29 on olanzapine in the olanzapine–haloperidol trial (probably the single trial of the 2009 Cochrane review that narrative reviews describe), 10 against 2 stopped early, and in one aripiprazole–risperidone trial 7 of 21 on aripiprazole and none of 21 on risperidone stopped because of adverse effects; in the usual-care trial, serious adverse events were one suicide in the aripiprazole arm and three paliperidone discontinuations (atrial fibrillation, QTc prolongation, acute renal failure with pneumonia). Two narrative reviews state that acute psychosis usually resolves with abstinence alone, citing early studies of amphetamine psychosis published between 1958 and 1980 or an online clinical reference entry. How often psychosis persists after stopping is described in section 9.
plain: Three reviews found eight small, short trials of medicines for meth psychosis, about 500 people in all. Six compared one medicine with another and found no clear winner. Two small trials against a dummy pill, in people already improving, and one two-year trial against usual care favoured the medicine on some measures, but these trials have serious flaws. Nobody has studied stopping the medicine.
population: Adults with methamphetamine psychosis (two trials are titled as amphetamine psychosis), mostly inpatients and men, in trials in Thailand, Iran, China and Malaysia; one 24-month trial in Hong Kong of mostly mild stimulant-induced psychosis (methamphetamine or cocaine), 17% with an earlier schizophrenia or schizoaffective diagnosis
exposure: Antipsychotic medication

risk_of_bias.note: Open-label head-to-head trials and unclear allocation concealment; placebo-controlled trials seen only through reviews; the usual-care trial changed its primary outcome after data collection and lost 30–46% of assessments (alone it would be rated down two levels).

inconsistency.note: Aripiprazole–risperidone trials without a consistent direction; paliperidone better than placebo after the acute phase but not than usual care; global and symptom ratings disagree in the usual-care trial; no explanation tested (status mixed). Certainty already at its floor.

indirectness.note: Indirect network estimates rest on transitivity; placebo-controlled trials enrolled people already improving; the usual-care trial included cocaine psychosis, 17% with earlier schizophrenia, and usual care that mostly included antipsychotics; no acute-phase comparison with no antipsychotic.

imprecision.note: 37 to 120 participants per short trial; no direct head-to-head interval excludes no difference; the usual-care trial's CGI-S interval (−1.03 to −0.07) rests on 116 people assessed.

grade.reasoning: Randomized evidence, read through three systematic reviews that share their trials (Srisurapanont et al., 2021, a network meta-analysis, AMSTAR 2 low confidence; Fluyau et al., 2019, critically low; Hall et al., 2026, critically low after adjudication of its card) and one trial against usual care read in full together with its registry record (Chung et al., 2026; RoB 2 high); the eight shorter trial reports themselves have not been read. Starts high. Risk of bias −1: two of the six head-to-head trials were open-label and allocation concealment was unclear in four; both indirect advantages over risperidone, and three of the four against aripiprazole, are chained through the open-label haloperidol–risperidone pilot trial (44 participants); the two placebo-controlled trials are known only through reviews that describe their analyses inconsistently; and the usual-care trial changed its primary outcome after the data were collected, lost 30% of assessments at 12 months and 46% at 24 months, and rated its second year unblinded. Taken alone, the comparison with usual care would be rated down two levels for risk of bias; certainty would be very low either way. Indirectness −1: the network is a chain without a closed loop, so every indirect estimate rests on transitivity, which the authors themselves doubt (participants and designs differ); two trials are titled as amphetamine psychosis; the placebo-controlled trials enrolled people whose symptoms had largely settled; the usual-care trial included cocaine-induced psychosis and 17% with an earlier schizophrenia or schizoaffective diagnosis, and its usual care included antipsychotics for most participants by 24 months. No trial compares an antipsychotic with none during an acute episode, the claim's open question. Imprecision −2: 37 to 120 participants per short trial, every direct head-to-head interval includes no difference, dropout odds ratios have intervals as wide as 0.00 to 218, and the usual-care trial's 12-month CGI-S difference (−0.55, −1.03 to −0.07) comes from 116 people assessed. Inconsistency −1: the only drug pair tested twice, aripiprazole against risperidone, has one trial without a between-group difference (Wang et al., 2016) and one whose significant positive-symptom result the reviews read in opposite directions (Farnia et al., 2014); paliperidone did better than placebo after the acute phase but not better than usual care on global severity; and in the usual-care trial the global ratings and the symptom ratings disagree. Differences in comparator, population, outcome and duration could explain this, but none has been tested, and the network's global I² of 0% for main symptoms rests on one degree of freedom (six two-arm trials of six drugs, no closed loop), so it shows nothing about consistency. These disagreements are counted here and not again under indirectness, which concerns whether any trial answers the claim's open question. With this level the downgrades total five from high; certainty cannot fall below very low. Publication bias not assessable with so few trials; not downgraded, noted. Very low. The network estimates are differences in end-of-treatment scores (the review used final values for all symptom analyses), not in how much symptoms fell. Status mixed (adjudicated): several independent trials with inconsistent findings and no adequate explanation (METHODS §6.4). The three reviews share their trials and count once (§6.3), and the claim also rests on three trials against placebo or usual care from three independent groups (Malaysia, China, Hong Kong); their findings disagree as set out under inconsistency, and no explanation has been tested. Not replicated: no comparison has been tested twice with a consistent, checkable direction (the aripiprazole trials against placebo and against usual care use different comparators, the first is known only through reviews that report its analysis inconsistently, and the second changed its primary outcome after the trial ended). Not single study: several independent trials. The two Chinese head-to-head trials share authors, and the narrative reviews describe some of the same trials. The olanzapine–haloperidol trial (Leelahanaj et al., 2005), probably the trial the narrative reviews describe as the 2009 Cochrane review's single trial with 58 participants, is listed with 58 (29 and 29) by the 2019 and 2026 reviews and with 56 (29 and 27) by the network meta-analysis. The placebo-controlled aripiprazole trial (Sulaiman et al., 2013) may have randomized people after an open-label aripiprazole phase reported in a dissertation (Sulaiman, 2011): that phase's end PANSS (51.6) equals the trial's entry PANSS in the network meta-analysis (editors' inference; the trial report has not been read).

statement: The US National Comorbidity Survey (1990–1992; household sample aged 15–54; structured CIDI interview) reported, for each drug class separately, the proportion of people who had ever used it who had ever met DSM-III-R criteria for dependence, with non-medical use of stimulants other than cocaine counted as one class. Among people who had ever used psychostimulants other than cocaine extramedically (15.3% of the population; dextroamphetamine and methamphetamine are the examples given), 11.2% (SE 1.6; about 8.1% to 14.3%, editors' calculation) had ever met the criteria, against 31.9% for tobacco (no standard error; tobacco use came from a separate 1991 survey and dependence was assessed for daily smoking in a subsample), 15.4% for alcohol, 16.7% for cocaine, 23.1% for heroin and 9.1% for cannabis. Such proportions are taken at a single interview among everyone who had ever used, including once (the dependence questions were asked only of people reporting more than a few occasions of use), and do not account for people who started recently; the data are three decades old, grouped across stimulants and based on DSM-III-R criteria. The source calls the class psychostimulants other than cocaine; it includes extramedical use of prescription stimulants. A 2007 Australian national household survey (8,841 people aged 16–85; response 60%; WMH-CIDI 3.0 interview) measured something different. Its outcome was broader, DSM-IV stimulant abuse or dependence, in a stimulant class the paper does not define. Of 579 people who had used stimulants, 45.7% (95% CI 39.5–51.8) had met the criteria by the interview. A survival analysis, which uses the years since each person first used and so allows for people who had started recently, estimated a cumulative probability of 50.4% (no interval given) of developing the disorder within 14 years of first use, 12.2% within the first year. The criteria were asked only of people who had used at least five times, and the authors note that counting abuse as well as dependence gives higher estimates than studies of dependence alone. The two surveys therefore measure different quantities and cannot be compared directly, and neither gives a figure for methamphetamine alone.
plain: A large US survey from the early 1990s counted, for each kind of drug, how many of the people who had ever used it had ever been dependent on it. About 11 in 100 of the people who had ever used stimulants other than cocaine (such as amphetamine or meth) without a prescription, or not as prescribed, had been dependent on them at some point, compared with about 32 in 100 for tobacco, 15 in 100 for alcohol and 17 in 100 for cocaine. That survey counted everyone who had ever tried a drug, even once, on the day of the interview, so people who had started only recently had had little time to become dependent. An Australian survey from 2007 asked a different question. It estimated how many of the people who had used stimulants (it does not say which ones) would develop dependence or a related diagnosis called abuse within 14 years of first using them: about 50 in 100. About 46 in 100 had already had one of these diagnoses at some point by the time they were interviewed; the questions were asked only of people who had used at least five times. Because the two surveys measure different things, the higher Australian number does not show that the risk has gone up. Both surveys lump stimulants together, and neither gives a number for meth alone.
population: US household (noninstitutionalized) population aged 15–54 in 1990–1992 who had ever used psychostimulants other than cocaine extramedically; Australian household population aged 16–85 in 2007 who had ever used stimulants (class not defined)
exposure: lifetime extramedical use of psychostimulants other than cocaine, including prescription stimulants used without or beyond a prescription (US); lifetime use of stimulants, class not defined (Australia)
comparator: other substance classes
outcome: lifetime DSM-III-R dependence, as a proportion at interview (US); lifetime DSM-IV abuse or dependence, as a proportion at interview and as a cumulative probability by years since first use (Australia)
magnitude: US NCS (weighted, n = 8,098; Table 2): proportion ever dependent (DSM-III-R) among people who had ever used extramedically: psychostimulants other than cocaine 11.2% (SE 1.6; editors' 95% CI about 8.1% to 14.3%), from 15.3% lifetime use and 1.7% lifetime dependence in the population; tobacco 31.9% (no SE), alcohol 15.4% (0.7), cocaine 16.7% (1.5), cannabis 9.1% (0.7), heroin 23.1% (5.6). Stimulants by age: 13.5% (15–24), 13.9% (25–34), 7.7% (35–44), 6.5% (45–54); by sex: men 9.7%, women 13.3% (Tables 4–5). Australia 2007 (NSMHWB; weighted; stimulant class not defined; DSM-IV abuse or dependence): 45.7% (95% CI 39.5–51.8) of 579 people who had used stimulants had ever met the criteria at interview; cumulative probability by years since first use (discrete-time survival analysis, no interval) 12.2% within the first year and 50.4% within 14 years; among those who developed the disorder, half did so within about 3 years (IQR 1–5) of first use.

evidence.extracted: National Comorbidity Survey, September 1990 to February 1992: probability sample of the noninstitutionalized population aged 15–54 in the 48 coterminous states, response rate 82.4%, n = 8,098; DSM-III-R dependence by lay-administered CIDI. Of the population, 15.3% (SE 0.7) had ever used psychostimulants other than cocaine extramedically (examples given: dextroamphetamine, methamphetamine) and 1.7% (SE 0.3) had ever been dependent on them, so 11.2% (SE 1.6) of those who had used them had ever met the criteria. Corresponding proportions: tobacco 31.9% (no SE; tobacco use from the 1991 NHSDA, dependence assessed for daily smoking in a subsample of 4,414), alcohol 15.4% (SE 0.7), cocaine 16.7% (1.5), cannabis 9.1% (0.7), heroin 23.1% (5.6), any controlled substance or inhalant 14.7% (0.7). Each proportion is the lifetime prevalence of dependence divided by the lifetime prevalence of use on at least one occasion. Editors' calculation: 95% CI for the stimulant proportion about 8.1% to 14.3%.

Of the 579 people who had used stimulants and gave a valid age of first use, 45.7% (95% CI 39.5–51.8) had a lifetime stimulant use disorder at the interview (a descriptive conditional probability); median age of onset 20 years (IQR 18–24). risk_of_bias.note: Not downgraded for the US figures (JBI items met or largely met, study card overall low: national probability sample, response 82.4% with weighting, a standardized CIDI interview and design-based standard errors; frame, deaths and self-report could move the figure in either direction but not materially). Downgraded one level for the Australian figures (JBI moderate on the study card): response 60% with no non-response analysis reported, ages of first use and onset recalled at one interview and coded by inconsistent rules, and a denominator that may or may not include people who had used fewer than five times.

inconsistency.note: Not downgraded: the two surveys do not estimate the same quantity (outcome, measure, stimulant class, country and decade differ), so the gap between 11.2% and 45.7–50.4% is not heterogeneity in the GRADE sense; the statement presents the figures separately and says they cannot be compared.

indirectness.note: US: psychostimulants other than cocaine, of which methamphetamine is one example, including extramedical use of prescription stimulants; DSM-III-R; 1990–1992. Australia: a stimulant class that is not defined (it may include cocaine and other stimulants), an outcome that includes DSM-IV abuse; 2007. Neither gives a methamphetamine-specific figure.

grade.reasoning: A descriptive claim (proportions and a cumulative probability in survey populations): starts low. Risk of bias, one level, for the Australian figures only (60% response, recalled timing, unclear denominator); the US figures are not downgraded (JBI low; the authors discuss frame, deaths and self-report, pp. 263–265). Indirectness, two levels: neither survey isolates methamphetamine, the US class includes extramedical use of prescription stimulants, and the Australian class is undefined and its outcome includes abuse; the criteria are DSM-III-R (1990–1992) and DSM-IV (2007). Not downgraded for inconsistency, because the two figures measure different things: a proportion ever dependent among everyone who had ever used, at one interview, against a projected cumulative probability of abuse or dependence by 14 years after first use. Certainty very low. The tobacco proportion is less comparable than the others: it combines tobacco use from a separate 1991 survey with dependence assessed for daily smoking in a subsample, and has no standard error. Status single study: the two surveys measure different quantities (see inconsistency), so they neither replicate nor contradict each other, and each figure rests on one survey; the four- to five-fold gap between them has candidate explanations (abuse counted, undefined class, a denominator that may exclude people with few uses, country and decade) that have not been tested. Imprecision not downgraded: the US proportion has a standard error and the Australian 45.7% an interval; the 50.4% has none, so its precision cannot be judged, which changes nothing at the floor. The US authors conclude from their figures that many, perhaps most, people who use a drug do not become dependent (p. 265); for stimulants, the Australian survival estimate (about half within 14 years, abuse included) shows that this conclusion depends on the measure and on how the outcome is defined.

statement: Among 56 people with methamphetamine dependence who were not seeking treatment and had no other current psychiatric disorder, followed during abstinence on a research ward (analyses used 25–32 of them), the commonest symptoms at entry on a rater-scored checklist (n=32) were preoccupation with methamphetamine (72%), craving (68%), increased appetite (63%) and tiredness (56%). On self-report scales most symptoms, including psychotic-type distress ratings, fell during the first one to two weeks, but on the rater-scored checklist only 8 of 30 items changed significantly, and its craving and depressed-mood items did not; depressive scores stayed above controls' for about three weeks and were still higher, though not significantly (p=0.07), at week 4; craving persisted at a reduced level to week 5. Participants had been admitted for neuroimaging studies lasting two or five weeks, so results after week 2 come only from those in the five-week studies, whose number the paper does not report. All participants had used within the 7 days before admission, so entry could be up to a week after last use; and without an inpatient comparison group the decline cannot be separated from hospitalization, the end of a period of use, or repeated testing.
plain: People dependent on meth who were not seeking treatment, and had no other current mental-health diagnosis, stopped using on a hospital research ward. At the start, the most common symptoms were thinking about meth, craving, hunger and tiredness. On questionnaires they filled in themselves, most symptoms eased within one to two weeks; on the checklist filled in by staff, only a few symptoms changed clearly. Low mood stayed higher than in people who don't use for about three weeks and was still slightly higher at week four. Craving lasted to week five at a lower level. After week two, only the people taking part in the longer, five-week studies were still measured, and the paper does not say how many there were.

statement: In a laboratory study of 13 men who used methamphetamine about 9 days a month (3 met criteria for current dependence) and were not seeking treatment, participants who had sampled an intranasal study dose chose, at each of ten opportunities, between a 10% portion of that dose and a 10% portion of the money sampled, each portion earned by finger presses whose required number rose from 50 to 2,800 over the session. Drug portions (methamphetamine and d-amphetamine pooled) were chosen on 41% of opportunities overall when the alternative was $5 (7 participants; about half at the larger study dose of either drug) and on 17% when it was $20 (6 participants). The two amounts were given to different, very small groups whose assignment is not described as randomized, and they were not compared statistically, so the difference may reflect the people as much as the money. In an earlier 20-day residential study from the same laboratory group, 8 volunteers with stimulant experience (only 3 of whom reported ever having used methamphetamine) chose an oral capsule over a $1 voucher on a mean of 4.3 of 8 occasions when it contained 5 mg of methamphetamine and 4.4 when it contained 10 mg, against 1.4 and 1.3 in the matched placebo conditions (P<0.02 and P<0.01), with no difference between the two doses; that comparison was double-blind and within person, but the two studies share investigators and setting, so they are not independent replications (Hart et al., 2001).
plain: In a lab study, 13 men who used meth but were not seeking treatment could choose between small portions of a stimulant dose, taken through the nose, and small amounts of cash. Seven men chose, ten times in a session, between a tenth of the drug dose they had tried and a tenth of $5; six chose between a tenth of the dose and a tenth of $20. Each portion, drug or cash, had to be earned by pressing a button, from 50 presses at first up to 2,800 by the end of the session. The $5 group chose the drug about 4 times in 10; the $20 group fewer than 2 times in 10. Different men got different amounts and the groups were tiny, so the study cannot show that more money caused the difference. In an earlier study from the same lab, eight volunteers who lived in a laboratory for 20 days chose a capsule over a $1 voucher about four times out of eight when it contained meth, and about once when it was a dummy capsule.
population: Adults with stimulant experience, not seeking treatment, in laboratory choice studies (13 men in the intranasal study; 8 residential volunteers, 1 of them a woman, in the oral study)
exposure: Opportunity to self-administer portions of a methamphetamine or d-amphetamine dose, or an oral methamphetamine capsule (study conditions: 5 and 10 mg)
comparator: An alternative of money: $5 (7 participants) or $20 (6 participants) sampled and chosen in 10% portions in one study; a $1 voucher per choice occasion in the other; placebo capsules in the matched conditions
outcome: Proportion of choices for the drug
magnitude: Drug choices 41% ($5) vs 17% ($20) overall (Abstract); about 47–50% at the 50 mg/70 kg condition with $5 (Discussion). Oral study: mean 4.3 of 8 choices at 5 mg and 4.4 at 10 mg against 1.4 and 1.3 in the matched placebo conditions (P<0.02 and P<0.01), with vouchers chosen on about 80% of occasions under placebo.

statement: In cross-sectional studies, people with methamphetamine dependence or use disorder score lower on average than healthy comparison groups without stimulant dependence on neuropsychological tests: pooled standardized differences mostly between about 0.3 and 0.9 SD across domains. Verbal learning and memory differences are found in every meta-analysis (visual learning did not differ in one meta-analysis); the largest estimates (impulsivity, social cognition, visuospatial, set-shifting and planning measures, up to about 1.1 SD) rest on fewer studies, include questionnaires or vary widely between studies. In a meta-analysis restricted to people abstinent from methamphetamine, 6 of 9 abilities differed, but only learning efficiency (g −0.47) held consistently across studies and in sensitivity analyses; in the largest meta-analysis the prediction interval for the overall difference runs from a large deficit to a small advantage (−1.58 to 0.22). Groups were often unmatched on education (in two meta-analyses the size of the education gap did not significantly predict the size of the difference, a weak, study-level test); one meta-analysis found strong small-study bias in its overall estimate, and two others found small-study effects in some domains, including learning and memory (trim-and-fill gave −0.40 for learning efficiency in one; in the other it imputed no missing studies for the overall estimate, −0.65 vs −0.68).
plain: On average, people dependent on meth score somewhat lower on thinking and memory tests than healthy volunteers who had never been dependent on meth or similar drugs. The gap is usually between a third and almost a whole standard deviation (the typical spread of scores between people), and differences in learning and remembering words were found in every review that combined the studies, though their size varied. Results vary a lot between studies, small studies with large gaps may be over-represented in what was published, the comparison groups often had more schooling (though studies with bigger schooling gaps did not clearly show bigger differences), and none of this shows that meth caused the difference. Group averages still mostly fall in the normal range (see the next claim).

comparator: Healthy comparison participants without a history of stimulant dependence (usually recruited separately, often with more education)
outcome: Neuropsychological test performance
