Publication bias: strong small-study bias for global cognition in one meta-analysis (Egger p=0.00003, no adjusted estimate); Egger signals for learning efficiency (p=.01) and working memory (p=.05) in a second (trim-and-fill −0.40 for learning efficiency); domain signals for verbal learning and memory (p=0.005) and working memory (p<0.001) in a third (overall Egger p=0.32; trim-and-fill imputed no missing studies, −0.65 vs −0.68); visual funnel inspection only in the fourth. Scott et al. (2007), Potvin et al. (2018) and Basterfield et al. (2019) share many primary studies, so their agreement is not independent; Cao et al. (2026) covers only studies published from May 2017, sharing none with Scott et al. or Potvin et al. and at most a few with Basterfield et al., so the direction of the difference has been found in independent bodies of primary studies.

statement: In the studies that compared group means with population norms, average test scores of people with methamphetamine dependence mostly fell in the low-average to average range: between the 16th and 55th percentiles after about 6 days of verified abstinence in one study, whose authors set the impaired range at the 2nd percentile or below. A group mean in the normal range does not show that every individual is, nor does it exclude a decline from a higher starting point. No study tested people before they began to use. One study from the same laboratory as the percentile study (Dean et al., 2018; 37 people with methamphetamine dependence after about a week of abstinence, 41 controls) predicted each person's adult score from school grades before first use, parental income, age and adult smoking status, with a model fitted in the controls that explained about 40% of their variance: the methamphetamine group's grades before first use were already lower (grade point average 2.1 against 2.5), and their adult scores fell below the prediction (overall, a standardized paired difference of 0.61; attention 0.69, memory 0.46; executive function not below). These scores were standardized to the controls, not to population norms, the model's own uncertainty was not carried into the tests, and other substance use disorders were far more common in the methamphetamine group. One review disputes reading normed scores as a categorical line, arguing that mild deficits can still matter, and cites initial evidence of lower scores on performance measures of everyday functioning (Dean et al., 2013). A minority met impairment criteria, more often than controls: about 7 of 27 people who used methamphetamine versus 2 of 18 controls met a 2-SD criterion in at least one domain in one study (as summarized, with ambiguous wording, in a review; for working memory alone, 1 versus 2; the primary paper is still to be read), and 34% of the methamphetamine group versus 16% of controls had a global deficit score above 0.5 in another (a cut-off the authors equate with roughly the 16th percentile and describe as relatively liberal, though validated and widely used), in which only the group that kept using differed significantly (38%; abstainers 24%), more than half of the methamphetamine group but no controls had HIV, and controls were also screened free of hepatitis C, ADHD and antisocial personality disorder.
plain: In the studies that compared them with test norms, groups of people dependent on meth scored on average in the low-average to average range, not in the range the authors called impaired. An average in the normal range does not mean every person is, and it cannot show whether someone's scores dropped from a higher starting point. No one was tested before they started using meth. One study used school grades from before first use to estimate how well people should do as adults: people dependent on meth scored lower than expected, mostly on attention and memory tests, but their school grades had already been lower than the comparison group's, many had also had alcohol or other drug problems, and they were tested only about a week after stopping. One review argues that even a small drop within the normal range can matter, pointing to early evidence of lower scores on tests of everyday tasks. In two studies that counted individuals, about a quarter to a third of people who used meth met a definition of impairment, compared with about one in nine to one in six people who didn't. The two studies drew the line differently: one counted very low scores (about the bottom 2%) in any one area, the other an overall score in roughly the bottom sixth. In one of them, more than half of the people who used meth had HIV and none of the comparison group did, which could explain part of that difference.

Against a prediction from pre-use school grades, parental income, age and adult smoking status (Dean et al., 2018; 37 vs 41): overall d 0.61 (paired t(36) 3.73, p = 0.001), attention 0.69, memory 0.46, executive function not below; pre-use grade point average 2.1 vs 2.5 (p = 0.016).

grade.reasoning: Observational, starts low. Risk of bias: different impairment definitions and norm sets; group means compared with norms without demographic matching; in the impairment-rate study, HIV, hepatitis C, ADHD and antisocial personality disorder present only in people who used methamphetamine. Imprecision: the proportions come from samples of 27 vs 18 and 83 vs 38. Status replicated for group means; the higher impairment rate in people who used methamphetamine rests on two studies, one reported second-hand and one confounded by HIV. Dean et al. (2018; ROBINS-E high, on which both card readers agree), from the same laboratory as Simon et al. (2010) and the review by Dean et al. (2013), though with participants whose cognitive data had not been published before, qualifies the caveat that no starting point was measured: it estimates one from school grades before first use, a proxy rather than a pre-use test, with a prediction model fitted in 41 controls that explains about 40% of the variance and whose uncertainty the paired tests ignore, scores standardized to the controls rather than to norms, testing after about a week of abstinence, and far more other substance use disorders in the methamphetamine group. It bears on whether scores fell from a higher starting point, not on whether group means lie within norms, so it changes neither the rating nor the status.

statement: Whether test performance improves with abstinence beyond practice effects is not established. In the two studies that retested a control group, people who had used methamphetamine did not improve significantly more than controls over about a month (composite change 0.14 vs 0.00 SD, p=0.33; 18 people who had used methamphetamine retested after a mean 25 days, 21 controls after 44 days) or about a year (group-by-time interaction p=0.13; 25 people reporting no use, 58 reporting any use, 38 controls). The first study was too small to exclude a moderate extra improvement (editors' standardized difference in change 0.32, 95% CI −0.31 to 0.96); in the year-long study, the abstainers' global score rose by about 3.0 T-points and the controls' by about 2.7 (editors' calculation from the printed means), and the printed data do not allow an interval for that difference. In the second study the 6 abstainers impaired at baseline gained more than other groups on processing speed (p=0.014, one of 8 domains tested without correction; motor skills p=0.051), while on the global score the 6 controls impaired at baseline also gained, about half as much (3.3 vs 6.7 T-points; three-way interaction p=0.061), and participants impaired at baseline gained more in every group, as regression to the mean predicts. At retest the gaps between the groups moved in both directions. After a month, the methamphetamine group still scored below controls on the four Repeated Memory Test scores (d about 0.7–0.8, against about 0.3–0.8 at the first test in the same people), while its gap on the Selective Reminding total shrank from about 1.0 to 0.2 SD (editors' calculations from Table 3; the authors did not test these differences). After a year, the abstainers' global score was no longer significantly below the controls' by the authors' test (the editors' recalculation from the printed means gives p≈0.025); by domain, the abstainer–control gap narrowed on processing speed (from 2.8 to 0.2 T-points) and motor skills (from 5.5 to 3.5; significant at baseline, not at follow-up), changed little on verbal fluency (from 1.8 to 1.5), and widened on executive functions (from 2.5 to 3.4) and working memory (from 3.3 to 5.0), which had not differed significantly at baseline and did at follow-up (editors' calculations from Tables 3–4; learning and memory are not compared because the paper prints identical follow-up values for the abstainers in the two domains). Two of three cross-sectional comparisons among people who had used methamphetamine found better executive performance in people abstinent longer (as summarized by Dean et al., 2013), which practice cannot explain but selection can. Across meta-analyses, length of abstinence did not moderate the size of group differences in most domains, and few studies tested people abstinent for more than a year.
plain: Does thinking get better after stopping meth? This is not known. Two studies retested both people who had stopped and people who don't use. In both, the people who had stopped did not improve clearly more than the people who don't use, who also improved from taking the tests a second time. The first study, over a month, was small, so a moderate extra improvement cannot be ruled out; in the second, over a year, both groups gained about the same. Over time some gaps between the groups narrowed and others widened. In the second study, the six people who had stopped and scored lowest at the start improved more than others on speed tests, but people who score low on a first test tend to score higher the next time anyway, and that group had only six people. Two of three studies comparing people who had stopped for shorter and longer times found better scores on some tests after longer abstinence, which may reflect who manages to stay stopped. Across many studies, groups tested after longer abstinence did not score closer to people who don't use, and very few studies have looked beyond a year.

Iudicello et al. (2010): all groups improved (time F(1,118)=55.12); group × time p=0.126; abstainer–control gap 3.0 T at baseline and 2.7 T at follow-up (editors' calculation from Tables 3–4). statement: In a Utah health-records cohort, a Parkinson's disease code on or after the date of the first stimulant code was recorded for about 0.30% of people with a methamphetamine- or amphetamine-related diagnosis and no code for other drugs, alcohol or HIV (15 of 4,935; about 7 in 10 people identified with such a diagnosis were excluded for other drug or alcohol codes) and 0.11% of people of the same sex and birth year without drug, alcohol or HIV codes (27 of 24,675) over a mean of about 7 years (editors' calculation; HR 2.8, 95% CI 1.6–4.8; HR 2.2, 1.2–4.0, after excluding diagnoses coded on the same date as the first stimulant code). A California hospital cohort of people aged 30 or over, likewise restricted to people with no alcohol, other drug or HIV code (the numbers excluded are not reported), found 51 against 29 Parkinson's disease diagnoses among 40,358 people hospitalized with a methamphetamine- or amphetamine-related diagnosis and 40,358 hospitalized for appendicitis, matched on age, race, sex, index date and number of later admissions, over a mean of about 6 years from the index admission to the end of the study (about 0.13% vs 0.07%, editors' calculation; HR 1.76, 95% CI 1.12–2.76; the abstract prints 1.12–2.75); the diagnoses came at a younger median age in the exposed cohort (57.2 vs 63.8 years). Against people with cocaine-related diagnoses the California HR was 2.41 (1.32–4.41), and people with cocaine-related diagnoses showed no increase against appendicitis patients (HR 1.04, 0.56–1.93). In Utah, people with cocaine-related diagnoses showed no clear increase (4 vs 22 events in the broader movement-disorder outcome, crude rates about 2.7 per 10,000 person-years in both, editors' calculation; the hazard ratio is shown only in a figure), but the numbers were too small to rule one out; compared directly, the methamphetamine cohort had more broader-outcome diagnoses than the cocaine cohort (HR 3.9, 95% CI 1.4–10.8), an outcome that includes tremor, and the tobacco-adjusted version of this comparison is misprinted. In both Utah groups, diagnoses in the broader outcome came young (median age 49 in the exposed cohort, 44 in controls), 2–3 years after the index date, and few had a levodopa order (3 of 30 exposed cases; 5 control cases), so the codes capture more than Parkinson's disease in both groups. Misclassification that differs between groups could still produce an excess: antipsychotic-induced parkinsonism was addressed in neither cohort, the broader outcome includes tremor, and tobacco codes went with more diagnoses, which suggests differences in medical contact; neither cohort validated its diagnosis codes against medical records. Misclassification and ascertainment therefore remain plausible explanations.
plain: In Utah health records, people with a meth- or amphetamine-related diagnosis, and no diagnosis for other drugs or alcohol, were given a Parkinson's disease diagnosis, on the same day or later, about three times as often as people of the same sex and age without drug or alcohol diagnoses: about 3 in 1,000 versus 1 in 1,000 over about 7 years. Most people with a meth-related diagnosis also had other drug or alcohol diagnoses and were left out of the study. A California hospital study found a smaller increase, about 13 versus 7 in 10,000 over about 6 years, and no increase in people with cocaine diagnoses. People with cocaine diagnoses showed no clear increase, but there were too few cases to rule one out; compared directly, people with meth diagnoses had more movement-disorder diagnoses of any kind than people with cocaine diagnoses. In both groups the wider set of movement-disorder diagnoses came at unusually young ages and few people got the usual Parkinson's medicine, so the records probably include other conditions; side effects of other medicines and how often people saw doctors were not accounted for.
population: People with methamphetamine- or amphetamine-related diagnoses in health records: in Utah, only those with no code for other drugs, alcohol or HIV (about 7 in 10 people identified with such a diagnosis were excluded for other drug or alcohol codes); in California, people aged 30 or over hospitalized with such a diagnosis and, likewise, no alcohol, other drug or HIV code at any time (the numbers excluded are not reported)

Cocaine cohort: 4 vs 22 broader-outcome events (1,867 vs 9,335 people), crude rates about 2.7 per 10,000 person-years in both (editors' calculation); hazard ratio shown only in a figure; methamphetamine vs cocaine cohort, broader outcome: HR 3.9 (1.4–10.8). grade.reasoning: Observational record-linkage, starts low. Risk of bias: outcome codes of low validity in both groups (young age at diagnosis, little levodopa treatment, tremor in the broader outcome), which alone would bias toward no difference, together with misclassification that could differ between groups (antipsychotic-induced parkinsonism not addressed; more medical contact, suggested by tobacco codes going with more diagnoses), which could create an excess. Unadjusted smoking would, if anything, bias toward no difference, because smoking is associated with lower Parkinson's risk. Imprecision: 15 exposed events in Utah and 51 in California (95% CI 1.12–2.76). Not upgraded for size because the biases do not all run toward the null. Indirectness not downgraded because the claim is worded for methamphetamine- or amphetamine-related codes, which do not identify methamphetamine itself. Status replicated: the California (Callaghan et al., 2012) and Utah cohorts, from different teams and record systems, agree in direction; both rest on diagnosis codes without validation or exposure measurement, and in California antipsychotic treatment and smoking were not recorded either, with matching on later admissions addressing medical contact only in part. An earlier California report by the same team (2010, not read) uses the same records system and does not count separately.

statement: In one UK study of 50 pairs of full siblings, in each of which one sibling met DSM-IV-TR criteria for stimulant dependence and the other had no personal history of substance dependence other than nicotine (the supplement's enrolment criterion; the main report says no history of chronic drug or alcohol abuse), both siblings had lower white-matter fractional anisotropy than 50 unrelated controls without a personal or family history of dependence, similar in age and verbal IQ, and shared three grey-matter clusters of difference from them: a larger left amygdala, a larger left putamen, and smaller volume across the left postcentral gyrus, superior temporal gyrus and posterior insula. The white-matter, putamen and posterior insula measures were more alike within sibling pairs than in random pairings (one-tailed permutation tests, not corrected for multiple testing); the amygdala measure was not. The imaging analyses included 146 people for grey matter and 145 for white matter; the grey-matter maps were thresholded to allow about one false-positive cluster per map, and the shared clusters are the overlap of two comparisons with the same control group. More of the non-dependent siblings than of the controls smoked (55% against 12%), and the share of men differed (51% of non-dependent siblings, 64% of controls, 92% of dependent siblings); a re-analysis of non-smokers kept the grey-matter differences, but no smoking check is reported for white matter, and neither this nor the single-sex re-analysis gives statistics. Differences shared by the two siblings suggest a familial vulnerability, genetic or from the shared family environment, that may predate drug use; the study cannot show that it does, because nobody was assessed before use began. Neither the main report nor its supplement names an orbitofrontal or anterior insular difference or compares the two siblings directly; a review describes a larger hippocampus in both siblings and smaller orbitofrontal and anterior insular volumes in the dependent siblings only: the hippocampal statement may come from the supplement, which labels the shared medial temporal cluster amygdala/hippocampus in places, while the orbitofrontal and anterior insular statement matches no difference that either document names. The supplement maps regions where lower fractional anisotropy and grey matter went with more years of stimulant use in the dependent siblings, without statistics or region names and with no adjustment described for age, which rises with years of use, or for their other dependence (55% on opiates, 26% on alcohol), so they do not separate an effect of stimulant use from these. The dependent siblings were still using stimulants when tested (urine positive in all but three); 94% were dependent on cocaine and 6% on amphetamines, and methamphetamine is not mentioned.
plain: Brothers and sisters of people dependent on stimulants, who had never been dependent on drugs or alcohol themselves (apart from nicotine), shared some of the same brain differences from unrelated volunteers. That suggests some differences run in families and may come before drug use, although nobody was scanned before they started using. More of the brothers and sisters than of the volunteers smoked, and the check that smoking did not explain the differences covered only part of the scans. The study shows pictures of brain areas that measured lower the longer people had used, but gives no numbers and does not say that it separated years of use from age or from other drugs. A review reports other differences found only in the dependent person, but neither the study's report nor its supplement names them. Almost all the dependent people (94 in 100) were dependent on cocaine; the rest were dependent on amphetamines, and the study does not mention meth.
population: Sibling pairs discordant for stimulant dependence (94% cocaine and 6% amphetamine dependence; UK)
exposure: Stimulant dependence
comparator: Biological full siblings with no personal history of substance dependence other than nicotine (the supplement's enrolment criterion; the main report says no history of chronic drug or alcohol abuse); unrelated controls without a personal or family history of drug or alcohol dependence, similar in age and verbal IQ
outcome: Brain structure (regional grey-matter volume; white-matter fractional anisotropy)
magnitude: No cluster statistics in the main report. Supplement, Table S2 (means over voxels selected because they differed between groups, so the differences are inflated): fractional anisotropy 0.55 in controls, 0.53 in non-dependent siblings and 0.52 in dependent siblings (SD 0.02); grey matter in the shared clusters, controls against non-dependent and dependent siblings: left amygdala 0.76 against 0.81 and 0.83, left putamen 0.34 against 0.38 and 0.38, left postcentral gyrus 0.89 against 0.75 and 0.74 (editors' calculation: standardized differences of about 0.7 to 1.3). Fractional anisotropy group difference F(2,141) = 26.3, P < 0.001 (main report; 145 participants with white-matter data, so the degrees of freedom fit one covariate, although the supplement names sex as a covariate only for the behavioural analyses; editors' calculation: η² about 0.27, inflated by the voxel selection). Within-family similarity (one-tailed permutation tests, uncorrected for multiple testing): white matter P = 0.004, putamen P = 0.013, posterior insula P = 0.012, amygdala P = 0.144 (not familial).

evidence.locator: Report text (no section headings; paragraphs counted from the first after the abstract): 3rd paragraph (design), 5th paragraph (FA) and 7th paragraph (grey matter; p. 602, right column, continuing on p. 603); Fig. 1B legend (p. 602); Fig. 2C and legend (p. 603)
evidence.extracted: 50 sibling pairs, one sibling with DSM-IV stimulant dependence and the other with no history of chronic drug or alcohol abuse, against 50 unrelated volunteers matched for age and IQ. Both siblings had lower white-matter fractional anisotropy than the volunteers (tract skeleton, F(2,141) = 26.3, P < 0.001), and it was more alike within true sibling pairs than within random pairs (permutation P = 0.004). Three grey-matter clusters were shared by both sibling groups: a larger left amygdala and left putamen, and a smaller left postcentral gyrus, superior temporal gyrus and posterior insula; the putamen (P = 0.013) and posterior insula (P = 0.012) differences were familial by the permutation test, the amygdala difference was not (P = 0.144). The main report names no hippocampal, orbitofrontal or anterior insular difference, reports no direct comparison of the two siblings and does not say which stimulants were used.

evidence.extracted: Recruited through advertisements and treatment services in East Anglia, UK; all assessed with the Structured Clinical Interview for DSM-IV. Sibling pairs had the same biological parents; one met DSM-IV-TR criteria for cocaine or amphetamine dependence and the other had no personal history of substance dependence except nicotine; controls had no personal or family history of drug or alcohol dependence; all were aged 18–55. Of 154 enrolled, 150 completed (three groups of 50); MRI scans were unavailable for three dependent participants and one sibling, leaving 47, 49 and 50. All dependent participants met DSM-IV-TR criteria for stimulant dependence, 94% for cocaine and 6% for amphetamines (which amphetamines is not stated; methamphetamine is not mentioned); they had used stimulants for a mean of 16.3 years (SD 7.6) from a mean age of 16.5 (SD 2.8); urine was positive for stimulants in all but three; most also met criteria for dependence on another substance (opiates 55%, alcohol 26%, cannabis 9%). Siblings and controls had very low drug and alcohol screening scores and drug-negative urine.

evidence.extracted: Grey matter was analysed in 50 controls, 47 dependent participants and 49 siblings, and FA in 50, 46 and 49 (one dependent participant could not tolerate the full session). Grey-matter maps were compared with the controls by permutation tests at a cluster-level threshold of one expected false-positive cluster per map (cluster-wise P = 9 × 10⁻⁴ for siblings and 8 × 10⁻⁴ for dependent participants), giving four clusters for the siblings and eight for the dependent participants; the voxels in both lay in three regions, and analyses restricted to men or to women did not change the results. FA: voxel-wise permutation tests with threshold-free cluster enhancement and 5000 permutations, corrected at P < 0.05; mean FA in the significant skeleton was then compared in SPSS. Table S2 (means, SD): FA across the 24,934 skeleton voxels that differed between groups 0.55 (0.02) in controls, 0.53 (0.02) in siblings and 0.52 (0.02) in dependent participants; grey matter in the left amygdala cluster (984 mm³) 0.76, 0.81 and 0.83 (0.07), left putamen (560 mm³) 0.34, 0.38 and 0.38 (0.05–0.06), left postcentral gyrus (1,152 mm³) 0.89, 0.75 and 0.74 (0.11–0.12). Editors' calculation: standardized differences from controls about 0.7, 0.7 and 1.2 SD (siblings) and 1.0, 0.8 and 1.3 SD (dependent participants) for the three grey-matter clusters; all inflated, because the values are means over voxels selected for differing.

risk_of_bias.note: ROBINS-E overall high on the study card, no longer provisional now that the supplement has been read: smoking was far more common in the non-dependent siblings than in the controls (55% against 12%) and was checked only for grey matter, by a re-analysis of non-smokers without statistics; the sexes were unbalanced (51% and 64% men; 92% among the dependent siblings), handled by a covariate in the behavioural analyses and by single-sex grey-matter analyses without statistics; and only the clusters shared by both sibling groups are described, with imaging values from voxels selected because they differed.

indirectness.note: 94% of the dependent siblings were dependent on cocaine and 6% (about 3 of 50, editors' calculation) on amphetamines, not further named; no participant is said to have used methamphetamine.

imprecision.note: 50 people per group (146 in the grey-matter and 145 in the white-matter analyses); a grey-matter threshold allowing about one false-positive cluster per map; one-tailed familiality tests without correction for multiple testing.

grade.reasoning: One cross-sectional study of 50 sibling pairs, read in full with its supplement. Starts low (observational). Risk of bias, one level: ROBINS-E overall high on the study card: smoking was far more common in the non-dependent siblings than in the controls (55% against 12%) and was checked only for grey matter, by a re-analysis of non-smokers without statistics; the sexes were unbalanced, handled by a covariate in the behavioural analyses and by single-sex grey-matter analyses without statistics; and only the clusters shared by both sibling groups are described, with imaging values from voxels selected because they differed. Indirectness, one level: 94% of the dependent siblings were dependent on cocaine and 6% on amphetamines, and methamphetamine is not mentioned. Imprecision, one level: 50 people per group (146 and 145 in the imaging analyses); grey-matter maps thresholded to allow about one false-positive cluster per map, the shared clusters coming from two comparisons with the same control group; familiality tests one-tailed and not corrected for multiple testing (three of the six would not pass a Bonferroni threshold, editors' calculation). Certainty very low. The familiality tests show that the measures are more alike within sibling pairs, as brain structure largely is; that the differences from the controls are shared rests on the two group comparisons with the same control group. The claim is rated as an association; whether the shared differences predate use cannot be settled by this design, and the correlations with years of use are shown only as maps, without statistics and with no adjustment described for age.

statement: In observational studies, mostly cross-sectional and mostly in treatment, psychiatric, emergency or criminal-justice samples in which the comparison group often also used other drugs, people with an amphetamine use disorder (amphetamine or methamphetamine) had higher odds of psychosis than people without one: odds ratio 2.4 (95% CI 1.6–3.5; 4 studies, I² 35%) in studies that adjusted for some combination of demographics, other substance use and premorbid risk. The review grades this estimate at its lowest level of evidence (cross-sectional associations within samples of people who use drugs); its four studies were of young offenders, people in methamphetamine rehabilitation, people using methamphetamine at least monthly, and people released from prison (a cohort): in two of them everyone used methamphetamine, so the comparison was with methamphetamine use without a use disorder, and for the prison cohort the review reports no significant relation with later primary psychosis (later substance-induced psychosis was raised). Unadjusted estimates were 3.0 (1.9–4.8; 13 studies, I² 90%) for use disorder and 2.0 (1.3–3.3; 7 studies, I² 80%) for any use; the review's authors consider unadjusted estimates likely inflated by co-occurring risk factors, and comparisons made within samples of people who use other drugs likely to understate the difference from the general population. In post hoc subgroups the association was stronger for psychotic symptoms than for diagnosed psychotic disorders; for any use, the association with a diagnosed disorder was not statistically clear (1.3, 1.0–1.9). Most studies cannot show whether use preceded psychosis. In a general-population birth cohort in Christchurch, New Zealand (962 to 1,025 people at each of five interviews from age 18 to 35), use of methamphetamine or other amphetamine-type stimulants since the previous interview went with reporting at least one psychotic symptom at the same interview (symptoms over the past month at ages 18, 21 and 25, since the previous interview at 30 and 35): odds ratio 1.88 (95% CI 1.55–2.30) unadjusted and 1.33 (1.03–1.72) after adjustment for childhood, family and adolescent factors and for concurrent cannabis use, alcohol use disorder, depression, anxiety and life stress; the outcome was self-reported psychotic experiences on checklist and interview items (35–42% of the cohort reported at least one in each period to age 25), not diagnosed psychosis, and use and symptoms were reported at the same interviews, so this cohort cannot show which came first either. The higher odds were concentrated in the 5% who had ever used at least weekly (2.85, 1.21–6.69, adjusted for childhood, family and adolescent factors only, not for concurrent cannabis use; about 1.3 and not statistically significant for less frequent use). No threshold level of use could be estimated; more frequent use went with more psychotic symptoms in 4 of the 8 study populations that examined it; the systematic review that counted them judged the studies finding this to be of higher quality and rated the evidence on frequency moderate, the only risk factor it rated above low. A registry cohort in Taiwan (2007–2016) followed 74,601 adults from their first arrest for using an amphetamine-type substance (urine-confirmed; the 23 substances counted include MDMA and others besides methamphetamine, with no breakdown by substance) and 298,404 insured adults of the same age, sex and index year with no record of illicit drug use, after excluding people with a psychosis diagnosis recorded before the index date: a first psychosis diagnosis was recorded at 4.68 against 0.77 per 1,000 person-years (Kaplan–Meier cumulative incidence at 10 years 3.75% against 0.63%; hazard ratio 5.28, 95% CI 4.90–5.70). This orders the first arrest before the first recorded diagnosis, not the start of use before the onset of symptoms. The hazard ratio is adjusted only for age, sex and five diagnoses (depression, anxiety and three cardiovascular conditions) recorded at any time during the study, including after the arrest; other drug and alcohol use, socio-economic position and family history were not adjusted for; the listed outcome codes omit the drug-induced psychosis codes that the text says were included; and the authors describe the analysis as exploratory and not preregistered. The hazard ratios rose with the number of arrests (4.49 for one, 6.25 for five or more), but arrests were counted over the whole follow-up, reflect police contact and are not a validated measure of the amount used.
plain: In studies mostly in treatment, hospitals or prisons, a meth or amphetamine use disorder went with about two and a half times the odds of psychosis, allowing for some other differences. A study following about 1,000 New Zealanders from birth found any use went with slightly more self-reported psychotic experiences, mostly in people who had ever used at least weekly. In Taiwan, an estimated 4 in 100 adults arrested for using amphetamine-type drugs were diagnosed with psychosis within 10 years, against under 1 in 100 people with no drug record; few other differences were allowed for. None of these studies settles which came first.
population: Mostly treatment, psychiatric, emergency and criminal-justice samples and samples of people who use drugs; the unadjusted estimates also include a population-wide hospital-admissions cohort and a sample of dance-venue patrons; one general-population birth cohort (New Zealand) gives within-cohort estimates; one national registry cohort (Taiwan) compares adults arrested for amphetamine-type substance use with insured adults without a drug record
exposure: Any amphetamine use; amphetamine use disorder; first arrest for use of an amphetamine-type substance (registry cohort)

grade.reasoning: Observational, mostly cross-sectional; starts low. The claim is an association and rests on the adjusted use-disorder estimate (2.4, 1.6–3.5; 4 studies, I² 35%); the unadjusted estimates are context, labelled as likely inflated. Risk of bias not downgraded: the adjusted studies accounted for some combination of demographics, other substance use and premorbid risk, the adjusted pool's weighted quality score is 88% in the review, and comparison groups mostly also used other drugs (in two of the four adjusted studies, methamphetamine without a use disorder), which the authors argue makes estimates understate the difference from the general population; residual confounding by unmeasured premorbid factors (family history of psychosis, childhood trauma) remains and is why the claim is worded as an association. Inconsistency not downgraded for the adjusted estimate; the unadjusted estimates are heterogeneous (I² 80–90%). Publication bias could not be assessed (too few studies; AMSTAR 2 critically low); not downgraded, noted. Not upgraded for dose–response: frequency was associated in 4 of 8 populations (evidence the risk-factor review rates moderate), but across different studies and measures rather than as a gradient within one body of evidence; the within-person gradient is rated in the claim on frequency of use within the same people (section 9). McKetin et al. (2013), rated separately in that claim, is inside the unadjusted any-use estimate and is the review's only adjusted any-use estimate (5.3); it is not in the adjusted use-disorder estimate on which this claim rests. Boden et al. (2023), a general-population birth cohort read in full (ROBINS-E high on the first reading, from concerns in several domains), agrees in direction and is smaller after fuller adjustment (any use, OR 1.33, 1.03–1.72, after adjusting for concurrent cannabis use and other time-varying factors; 1.88 unadjusted), which fits the meta-analysis authors' view that unadjusted estimates are inflated; it is not counted as inconsistency, because exposure (any use rather than use disorder), population and outcome (self-reported psychotic experiences) differ. Not upgraded for dose–response: its gradient (2.85 for ever at least weekly use against about 1.3, not significant, for less frequent use) is adjusted only for fixed confounders, is not monotonic (1.37, 1.32, 2.85) and rests on 51 people in the top category. It is an independent sample, though it shares an author with McKetin et al. (2013) and the meta-analysis. Huang et al. (2022), a Taiwanese registry cohort read in full (ROBINS-E very high, from confounding, on which both card readers agree), agrees in direction with a much larger estimate (HR 5.28, 4.90–5.70) for a first recorded psychosis diagnosis after a first arrest for an amphetamine-type substance, against insured people with no drug record. It is not counted as inconsistency, because exposure (arrest, with MDMA and other substances pooled with methamphetamine), comparator (no record of any illicit drug use) and outcome (claims diagnoses) differ and the adjustment is minimal: age, sex and five comorbidity codes partly recorded after the arrest, nothing for other drug or alcohol use, socio-economic position or family history. It does not earn an upgrade for large effect, because these remaining biases, and more contact with services after arrest, all run away from the null; nor for dose–response, because its gradient by number of arrests uses arrests counted over the whole follow-up (more arrests go with longer observation) and its printed trend test is reproduced by a regression on five category rates. Its rehabilitation comparison (HR 0.74 for the roughly 10% offered treatment under deferred prosecution, chosen by prosecutors for promising outcomes) is not used. It is an independent sample from a different country and design, so it adds to the replication of the direction, not to the precision of any one estimate.

statement: In 278 people with methamphetamine dependence, assessed in up to four one-month windows over 3 years (230 of them at the last; injecting was the main route in 79% of months of use), psychotic symptoms were more likely in months of methamphetamine use than in months without use in the same individuals: odds ratio 5.3 (95% CI 3.4–8.3) for any use, 4.0 (2.5–6.5) for 1–15 days and 11.2 (5.9–21.1) for 16 or more days of use in the month, after adjustment for heavy cannabis and alcohol use; in months without heavy cannabis or alcohol use, predicted risk rose from about 7% of months without methamphetamine to about 48% of months with 16 or more days of use. Adding concurrent unemployment, unstable housing, low income, distress and disability to the model reduced the odds ratios to 2.25 and 3.90; those factors may be consequences of use or of psychosis as well as confounders. Use and symptoms were measured over the same month, so the study cannot show which came first; the authors limit the findings to people with methamphetamine dependence.
plain: In about 280 people dependent on meth in Australia, most of whom injected it, each person was compared with themselves at up to four points over three years. The study's model predicted psychotic symptoms such as paranoia or hallucinations in about 7% of months without meth and in about half of months with meth on 16 or more days (in both cases for months without heavy cannabis or alcohol use). The link was smaller, but still there, after also accounting for unemployment, housing, income, distress and disability at the time, which may themselves be results of use. Because use and symptoms were measured over the same month, the study cannot show which came first.
population: Adults with DSM-IV methamphetamine dependence and no lifetime schizophrenia or mania (Australian treatment and community cohort)
exposure: Days of methamphetamine use in a month (1–15; 16 or more)
comparator: Months without methamphetamine use in the same individuals
outcome: Psychotic symptoms in the month (BPRS score of 4 or more on suspiciousness, unusual thought content or hallucinations)
magnitude: Any use OR 5.3 (3.4–8.3); 1–15 days 4.0 (2.5–6.5); 16+ days 11.2 (5.9–21.1); predicted risk about 7% vs 48% of months; with additional adjustment for concurrent social and health factors 2.25 (1.29–3.90) and 3.90 (1.80–8.45).

grade.reasoning: Prospective within-person cohort; starts low. Comparing each person with themselves removes stable confounders, the main weakness of the cross-sectional literature. Risk of bias −1 (ROBINS-E overall high): selection (278 of 501 in the parent cohort analysed; 138 excluded for missing follow-up interviews; the number contributing to the fixed-effects estimates is not reported), self-reported use, and symptom ratings for which the paper does not say whether the interviewers knew that month's use. Dose–response +1: within the same people the odds rose from 4.0 (1–15 days) to 11.2 (16 or more days), and the point estimates kept the same order under the most adjusted model (2.25, 1.29–3.90; 3.90, 1.80–8.45), although those intervals overlap widely and no test for trend is reported. The upgrade is kept because the within-person design addresses the main reason observational evidence starts low; upgrading evidence already rated down for risk of bias is a judgment call, and without it certainty would be very low. Not upgraded for large effect (§6.3): under the most adjusted model the estimates are 2.25 (1.29–3.90) and 3.90 (1.80–8.45); symptoms were present in 25% of person-months, so odds ratios overstate risk ratios; ratings by interviewers who knew that month's use, if they did, could bias away from the null; and this is one cohort.

statement: In a systematic review of studies of methamphetamine-associated psychosis to March 2018, mostly of hospital patients and without appraisal of study quality, 27 studies reported the share of participants still psychotic more than a month after stopping use: the median study reported 25%, ranging from none in six laboratory studies in which volunteers were given the drug (symptoms resolved within 12 hours to 7 days) to 96%, with a median of 40% in longitudinal studies; Japanese studies reported more persistence (median 44%) than studies elsewhere (12%), which the review's authors attribute to the ICD rule allowing psychosis to last up to 6 months before a primary psychotic disorder is diagnosed, although only about a third of the Japanese studies (35%, against 6% elsewhere) used ICD-10. Second-hand reports of hospital series add 27% and 17% still psychotic beyond one and three months despite abstinence and antipsychotic treatment in 104 Japanese inpatients (cited by the systematic review); 16% and 17% after 1 and 3 months of abstinence in two reports from one Taiwanese research group, probably on one sample (a systematic review combines them as one study population of 445), with the denominator not explained and conflicting statements on family history in the narrative review that quotes them; and 10–28% beyond 6 months (narrative reviews). A 2020 meta-analysis of cohorts of substance-induced psychosis (searches 1980 to 2018, English only) pooled five estimates for amphetamine-type psychoses, 2,284 people, into an average of 22% (95% CI 14% to 34%) later diagnosed with schizophrenia, with extreme heterogeneity between studies (I² 96%) and no prediction interval; the five studies are not named in the article, and its methods group cocaine with methamphetamine and amphetamine as stimulants. Across all substance-induced psychoses the pooled figure was 25% (18% to 35%; 25 studies, I² 99%), highest after cannabis (34%) and lowest after alcohol (9%), and no categorical study feature met the review's significance threshold, nor were length or completeness of follow-up associated with it; older cohorts had somewhat lower rates (P = .03), which the review suggests may be an ecological association. Single-study figures range from 5% (China, second-hand) to about 39% in a Thai cohort of 1,116 people with methamphetamine psychosis after a first hospitalization, which four reviews report four ways: 38.8% at 5 years, nearly 40% within 6 years, 33–38% after 6–7 years together with a small cohort of 28 people, and, in the meta-analysis, 39% after 5 years with only 40% of the cohort followed up. The 2019 systematic review gives 16% within 16 years for a Finnish register study of 825 people, a narrative review gives 19–30% for register studies of amphetamine-induced psychosis, and in a 24-month randomized treatment trial in Hong Kong 7 of 137 people (5.1%) with stimulant-induced psychosis and no earlier diagnosis were newly diagnosed with schizophrenia. These figures cannot show whether methamphetamine caused a lasting illness or revealed an existing vulnerability, whether some first episodes were primary psychoses attributed to drug use, or whether some later diagnoses relabel a persistent methamphetamine psychosis, since one review notes that diagnostic rules call for a primary psychotic diagnosis once psychosis persists. Recurrence with renewed use is common in clinical series, and in one follow-up positive symptoms rose in former patients who resumed use; Japanese researchers, as one review reports, describe spontaneous relapses after remission, which stressful situations seem to trigger in susceptible people. None of the single-study figures has been checked in the primary studies.
plain: Across 27 studies of meth-related psychosis, mostly in hospital patients, the typical study found 1 in 4 people still had symptoms over a month after stopping; studies ranged from none to almost all. Later diagnoses of schizophrenia varied from about 1 in 20 to about 2 in 5 between studies; a 2020 review that averaged five widely differing studies of amphetamine-type psychosis found about 1 in 5. This does not show meth caused it. Psychosis often returns with renewed use.
population: People with methamphetamine-associated psychosis, mostly hospitalized (for later schizophrenia, also pooled cohorts of amphetamine-type substance-induced psychosis)

magnitude: Systematic review, 27 studies with duration data: median 25% still psychotic beyond one month (laboratory studies 0%; longitudinal studies median 40%, range 14–96%; Japanese studies median 44%, range 18–96%, against 12%, range 0–39%, elsewhere; t = 4.79, p = .0001); case reports 2 of 24. Later schizophrenia diagnosis, meta-analysis (searches to 2018): amphetamines 22% (95% CI 14–34%), 5 estimates, 2284 people, I² 96%; all substance-induced psychoses 25% (18–35%), 25 studies, 34,224 people, I² 99%; cannabis 34% (25–46%); alcohol 9% (6–15%); no categorical moderator significant; lower in older cohorts (meta-regression P = .03, possibly ecological). Systematic review: 33–38% after 6–7 years (two studies, 1116 and 28 people; the meta-analysis lists the Thai cohort as 39% after 5 years with 40% followed up); 16% within 16 years (825 people). Randomized treatment trial, Hong Kong: 7 of 137 (5.1%) within 24 months. Second-hand in narrative reviews: 16% and 17% still psychotic after 1 and 3 months (one research group, probably one sample); beyond 6 months 10–28%; later schizophrenia 5.0% (China) to 38.8% at 5 years (Thailand; nearly 40% within 6 years in another review); 19.1–30% in register studies of amphetamine-induced psychosis. Japanese inpatient series cited by the systematic review: 27% beyond one month, 17% beyond three months (n=104). No pooled estimate or interval for persistence.

risk_of_bias.note: Mostly hospital samples with unverified abstinence and untreated confounding by medication and other drugs; transition from register or routine diagnoses with follow-up as low as 40%.

inconsistency.note: Persistence 0% to 96% across studies, only partly explained; transition I² 96% for amphetamines in the meta-analysis, single studies 5% to about 39%.

indirectness.note: Not downgraded; the pooled transition figure covers amphetamine-type psychoses and may include some cocaine psychoses.

grade.reasoning: Descriptive claim (base rates of persistence and of later diagnosis); observational, starts low. The claim rests on a systematic review read in full (Voce et al., 2019; AMSTAR 2 critically low), which reports persistence and transition figures second-hand from primary studies it did not appraise, as unweighted medians without intervals, and now also on a meta-analysis of transition read in full (Murrie et al., 2020; AMSTAR 2 critically low confidence, provisional, after adjudication of its card), which pools five estimates for amphetamine-type psychoses (22%, 14% to 34%) but does not name the studies and groups cocaine with methamphetamine and amphetamine as stimulants. Risk of bias −1: mostly hospital samples, abstinence not verified, antipsychotic treatment and polydrug use not accounted for, a persistence median that includes six laboratory studies of volunteers given the drug, which observed no persistence (symptoms resolved within 12 hours to 7 days), and transition figures from register or routine diagnoses with follow-up as incomplete as 40% (the Thai cohort). Inconsistency −1: persistence ranges from 0% to 96% across studies, which the review's authors attribute to diagnostic rules (median 44% in Japanese studies against 12% elsewhere), although only 35% of the Japanese studies used ICD-10 (25% DSM-IV; elsewhere 6% and 42%), so the explanation covers about a third of them at most and is untested; the pooled transition estimate for amphetamines carries an I² of 96%, unexplained by the moderators the meta-analysis tested (only the cohorts' average age was associated, which the review suggests may be ecological), single studies range from 5% to about 39%, and the Thai cohort is reported four ways by four reviews. Indirectness not downgraded: the persistence figures concern methamphetamine; the pooled transition figure covers amphetamine-type psychoses and may include some cocaine psychoses, which the statement says. Imprecision not downgraded: the pooled interval (14% to 34%) is wide, but the claim describes a range. Very low. Status mixed: persistence beyond a month ranges from 0% to 96%, and the review's partial explanations (laboratory against clinical designs; Japanese against other studies) leave a wide unexplained spread within groups (18–96% in Japan, 0–39% elsewhere); later schizophrenia diagnoses run from 5% to about 39% in single studies, with a pooled 22% and I² 96%. The inconsistency is in size, not in whether persistence or later diagnosis occurs in clinical samples. The meta-analysis and the systematic review share at least three studies (the Thai cohort, a small prospective amphetamine cohort and the Finnish register study), so they are not independent. The 5.1% within 24 months comes from a treated trial sample that included cocaine-induced psychosis and excluded, after the fact, 28 people with an earlier diagnosis. Not yet read: the register cohorts the currency check of 2026-10-16 lists.

statement: In a meta-analysis of 12 observational studies to December 2022 (624 people with methamphetamine-induced psychosis and 527 with schizophrenia or a related disorder, mostly treated outpatients described as stable; antipsychotic doses reported in six studies), negative symptoms were less severe in methamphetamine psychosis (standardized mean difference −0.35, 95% CI −0.54 to −0.16; I² 54%; −0.44, −0.82 to −0.07, in studies rated at lower risk of bias), a small-to-moderate difference, consistent in direction (10 of the 12 study estimates lie on that side and none is significant the other way) and significant in 5 of the 12 studies, from four research groups; pooled from three studies, neither diminished expression nor amotivation differed significantly. Positive symptoms did not differ significantly as reported (−0.01, −0.13 to 0.11, with no heterogeneity), but none of the 12 study values behind that result can be reproduced from the review's own table of study means; recalculated from that table, the comparison is imprecise and very heterogeneous, with study values significant in both directions (editors' recalculation −0.29, −0.67 to 0.10, I² 89%, reading the dispersions printed for two studies as standard errors, as the review's negative-symptom values require; −0.35, −0.90 to 0.20, I² 94%, taking them as printed), so the evidence shows no significant difference rather than similarity. The pooled groups mix acute and persistent psychosis and current and past methamphetamine use; at least one comparison group with a primary psychotic disorder also used methamphetamine, two of the studies, from one research group, probably share participants, and the designs are cross-sectional. As reported in one narrative review of 12 direct comparisons (figures second-hand; at least three of its studies are also in the meta-analysis), more visual and tactile hallucinations in methamphetamine psychosis were found in one comparison of persistent psychosis (about 53 people per group), and a second comparison, of lifetime symptoms in 284 people who all had methamphetamine dependence, is reported in opposite directions in the review's table and text; in one comparison of acute psychosis (33 vs 69 people), voices conversing were more frequent in methamphetamine psychosis (48.5% vs 20.3%) and thought broadcasting in schizophrenia (42% vs 24%, significant only after adjusting for age). In one Taiwanese study, psychosis persisting more than a month into abstinence was comparable to schizophrenia on positive symptoms and on cognitive tests, while people whose psychosis had resolved within a month (abstinent for an average of 9 weeks when assessed) scored lower on positive symptoms and performed like people who used methamphetamine without psychosis. The narrative review's authors conclude that acute methamphetamine psychosis may be clinically distinguishable from schizophrenia while persistent psychosis appears similar, except for more pronounced negative symptoms in schizophrenia; the review reports no study validating any symptom for telling the two apart, and its evidence on thought disorder is mixed and, by its authors' account, indirect and inconclusive.
plain: Meth psychosis and schizophrenia can look alike. In 12 small studies pooled together, hallucinations and delusions were not clearly different in strength, though this result is less certain than reported. 'Negative' symptoms, such as flatness and withdrawal, were somewhat milder in meth psychosis. No symptom has been shown to reliably tell the two apart.
population: People with methamphetamine psychosis and people with schizophrenia
exposure: Methamphetamine psychosis (acute or persistent)
comparator: Schizophrenia or primary psychosis
outcome: Positive, negative and cognitive symptoms
magnitude: Meta-analysis, 12 studies, 624 vs 527 people: negative symptoms SMD −0.35 (−0.54 to −0.16), I² 54%; studies with Newcastle–Ottawa scores above 5: −0.44 (−0.82 to −0.07); leave-one-out as reported, without naming the study left out: −0.254 (−0.37 to −0.13), I² 58.0% (editors' recalculation without Mikami 2003, the funnel-plot outlier: −0.28, −0.44 to −0.12, I² 30%, with random effects; −0.25, −0.38 to −0.13, with a common-effect model). Positive symptoms −0.01 (−0.13 to 0.11), I² 0%, as reported; editors' recalculation from the review's Table 1, reading the dispersions of Dawe 2011 and Hajebi 2018 as standard errors: −0.29 (−0.67 to 0.10), I² 89%, study values −1.93 to 0.54; taking every dispersion as printed: −0.35 (−0.90 to 0.20), I² 94%, study values −1.98 to 1.20. grade.reasoning: Observational comparisons of diagnostic groups; start low. The claim no longer rests only on a narrative review: a systematic review and meta-analysis read in full (Cohen-Laroque et al., 2024; AMSTAR 2 critically low on the first reading) pools 12 studies, so the severity comparisons are no longer second-hand; the narrative review's study-level descriptions remain second-hand. Risk of bias −1: cross-sectional comparisons of treated patients, with acute and persistent psychosis and current and past use mixed, at least one comparison group using methamphetamine, two studies from one group probably sharing participants, and the meta-analysis's input values for positive symptoms not reproducible from its own table. Inconsistency −1: positive symptoms very heterogeneous on recalculation (I² 89%, or 94% taking Table 1 as printed), with study values significant in both directions, although reported as homogeneous; negative symptoms I² 54%, although 10 of the 12 study estimates point the same way and none significantly the other way. (The narrative review's table and text disagree on hallucination modalities in one study, a reporting problem rather than inconsistency between studies.) Imprecision not downgraded separately (already very low), although the recalculated positive-symptom interval (−0.67 to 0.10) includes both no difference and a moderate one. Very low. Status mixed: the positive-symptom comparison is inconsistent on recalculation, while the negative-symptom difference is consistent in direction across studies from four research groups. One claim is kept because both comparisons come from the same review, studies and biases and are read together, and the statement says which part is consistent. Overlap: at least three primary studies (Chen 2015, Srisurapanont 2011, Wang 2016) are in both the meta-analysis and the narrative review, which therefore do not count as independent replication.

statement: Use of methamphetamine or other amphetamines is associated with depressive symptoms in observational studies: pooled adjusted odds ratio 1.3 (95% CI 1.2–1.4; 6 studies, I² 0%) for any use in a 2019 review, whose authors note that all but one of the population surveys and cohorts supporting the association measured symptoms rather than diagnosed depression; and adjusted odds ratios of 1.60 and 1.50 in the two cohorts in its 2023 update that followed people over time while adjusting for earlier depressive symptoms (secondary-school students; men who have sex with men); the school cohort (Briere et al., 2012) is also one of the six studies in the 2019 estimate, so only the second cohort adds independent evidence. That update's pooled estimate for these cohorts (1.18, or 1.24 in its text) cannot be reproduced from its tables. In unadjusted post hoc subgroups of the 2019 review, the association was present in general-population samples (2.0) but not within samples of people who use other substances (1.1, 0.7–1.7). For amphetamine use disorder the reviews differ: 1.2 (0.5–2.7; 6 studies, unadjusted; major depression in all) in the 2019 review, mostly in samples with high levels of other substance use or clinical conditions, and 3.46 (2.04–5.89; 2 cross-sectional studies, unadjusted) in the 2023 update, which excluded comparisons with people who use other drugs. The 2023 review updates the 2019 one, with largely the same authors, so the two are not independent.
plain: People who use meth or other amphetamines report depressive symptoms somewhat more often than people who don't: about 1.3 to 1.6 times the odds after accounting for some other factors, including in two studies that followed people over time. When people who use meth were compared with other people who use drugs, there was no clear difference. For people with a meth use disorder, the two main reviews disagree.

grade.reasoning: Observational, mostly cross-sectional; starts low. Rated for the association as worded. Risk of bias not downgraded: the headline estimates are adjusted (different covariate sets); the adjusted pool has a weighted quality score of 87% at the review's evidence level C (cohorts of people who use drugs), against 62% at level E (cross-sectional associations in samples of people who use drugs) for the adjusted use-disorder estimate behind the suicidality claim, which is downgraded; and the two longitudinal cohorts adjusted for earlier depressive symptoms. Residual confounding by other drug use and life circumstances is plausible (no association within substance-using samples); under a stricter reading, in which it could account for an odds ratio of 1.3, certainty would be very low. Inconsistency not downgraded: adjusted any-use estimates agree (I² 0%) and the main heterogeneity is explained by sample type; the use-disorder estimates conflict between the reviews and are reported, not pooled. Indirectness not downgraded, but definitions range from mild screening thresholds (PHQ-9 of 5 or more) to diagnosed major depression, and methamphetamine is pooled with amphetamine. Publication bias was assessed in neither review. The 2023 review updates the 2019 one (same protocol, largely the same authors), so they are not independent; 'replicated' rests on the independent primary studies within them (6 adjusted studies in the 2019 review, one of which is the school cohort in the 2023 update, plus one further cohort in the update).

statement: In mostly cross-sectional studies, amphetamine use disorder (amphetamine or methamphetamine) is associated with suicidal ideation and attempts: pooled adjusted odds ratio 1.5 (95% CI 1.3–1.8; I² 0%) in 4 cross-sectional studies of psychiatric emergency patients, arrestees, outpatients with substance use disorders (compared with people with other substance use disorders) and people under community corrections, against 2.3 (1.8–2.9) unadjusted in 7 studies that include those 4. For any use, the 4 studies with adjusted estimates gave 1.7 (1.0–2.9; I² 77%; the review's text gives 1.4), an interval that reaches no association, against 4.4 (2.4–8.2) unadjusted in 7 partly different studies. The review found no longitudinal evidence on whether use preceded suicidal thoughts or attempts. The review's authors suggest the excess may be largely shared with substance use in general and related demographic and premorbid risk factors. Only one study in this review examined deaths by suicide: in a drug-treatment follow-up, suicide deaths were higher than expected but not significantly higher than among people using opioids, and most cases involved premorbid risk. A separate meta-analysis of cohorts of people with regular or problematic amphetamine use found suicide deaths about 12 times the rate in the general population of the same age and sex, a less certain figure (95% CI 4.89–30.47; cause of death often unclearly ascertained; see the mortality claim in section 10).
plain: People with an amphetamine or meth use disorder, in studies mostly of people in emergency rooms, the justice system or drug treatment, were more likely to report suicidal thoughts or attempts: about 1.5 times the odds after accounting for some other factors, against about 2.3 times in raw numbers across a larger set of studies. These studies measured both at one time, so they cannot show which came first, and the authors think the excess may be largely shared with drug use in general and with people's backgrounds and earlier problems. This review had little on deaths by suicide, but studies following people with regular or problematic use found suicide deaths about 12 times as common as in people of the same age and sex, a less certain figure (see the mortality claim).

statement: After accounting for other factors, amphetamine use (amphetamine or methamphetamine) is associated with more violence in two longitudinal studies by overlapping research groups, one in the general population and one in people dependent on methamphetamine; a meta-analysis of mostly cross-sectional studies found an adjusted association in the same direction that was not statistically clear, and none of these sources can show that use came before the violence, so whether use causes violence is not settled. In a systematic review and meta-analysis, the pooled adjusted odds ratio was 1.4 (95% CI 0.8–2.4; 6 studies), against 2.2 (1.2–4.1; 10 studies, I² 95%) unadjusted. In unadjusted post hoc subgroups, violent behaviour (hostility rating scales, violent behaviour or sexual exploitation reported in surveys, and violent or self-destructive behaviour in an emergency department) was associated (3.7, 3.1–4.5) and violent offending was not clearly associated (1.0, 0.4–2.7; I² 94%). For amphetamine use disorder the review has a single study: among offenders whose punishment was reduced or waived because of mental disorder, those with the disorder had more violent re-offending over 7 years (unadjusted OR 6.2, 3.1–12.3; 52 people with the disorder; quality score 43%). The violence studies had among the lowest quality ratings in the review, with poor measurement of use; the review's authors judge that large effects in two population surveys and two longitudinal studies suggest that an association may exist but needs confirmation. The review also describes a within-person analysis of the same Australian treatment cohort as the psychosis study in section 9, in which severe hostility was more frequent during periods of use after adjustment for concurrent other drug use; that paper has not yet been read. A later general-population birth cohort, not in the review (Christchurch, New Zealand; about 1,000 people interviewed at 21, 25, 30 and 35; 28% used methamphetamine or amphetamine at least once between 18 and 35), found that use in a period went with more self-reported violence in the same period after adjustment for childhood and adolescent factors and for concurrent depression, anxiety, alcohol and cannabis use disorders, life stress, unemployment and psychotic symptoms: perpetration OR 1.60 (1.01–2.54), victimisation 1.57 (1.00–2.47), intimate-partner violence perpetration 1.55 (1.04–2.30) and victimisation 1.09 (0.80–1.49). Odds were higher among the 51 people who had used at least weekly (perpetration 4.84, 2.48–9.46), in an analysis adjusted for childhood and adolescent factors only that related the heaviest use in any period to violence at any time from 18 to 35, so the two need not fall in the same period; less frequent use was not clearly associated with perpetration (1.13 and 1.40, intervals including 1). Use and violence were reported for the same periods, so which came first is unknown, and other illicit drug use was not adjusted for. A second longitudinal study, also later than the review, followed 469 people dependent on methamphetamine in Sydney and Brisbane (mostly people entering treatment, most of whom injected; the same cohort as the hostility analysis inside the review), with reports for the past month at entry, 3 months, 1 year and 3 years (2006–2010). Self-reported crime involving violence, such as violence in a robbery or assault, was reported in 113 of 927 months with methamphetamine use (12%) and 19 of 593 months without (3%). Comparing each person's months with and without use, a comparison designed to remove the influence of stable personal characteristics (the paper names both a random-intercept and a fixed-effects estimator), the odds were 8.2 times higher (4.2–15.9) unadjusted and 3.4 times higher (1.5–8.0) after adjustment for age, income, unemployment, unstable housing and concurrent alcohol, cannabis, cocaine, heroin and ecstasy use; unadjusted percentages rose with days of use, and the adjusted dose estimates are only in a supplement that has not been read. Use and crime were reported for the same month in the same interview, treatment and imprisonment during follow-up were not taken into account, and the analysis was exploratory; the authors say that their intervals are wide because few participants committed crime in months without use, and that the results apply to people dependent on methamphetamine, not to recreational use. The two longitudinal studies share three authors (McKetin, Boden, Foulds), and the second shares four with the review (McKetin, Foulds, Degenhardt, Farrell), so their agreement is not independent replication.
plain: Is amphetamine use, including meth, linked to violence once other factors are taken into account? Two long-term studies found a link even after other factors were taken into account, but neither can show that meth causes violence, and the two studies share authors. A review of mostly weak studies found that the link seen in raw numbers shrank and became uncertain after adjustment; in the raw numbers it was seen for violent behaviour but not clearly for violent offences. A study in New Zealand followed about 1,000 people from age 18 to 35. In periods when they used meth or speed, people were somewhat more likely to report attacking someone or being attacked, even after many other factors were taken into account. The few who had used at least weekly had higher odds, in an analysis that took fewer factors into account. A study in Australia followed 469 people dependent on meth for up to three years and compared each person's months of use with their own months without. Violent crime was reported in 12 of 100 months with meth use and 3 of 100 months without, and the link remained after age, money and housing problems and other drug use were taken into account. But in both studies people reported use and violence for the same periods, so the studies cannot show which came first, and the Australian study did not take treatment or time in prison into account. An earlier study of the same Australian people, which also compared each person with themselves, found more hostility in periods of use; it has not been read yet. The review's authors think a link may exist but needs to be confirmed.
population: General-population (a New Zealand birth cohort followed from 18 to 35), clinical and justice samples, including an Australian cohort of people dependent on methamphetamine
exposure: Any amphetamine use (in the birth cohort, self-reported use of methamphetamine or amphetamine in each interview period; in the dependent cohort, any self-reported methamphetamine use in the past month)
comparator: No use (in the dependent cohort, the same people's months without use)
outcome: Violent behaviour or violent offending (in the birth cohort, self-reported perpetration and victimisation, including intimate-partner violence; in the dependent cohort, self-reported crime involving violence in the past month)
magnitude: Review (any use): adjusted OR 1.4 (0.8–2.4), 6 studies, I² 25%; unadjusted 2.2 (1.2–4.1), 10 studies, I² 95%; violent behaviour 3.7 (3.1–4.5); violent offending 1.0 (0.4–2.7). Birth cohort (any use in a period, fully adjusted): perpetration 1.60 (1.01–2.54), victimisation 1.57 (1.00–2.47), intimate-partner perpetration 1.55 (1.04–2.30), intimate-partner victimisation 1.09 (0.80–1.49); at least weekly use against never (heaviest use in any period, violence at any time from 18 to 35), adjusted for childhood and adolescent factors only: perpetration 4.84 (2.48–9.46), victimisation 3.62 (1.88–6.96). Dependent cohort (within-person, months with any methamphetamine use against the same people's months without; self-reported violent crime in the past month): 12% against 3% of months (113 of 927 against 19 of 593); odds ratio 8.2 (4.2–15.9) unadjusted, 5.3 (2.6–10.7) adjusted for age and socio-economic factors, 3.4 (1.5–8.0) also adjusted for other drug use.

risk_of_bias.note: The review's violence studies had among the lowest quality scores (56–58%), with poor measurement of use. Both longitudinal studies are at high risk of bias overall on their study cards (ROBINS-E), without a single high domain: use and violence reported for the same periods (reverse causation possible) and by self-report, without corroboration; no adjustment for other illicit drug use in the birth cohort, whose fully adjusted estimates sit at the margin of no association; and, in the dependent cohort, no account of treatment, imprisonment or other changes over time, in an exploratory analysis.

inconsistency.note: Not downgraded: the adjusted estimates agree in direction (review 1.4; birth cohort 1.55–1.60 for perpetration, victimisation and intimate-partner perpetration; dependent cohort 3.4 for violent crime). The larger estimate in the dependent cohort fits its population (people dependent on methamphetamine) and its scale: odds ratios comparing months within the same person are not on the same scale as population-averaged or between-person odds ratios. The high heterogeneity of the review's unadjusted pools is partly explained by the post hoc split between violent behaviour and violent offending.

imprecision.note: The review's adjusted interval includes no association (0.8–2.4), the birth cohort's fully adjusted lower limits are 1.00–1.04, and the dependent cohort's interval is wide (1.5–8.0), resting on 19 months with violent crime among the 593 months without use.

large_effect.note: Not applied: the dependent cohort's adjusted odds ratio for violent crime (3.4) has a lower limit of 1.5, and the biases that remain (same-month self-report, changes around treatment entry, drug-market involvement) can run away from the null.

dose_response.note: Considered and not applied: the birth cohort's gradient comes from an analysis adjusted for childhood and adolescent factors only, which relates the heaviest use in any period to violence at any time from 18 to 35, rests on 51 people who used at least weekly, is concentrated in that top category for perpetration, and could be produced by confounding that grows with frequency of use (other drug use, involvement in drug markets), which runs away from the null; in the dependent cohort the article shows the gradient only as unadjusted percentages pooled across people (Fig. 1), and the adjusted dose estimates are in a supplement that has not been read.

grade.reasoning: Observational: mostly cross-sectional studies in the review, plus two longitudinal cohorts; starts low. Risk of bias −1: the review's violence studies had among the lowest quality scores (56–58%), with poor measurement of use, and both cohorts are at high risk of bias on ROBINS-E (use and violence self-reported for the same periods; no adjustment for other illicit drugs in the birth cohort; no account of treatment or imprisonment in the dependent cohort). Imprecision −1: the pooled adjusted interval includes no association (0.8–2.4), the birth cohort's fully adjusted lower limits are 1.00–1.04, and the dependent cohort's interval (1.5–8.0) rests on few months with violent crime without use. Not upgraded for dose-response or large effect (see the domain notes). Certainty very low. Relation: is associated with, rather than insufficient evidence, because the adjusted association now appears in two longitudinal cohorts, in a general population and in people dependent on methamphetamine, with intervals that exclude no association, and the review's adjusted pooled estimate points the same way (its interval includes no association, so it adds direction, not independent support; the review's violence studies also include the 2014 analysis of the MATES sample); the birth cohort's fully adjusted lower limits (1.00–1.04) come without adjustment for other illicit drugs, which in the dependent cohort reduced the odds ratio from 5.3 to 3.4; the very low rating says how uncertain this association is, and whether use causes violence is a separate question that none of the sources can settle, because use and violence were reported for the same periods. Status: replicated by the same team. The adjusted estimates agree in direction, but the two cohorts share three authors (McKetin, Boden, Foulds), the dependent-cohort paper shares four with the review (McKetin, Foulds, Degenhardt, Farrell), and the dependent cohort is the same sample as the within-person hostility analysis inside the review's pooled estimate (McKetin et al., 2014, not yet read), so the agreement is not independent replication. In the review's unadjusted data, violent behaviour and violent offending point different ways (3.7 against 1.0, with I² 94% left unexplained within offending); the dependent cohort's within-person result for self-reported violent crime runs against the unadjusted offending estimate but does not explain that heterogeneity. The rating rests on the adjusted estimates, so this is noted rather than rated down. On the reading list: McKetin et al. (2014); a systematic review of drug-administration studies of aggression (O'Malley et al., 2022, DOI list item 110).
