statement: In people dependent on methamphetamine (one Australian cohort recruited mostly on entering treatment in Sydney and Brisbane; 469 people analysed, most of whom injected; 2006–2010), months with methamphetamine use, compared with the same people's months without use, are associated with more self-reported crime: any crime was reported in 515 of 927 months with use (56%) and in 104 of 593 months without (17.5%). Within-person odds ratios adjusted for age, income, unemployment, unstable housing and other substance use were 4.7 (95% CI 2.8–8.0) for any crime, 5.9 (3.0–11.9) for drug dealing and 5.5 (2.8–10.8) for property crime; fraud was not clearly associated (1.7, 0.8–3.3); crime involving violence is covered by the claim on violence (3.4, 1.5–8.0). Adding other substance use to the adjustment reduced the odds ratios by a third to nearly two-thirds; unadjusted percentages rose with days of use, and the adjusted dose estimates are only in a supplement that has not been read. Use and crime were self-reported for the same month in the same interview, so which came first is unknown; treatment and imprisonment during follow-up were not taken into account; the analysis was exploratory, and its methods describe both a random-intercept model and the fixed-effects option for the within-person effect. The authors limit the findings to people dependent on methamphetamine, not recreational use. Whether use causes crime is not shown.
plain: Is meth use linked to crime? In one Australian study, 469 people dependent on meth, most of them starting treatment, were followed for up to three years, and each person's months of meth use were compared with their own months without. Some crime was reported in 56 of 100 months with meth use and in about 18 of 100 months without. The link was strongest for selling drugs and for property crime such as theft or break-ins, and it remained after age, money and housing problems and other drug use were taken into account; fraud was not clearly linked. People reported their meth use and their crime for the same months in the same interview, so the study cannot show which came first, and it did not take treatment or time in prison into account. The results apply to people dependent on meth, not to people who use it now and then. Violent crime is covered in the answer on violence.
population: People with DSM-IV methamphetamine dependence at entry to an Australian cohort (MATES: Sydney and Brisbane, 2006–2010; recruited mostly on entering community-based treatment; most injecting)
exposure: Any self-reported methamphetamine use in the past month (Opiate Treatment Index)
comparator: The same people's months without methamphetamine use
outcome: Self-reported crime in the past month on the Opiate Treatment Index crime scale: any crime, drug dealing, property crime and fraud (crime involving violence is in the claim on violence)
magnitude: Shares of months with each crime, without against with methamphetamine use (Table 1; 593 and 927 interview-months): any crime 104 (17.5%, printed 17%) against 515 (56%); dealing 33 (6%) against 330 (36%); property crime 43 (7%) against 279 (30%); fraud 32 (5%) against 121 (13%). Within-person odds ratios, months with use against the same people's months without, unadjusted, adjusted for age and socio-economic factors (Model 1) and also for other substance use (Model 2): any crime 13.2 (8.5–20.6), 10.5 (6.6–16.7), 4.7 (2.8–8.0); dealing 18.2 (10.2–32.5), 15.8 (8.6–29.1), 5.9 (3.0–11.9); property crime 10.6 (6.3–18.0), 8.4 (4.8–14.5), 5.5 (2.8–10.8); fraud 3.4 (2.0–5.8), 2.8 (1.6–5.0), 1.7 (0.8–3.3), p = 0.158; all others p < 0.001. From Model 1 to Model 2 the odds ratios fell by 35% to 63% (editors' calculation). Odds ratios are not risk ratios: for any crime the raw shares are in a ratio of 3.2 (editors' calculation). Unadjusted shares of months by 0, 1–15 and 16 or more days of use (editors' reading of Fig. 1, which prints no values): any crime about 18%, 48% and 71%; dealing 6%, 27% and 53%; property crime 7%, 26% and 39%; fraud 5%, 12% and 16%.

Crime was more common in months with 16 or more days of use than in months with fewer (Fig. 1: unadjusted percentages of months by 0, 1–15 and 16 or more days of use, no values printed; editors' reading of the bars: any crime about 18%, 48% and 71%, dealing 6%, 27% and 53%, property crime 7%, 26% and 39%, fraud 5%, 12% and 16%); the authors report that the gradient remained after adjustment, in a supplementary table (Table S3) that was not available. The authors state that crime was self-reported, not convictions; that the direction of the same-month relationship could be disputed (they consider crime leading to more use unlikely, and the association more likely to reflect desisting from crime during abstinence); that the findings apply to people dependent on methamphetamine, most of whom injected, and should not be generalised to recreational use; that few participants committed crime in months without use, giving wide confidence limits, and small numbers limit the dose findings; and that unmeasured factors in the same months may have contributed.

risk_of_bias.note: ROBINS-E high overall on the study card, with some concerns in all seven domains: use and crime self-reported for the same month in the same interview, so crime could drive use within the month (dealing and property crime bring money or drugs); changes around treatment entry, treatment received and imprisonment not measured; other drugs measured coarsely; a third of participants lost by 3 years; and an exploratory analysis whose estimator is described ambiguously.

indirectness.note: None as worded: the population is restricted to people dependent on methamphetamine and the outcome to self-reported crime.

imprecision.note: The intervals for any crime, dealing and property crime are well clear of no association (lower limits 2.8–3.0); that the number of people contributing to each within-person estimate is not reported is a reason for caution, not a downgrade.

large_effect.note: Not applied: the adjusted odds ratios are large (4.7–5.9), but for common outcomes within-person odds ratios overstate risk ratios (for any crime the raw shares are in a ratio of 3.2), and the biases that remain can run away from the null: crime can drive use within the same month, and reports of use and crime in one interview can move together (METHODS §6.3).

dose_response.note: Not applied: the article shows the gradient only as unadjusted percentages pooled across people (Fig. 1); the adjusted dose estimates are in a supplementary table that was not available.

grade.reasoning: One within-person analysis of a prospective cohort, read in full (PDF pp. 1–6); observational, so it starts low. Risk of bias −1: ROBINS-E high on the study card (same-interview self-report of use and crime for the same month; changes around treatment entry, treatment and imprisonment not measured; an exploratory analysis). Inconsistency is not assessable with one study; indirectness 0 as worded; imprecision 0 (the intervals for any crime, dealing and property crime are far from 1). Not upgraded for large effect or dose-response (see the domain notes). Certainty very low. Relation: is associated with; causal wording is not supported, because use and crime were reported for the same month, and the authors' reading of the results as robust evidence of an increase beyond pre-existing risk, and of crime as a likely consequence of use, goes beyond what the design shows. Status: single study. The same cohort's psychosis and hostility analyses concern other outcomes, no other study of acquisitive crime or dealing has been read, and the authors overlap with those of the violence claim's other sources (three with the New Zealand birth cohort, four with the 2019 review). The study card also records that the number of people contributing to each within-person estimate is not reported, that the abstract and the methods describe the estimator differently, and that the paper reads its odds ratios as risk ratios. A separate claim from the one on violence, because the study's main results concern crime in general; the any-crime estimate includes the months with violent crime.

statement: Among US adults aged 18–64, estimated past-year methamphetamine use rose from about 1.61 million in 2015 to 1.97 million in 2019 (about +22%, editors' calculation) and past-year methamphetamine use disorder (DSM-IV criteria) from about 741,000 to 1.09 million (about +47%, editors' calculation), while overdose deaths involving psychostimulants other than cocaine rose from 5,526 to 15,489 (+180%). More than half of the 2019 deaths also involved opioids, but deaths not involving opioids also rose, from 3,220 to 7,051. The death code (ICD-10 T43.6) covers psychostimulants other than cocaine; the authors report that about 85–90% of such certificates mention methamphetamine. The survey excludes unsheltered and institutionalized people and relies on self-report, so use is probably underestimated. The paper's headline increases for use (43%) and for use disorder without injection (105%) are calculated from 2016, the lowest year, not from 2015. These 2015–2019 figures (ages 18–64, DSM-IV) are not comparable with the 2024 survey figures shown in this section (ages 12 and over, DSM-5). Counting all ages, overdose deaths that a later analysis of the national death records labels methamphetamine-involved (its ICD-10 codes are given only in a supplement, not read) rose from 547 in 1999 to 34,855 in 2023 (crude rate 0.20 to 10.41 per 100,000; 2023 data provisional). The increase averaged 18.5% a year, was steepest in 2018–2021 (37.4% a year) and slowed to 3.4% a year (95% CI 0.2–6.8) in 2021–2023. Deaths involving methamphetamine with fentanyl rose by 76% a year in 2012–2021 and 8.6% a year in 2021–2023, while those with other opioids fell by 27% a year in 2021–2023; no count or share of methamphetamine-involved deaths that also involved opioids is printed (a figure plots their rates, and the overlap of the fentanyl and other-opioid series is not given). The analysis gives two counts for 2023 (34,855 and 35,126), its rates are crude rather than age-adjusted, and its all-ages series is not directly comparable with the 2015–2019 counts for ages 18–64. A CDC report gives the same 2023 count (34,855), citing a national statistics brief, for deaths with the code for psychostimulants other than cocaine (T43.6), which suggests that the later analysis used that code (editors' inference); on that code, the age-adjusted death rate rose from 3.9 per 100,000 in 2018 to 10.4 in 2023, and the report says that, across racial and ethnic groups, the largest increases in stimulant-involved deaths (cocaine and psychostimulants together) were in deaths that also involved opioids, without giving those figures. The same report draws on a CDC surveillance system that counts methamphetamine as involved when the medical examiner or coroner listed it as a cause of death on the death certificate, in their report or in the toxicology report (49 states and the District of Columbia, four of them for only part of the period, pooled over January 2021 to June 2024): methamphetamine was involved in 96,614 of 309,274 overdose deaths (31.2%); 68.8% of these also involved opioids and 30,139 (9.7% of all overdose deaths) did not. This share comes from a different system and period than the 2019 share above, so the two are not directly comparable. Decedents without opioids were older (64% aged 45 or over, against 39% of those with opioids; editors' calculation) and, in the 46 states and DC with circumstance data, more often had a recorded history of cardiovascular disease (39.3% against 19.8%); both contrasts are crude, so age may account for part of the second. The report's authors expect stimulant-involved deaths to be undercounted, because some are certified as cardiovascular deaths without an overdose code and toxicology testing varies.
plain: In US household surveys of adults aged 18 to 64, the estimated number who said they had used meth in the past year rose by about a fifth between 2015 and 2019, and the number with a meth use disorder by about half; the surveys miss people who are homeless or in institutions. Over the same years, overdose deaths involving stimulants other than cocaine (mostly meth) nearly tripled; more than half of the 2019 deaths also involved opioids, but deaths without opioids also more than doubled. The bigger percentages often quoted from this paper start from 2016, the lowest year. Later US survey figures use different methods and are not directly comparable. Newer death records for all ages show that deaths involving meth kept rising, from about 550 in 1999 to about 35,000 in 2023, but the rise slowed after 2021 (the latest year's figures are provisional). Deaths involving both meth and fentanyl rose fastest. These newer counts come from the same death records and include all ages, so they extend the earlier figures rather than confirm them. A CDC report found that medical examiners or coroners listed meth among the causes of about 31 in 100 overdose deaths from 2021 to mid-2024; about 7 in 10 of those deaths also involved opioids, and about 3 in 10 did not. These reports are a different kind of record from the death records above, so this share cannot be compared directly with the 2019 one.

grade.reasoning: Repeated national survey (NSDUH) and death-certificate counts; observational, starts low (§6.3). Not upgraded: large effect concerns the size of an exposure's effect under adjustment, not a change in counts over time (§6.3, descriptive claims), and the survey trends (+22% use, +47% use disorder; intervals overlapping between 2015 and 2019; trend tests significant) are not large. Risk of bias not downgraded for the trend (JBI moderate): the frame excludes unsheltered and institutionalized people and about half of sampled people completed an interview, which lowers the levels more than it changes the trend. The death series is a code (ICD-10 T43.6), about 85–90% of whose certificates mention methamphetamine, and about 6% of 2019 overdose certificates named no drug, so the counts are a proxy and an undercount. The all-ages extension to 2023 (Zhu et al., 2025; JBI moderate on its study card) draws on the same national death records, so it extends the series rather than replicating it (status stays single-study); its codes are not shown in the article, 2023 data are provisional, two different 2023 counts are given and two subgroup averages in its table appear transposed. These faults affect exact figures, not the direction of the rise or the timing of the slowdown after 2021, so the rating is not downgraded; the 2021–2023 slowdown is a segment fitted to three yearly values, the last of them provisional. The CDC report (Tanz et al., 2025; JBI moderate, on which both card readers agree), read in full, uses the same national death records for its 2018–2023 rates, so it too extends rather than replicates the series (status stays single-study); its 2023 count matches the later analysis, which suggests that both use the T43.6 code. Its SUDORS figures come from a partly separate source (medical examiner, coroner and toxicology reports naming methamphetamine) and give a methamphetamine-specific opioid share from medical examiner and toxicology records, which the all-ages death-code analysis (Zhu et al., 2025) lacked, but they are pooled over one period, cover four states for only part of it, and cannot show a trend. The authors expect an undercount; in the editors' reading it may fall more on deaths without opioids (deaths certified as cardiovascular are the ones missed, and decedents without opioids were older and more often had cardiovascular disease), so the share with opioids may be somewhat overstated. Not downgraded: these limits affect exact shares, not the order of magnitude.

statement: In 23 cohorts (115,223 people) of people with regular or problematic use of amphetamines (amphetamine or methamphetamine), mostly people in treatment, people who inject drugs, people with hospital diagnoses and people in contact with the criminal justice system, found through a search covering 2008 to February 2018 and, for 1980–2007, the authors' earlier review, all-cause mortality was 1.11 deaths per 100 person-years (95% CI 0.90–1.37), 6.83 times (5.27–8.84) that of the general population of the same age and sex (5.71 in the 8 cohorts that reported their own ratios; ratios for 13 cohorts were imputed by the reviewers). In the 4 to 7 cohorts reporting each cause, crude death rates per 100 person-years were 0.20 for accidental injury, 0.20 for suicide, 0.14 for drug poisoning, 0.13 for cardiovascular disease and 0.03 for homicide; relative to the general population the excess was largest for drug poisoning (24.7 times), suicide (12.2) and homicide (11.9). These cause-specific figures come from few cohorts, in which the cause of death was often unclearly ascertained, and most are highly heterogeneous (I² 94–98% for the crude rates except homicide), so they are less certain than the all-cause estimates. Heterogeneity was very high (I² 97–98% for the all-cause estimates). The ratios compare each cohort with the general population of the same age and sex (for the 13 imputed ratios, also of the same location and calendar years) and adjust for nothing else, so they describe the excess mortality of these populations, which includes the effects of opioid and other drug use, injecting, infection, poverty and imprisonment, not the effect of amphetamines alone; older cohorts probably involved less methamphetamine, relative to amphetamine, than recent ones, which the reviewers could not examine.
plain: In studies that followed people with regular or problematic use of amphetamines, including meth, about 1 in 90 died each year, nearly 7 times the rate of people of the same age and sex. Deaths from injuries, suicide, overdose and heart disease each occurred at roughly 1 to 2 per 1,000 people per year, and deaths from homicide less often; compared with people of the same age and sex, overdose deaths were about 25 times as common, and suicide and homicide about 12 times. These figures for single causes come from fewer studies and are less certain than the overall figure. These were people in treatment, people who inject, people in hospital records or in contact with the justice system, not everyone who uses. Many also used opioids or other drugs, and the comparison takes account of age and sex (and, for some studies, place and calendar years), not of injecting, infections, poverty or prison, so these figures do not show how much of the excess is caused by the stimulant itself.

exposure: Regular or problematic amphetamine use
comparator: General population of the same age and sex (for the 13 imputed ratios, also of the same location and calendar years)
outcome: All-cause and cause-specific mortality
magnitude: Crude all-cause 1.11 per 100 person-years (0.90–1.37); SMR 6.83 (5.27–8.84); 5.71 (4.44–7.35) in the 8 cohorts reporting their own SMR; 6.47 (4.96–8.43) without the HIV-positive cohort. Cause-specific crude rates per 100 person-years: accidental injury 0.20 (0.08–0.47; 7 cohorts), suicide 0.20 (0.07–0.55; 6), drug poisoning 0.14 (0.06–0.34; 5), cardiovascular 0.13 (0.06–0.29; 4), homicide 0.03 (0.02–0.06; 4). Cause-specific SMR: drug poisoning 24.70 (16.67–36.58), suicide 12.20 (4.89–30.47), homicide 11.90 (7.82–18.12), cardiovascular 5.12 (3.74–7.00), accidental injury 5.12 (2.88–9.08).

grade.reasoning: Observational, starts low. Rated as a description of mortality in these cohorts relative to the general population, not as an effect of amphetamine use. Not upgraded for large effect: the ratios adjust for nothing beyond age and sex (and, for the imputed ones, location and calendar years), and the differences left unadjusted (opioid and other drug use, injecting, infection, poverty, imprisonment) run away from the null (§6.3); descriptive claims are not upgraded for large effect. Not downgraded for inconsistency: I² is 97–98%, but every regional point estimate (4.5–10.5) and both sensitivity analyses (5.71 in cohorts with their own ratios; 6.47 without the HIV cohort) show a several-fold excess, so the heterogeneity concerns the size of the excess, not its presence. Not downgraded for indirectness because the claim is restricted to the populations sampled; older cohorts probably involved less methamphetamine, relative to amphetamine, than recent ones. Risk of bias: cause-of-death ascertainment was often unclear and 13 of 23 ratios were imputed; not downgraded for the all-cause estimate. The cause-specific figures rest on 4 to 7 cohorts each, with cause of death often unclearly ascertained, I² 94–98% for the crude rates except homicide, and wide intervals (suicide SMR 4.89–30.47); taken alone they would be rated very low (risk of bias and inconsistency), so the rating of low applies to the all-cause estimates and the statement labels the cause-specific figures as less certain.

statement: In adults with moderate or severe methamphetamine use disorder (403 randomized at eight US sites), extended-release injectable naltrexone plus oral bupropion was followed by a urine-verified response (at least 3 of 4 negative samples at the end of each 6-week stage) in 13.6% versus 2.5% on placebo, weighted across two stages: a difference of 11.1 percentage points (95% CI about 6.3 to 15.9; number needed to treat 9). Nausea and vomiting were more frequent on treatment; serious adverse events were similar. The response was measured in the last two weeks of each stage, the estimate combines a first-stage comparison with a second-stage comparison among placebo non-responders, and participants had to be free of opioid use and not in other treatment. Most participants in both groups did not respond, and no outcome after the 12-week medication period is reported.
plain: In one large US trial of adults who used meth almost every day, about 1 in 7 people given an injected medicine (naltrexone) plus a daily tablet (bupropion) had mostly meth-free urine tests in the last two weeks of a 6-week treatment period, compared with about 1 in 40 on placebo: about 1 extra person for every 9 treated. Most people on the medicines did not reach this, the trial did not report what happened after treatment ended, and people using opioids were not included. Nausea was common on the medicines.
population: Adults with moderate or severe DSM-5 methamphetamine use disorder (mean use 26.7 of 30 days; 73% mainly smoking)
exposure: Extended-release injectable naltrexone (every 3 weeks) plus extended-release oral bupropion
comparator: Placebo injections and tablets
outcome: Response: at least 3 of 4 methamphetamine-negative urine samples at the end of each stage
magnitude: Weighted response 13.6% vs 2.5%; difference 11.1 percentage points (Wald z 4.53; 95% CI about 6.3–15.9, editors' calculation matching the printed lower limit); NNT 9. Stage 1: 16.5% vs 3.4%; stage 2: 11.4% vs 1.8%.

grade.reasoning: Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled; starts high. Risk of bias (RoB 2 some concerns in randomization, deviations, missing data and selection of the reported result) not downgraded: the outcome is an objective urine result; participants missing two or more of the four samples, or who left the trial, were counted as non-responders, which here penalizes the active arm, whose samples were more often missing (all four provided by 47.7% vs 60.2% in stage 1; the complete-case difference was 18.7 points); the registry's stage-specific outcomes are reported and each favours treatment (13.1 and 9.6 points, editors' calculation); functional unblinding is plausible (nausea 37.6% vs 15.3%) and could affect the size of the effect but would not plausibly create it. Imprecision −1: one trial with 31 responders on active treatment; the number needed to treat is 9 as printed and about 6 to 16 across the two-sided interval (editors' calculation: 100 divided by 15.9 and by 6.3, rounded to the nearest whole number as the printed 9 is). Indirectness not downgraded because the claim is restricted to the trial population (opioid-free, not in other treatment) and to the end-of-stage response.

statement: Whether methamphetamine use causes lasting cognitive impairment in humans has not been established: people with methamphetamine use disorder score lower than non-using volunteers on average (by about half to two-thirds of a standard deviation overall in the two meta-analyses that pooled all domains; see the claim on group differences), but none of the studies in these reviews measured cognition before use began, groups differ in education and other risk factors, scores are mostly unrelated to how much or how long people used, and the differences have not been shown to change with abstinence more than practice effects do.
plain: Does meth cause lasting problems with thinking and memory? Not shown. People dependent on meth score somewhat lower on average than people who don't use (about half to two-thirds of a standard deviation overall; see the claim on group differences), but none of these studies tested people before they started using, the groups differ in other ways, and scores are mostly unrelated to how much people used. After stopping, scores have not been shown to rise more than those of people who don't use, who also improve when retested; that fits both lasting harm and differences that were there before. See the contested question.

exposure: Methamphetamine use
comparator: No use

magnitude: Not estimable from current designs; the size of the association is given in the claim on group differences (section 9).

grade.reasoning: Causal inference from cross-sectional and short follow-up studies. Risk of bias: confounding by education and pre-existing differences, no pre-use baseline. Indirectness: animal regimens and a twin study of mixed stimulants.

debate.question: Does methamphetamine use cause lasting cognitive impairment?
debate.evidence_yes: Four meta-analyses agree in direction, two of them with no primary studies in common: people with methamphetamine use disorder score on average about 0.5–0.7 SD below non-using controls overall (0.46 and 0.68 in the two that pooled all domains), with domain differences mostly between 0.3 and 0.9 SD, most consistently on verbal learning and memory (Scott et al., 2007; Potvin et al., 2018; Basterfield et al., 2019; Cao et al., 2026). In well-matched studies people who used methamphetamine did worse on some tests in 6 of 7, and no matched study found them better on any test (Dean et al., 2013). In the one co-twin study, twins who had used stimulants weekly (80% amphetamines), matched with their co-twins on IQ and education and without stimulant use in the year before testing, did worse on four timed attention and psychomotor tests (Dean et al., 2013). In animals, chronic moderate and binge regimens produce deficits, and escalating regimens still did so in rats that self-administered the drug and in vervet monkeys, whose deficits improved with abstinence (Dean et al., 2013). More people who use methamphetamine than controls meet impairment criteria: about a quarter to a third versus one in nine to one in six (Iudicello et al., 2010; Kalechstein et al., 2003, as reported in Hart et al., 2012). Participants who drop out of studies may be in poorer health, which would make the differences look smaller (Basterfield et al., 2019). In one meta-analysis, longer use went with larger differences in fluid reasoning (11 studies), the only one of four abilities in which duration was related to the size of the difference, although fluid reasoning showed no average difference; its authors read this as support for longer use going with larger deficits (Basterfield et al., 2019). In four meta-analyses, study-level differences in education between the groups, or the groups' education level, did not predict the size of the cognitive differences (Scott et al., 2007; Potvin et al., 2018; Basterfield et al., 2019; Cao et al., 2026), which one of them reads as tentatively suggesting that the deficits follow use (Potvin et al., 2018). The review that weighed animal, cross-sectional, twin, abstinence, imaging and dose evidence concluded that the preponderance of the evidence suggests methamphetamine causes mild cognitive decline in at least some people, weighting the animal experiments most heavily because their designs support causal inference (Dean et al., 2013).
debate.evidence_no: No study in these reviews has a pre-use baseline. People who used methamphetamine had about 1.4–1.6 fewer years of education than controls (Scott et al., 2007; Basterfield et al., 2019; editors' calculation from the reviews' weighted means); in one small study (27 people who used methamphetamine, 28 controls) the composite difference was no longer statistically significant after adjusting for education, with no adjusted estimate reported (Simon et al., 2010). Most studies found no relation between test scores and how long, how often or how much people had used; positive findings came from uncorrected post hoc analyses, and in the twin study more days of stimulant use went with better scores on a few tests (Dean et al., 2013); duration of use did not moderate the group differences in two meta-analyses (Scott et al., 2007; Cao et al., 2026) and moderated only fluid reasoning, an ability with no average difference, in a third (Basterfield et al., 2019). In the same twin study the using twins did better on one sustained-attention test and no differently on nine of 14 (Dean et al., 2013). There is strong small-study bias in one meta-analysis and small-study signals, including for learning and memory, in two others (Potvin et al., 2018; Basterfield et al., 2019; Cao et al., 2026), and a meta-analysis restricted to people abstinent from methamphetamine found a reliable difference only for learning efficiency (Basterfield et al., 2019). The comprehension-knowledge difference, a measure close to premorbid ability, was found only in studies at high risk of bias (Basterfield et al., 2019). Group means usually fall in the low-average to average range (Simon et al., 2010; Hart et al., 2012). In the study with the 34% versus 16% impairment rates, more than half of the methamphetamine group had HIV and controls were screened free of HIV, hepatitis C, ADHD and antisocial personality disorder, and only the group that kept using differed significantly from controls (Iudicello et al., 2010). In three rat studies, escalating pre-exposure largely prevented the deficits that a later binge dose produces (Dean et al., 2013).
debate.neither_can_show: Cross-sectional comparisons cannot separate effects of the drug from differences that predate use. The one co-twin study mixed amphetamine with other stimulants, did not test urine and did not establish dependence (Dean et al., 2013). Education is both a possible confounder and a possible consequence: in one study, people who started using earlier had less education than their test scores predicted, which the authors read as use cutting schooling short, so matching or adjusting for education may remove part of a real effect (Dean et al., 2013; Basterfield et al., 2019). That differences do not shrink with abstinence across studies fits lasting damage and pre-existing differences equally. Statistical group differences are not the same as impairment in daily life, and the literature uses the word for both (Hart et al., 2012).
debate.editors_reading: Editors' reading (certainty: very low). A modest average difference, about half to two-thirds of a standard deviation overall and clearest for verbal learning and memory, is consistently found between people with methamphetamine use disorder and healthy volunteers (Basterfield et al., 2019; Cao et al., 2026; Potvin et al., 2018; Scott et al., 2007). Whether methamphetamine caused it, how much predates use, and how much reverses with abstinence are open questions: no study in these reviews measured cognition before use, the one co-twin study is small and mixed stimulants (Dean et al., 2013), dose–response is mostly absent (Cao et al., 2026; Dean et al., 2013; Scott et al., 2007), and the animal deficits come from regimens whose equivalence to human use is uncertain (Dean et al., 2013).
debate.what_would_settle_it: Cohorts that test cognition before regular use begins, with later follow-up of drug use; co-twin or sibling designs restricted to methamphetamine; abstinence studies that retest controls over one to several years with verified abstinence; and reporting of individual impairment rates against norms, not only group means.

statement: In a meta-analysis of five placebo-controlled trials of bupropion or modafinil in people with methamphetamine dependence (642 participants), urine-verified abstinence in the final two weeks of treatment was about one in five with medication and with placebo (70 of 353, 19.8%, vs 62 of 289, 21.5%; OR 0.97, 95% CI 0.65–1.45; 5 fewer per 1,000, from 64 fewer to 69 more, the review's GRADE estimate from an assumed placebo rate of 215 per 1,000), with no significant difference between the two drugs in a subgroup test (p = 0.59). The five trials come from two investigator groups, two from one and three from the other, so they are not five independent replications. A later meta-analysis of bupropion (Bakouni et al., 2023; searched to October 2022) pooled a different outcome, the share of amphetamine-positive urine samples, from seven reports of six trials, each of which shares at least one investigator with another: risk ratio 0.90 (95% CI 0.84–0.96; very low certainty by the review's own rating); for bupropion alone (five trials, 357 participants) 0.90 (0.81–1.00), the rest coming from the two stages of a trial that combined bupropion with injectable naltrexone. By the editors' reading of its tables (it does not state its unit of analysis), that analysis counts each of 15,664 urine samples as an independent observation, so its intervals are too narrow; it reports no absolute rates, the largest bupropion-alone trial gave it no urine data, and retention did not differ (risk ratio 0.97, 0.89–1.05). No dexamphetamine or methylphenidate trial entered this analysis, because none reported abstinence in a form the review could pool; of the six methylphenidate trials, four reported fewer positive urine tests than placebo on their own measures (for example OR 0.42, 0.24–0.72), two of them in people dependent on amphetamine rather than only methamphetamine, and two reported no difference. Across 14 trials of the four drugs, retention to the end of treatment was 53.0% vs 48.0% (OR 1.20, 0.91–1.58; 46 more per 1,000, from 23 fewer to 113 more, the review's estimate from an assumed placebo rate of 480 per 1,000).
plain: Pooling five trials, two medicines tested to help people stop using meth, bupropion and modafinil, did not lead to more people stopping than a placebo did: about 1 in 5 had stopped by the end of treatment in each group. The trials were small and uneven in quality, so a modest benefit or harm cannot be ruled out. A later review of bupropion trials found about one-tenth fewer meth-positive urine tests than with placebo, but this is uncertain: it appears to have counted every test as if it came from a different person, part of the data came from a trial that also gave a second medicine (naltrexone), and for bupropion on its own the result could also mean no effect. Stimulant medicines such as dexamphetamine or methylphenidate were not part of this comparison; in the same review, four of six trials of methylphenidate reported fewer positive urine tests than a placebo, each measured in its own way, and two found no difference.
population: People with methamphetamine dependence in placebo-controlled trials (five trials for abstinence; 14 trials of amphetamine or methamphetamine use disorder for retention); eight placebo-controlled trials of bupropion in amphetamine-type stimulant use disorder (later meta-analysis of the share of positive urine samples)
exposure: Bupropion or modafinil (abstinence); bupropion, modafinil, methylphenidate or dexamphetamine (retention); bupropion alone or with injectable naltrexone (share of positive urine samples)
comparator: Placebo
outcome: Urine-verified abstinence in the last 2 weeks of treatment; retention to the end of the trial; share of amphetamine-positive urine samples (bupropion meta-analysis)
magnitude: Abstinence 19.8% vs 21.5%, OR 0.97 (0.65–1.45), I² 2%; 5 fewer per 1,000 (64 fewer to 69 more). Retention 53.0% vs 48.0%, OR 1.20 (0.91–1.58), I² 15%; 46 more per 1,000 (23 fewer to 113 more) against an assumed placebo retention of 480 per 1,000. Bakouni et al. (2023): share of amphetamine-positive urine samples, 7 reports, 15,664 samples, RR 0.90 (0.84–0.96), I² 89%; bupropion alone (5 trials, 357 participants) 0.90 (0.81–1.00); the two stages of the naltrexone-plus-bupropion trial 0.92 (0.89–0.94); intervals too narrow because samples, not people, appear to be the unit of analysis (editors' reading; the review does not state it); no event rates reported. Retention RR 0.97 (0.89–1.05), 7 reports, 786 participants (8 reports are marked as having retention data; stage 1 of the combination trial appears to have been left out, editors' calculation).

grade.reasoning: Randomized trials. Risk of bias: allocation concealment inadequately reported in more than three-quarters of trials, outcome assessment unclear or high risk in all, incomplete outcome data at high risk in half. Imprecision, two levels: the interval runs from about a third fewer to nearly half again as many abstinent people, so neither a useful benefit nor a harm is excluded, and only 132 people were abstinent. The review's own downgrade for inconsistency is not applied (I² 2% and 15%). Nor are its indirectness downgrades (serious for abstinence, for pooling different drugs and doses; very serious for retention, which also pooled populations that included people who inject drugs, incarcerated people and people with ADHD): the claim is worded to the pooled drugs, doses and populations and speaks for no single drug or dose, and the test between the two drugs for abstinence was not significant (p = 0.59). The five abstinence trials come from two investigator groups, so 'replicated' rests on two groups, not on five independent trials (METHODS §6.3); in the author lists available (Bakouni et al., 2023, reference list), Anderson et al. (2015) shares no author with Shoptaw et al. (2008) or Heinzerling et al. (2014), although both groups have authors on a third bupropion trial outside the abstinence pool (Elkashef et al., 2008). Very low certainty means the result cannot be read as showing that these drugs do not work. The later bupropion meta-analysis (Bakouni et al., 2023) does not change the rating: its outcome (share of positive urine samples) differs from this claim's abstinence outcome; its intervals are too narrow because samples rather than people appear to be the unit of analysis; its bupropion-alone estimate reaches no effect (0.90, 0.81–1.00); much of its estimate comes from a combination trial covered by the claim on naltrexone plus bupropion; it shares two of this claim's three bupropion trials (Shoptaw et al., 2008; Heinzerling et al., 2014), while the third (Anderson et al., 2015) gave it no urine data; and it rated its own urine result very low. Its urine reports are not independent of one another either: Steven Shoptaw is an author of the trials behind six of the seven, and the seventh (Elkashef et al., 2008) shares Walter Ling with two of them (reference list, pp. 11–12).

statement: In a meta-analysis of placebo-controlled trials of medications for methamphetamine or amphetamine withdrawal searched to December 2020 (nine trials of six medications, about 240 participants, six trials at high risk of bias), only six trials of four medications could be pooled; the ibudilast and varenicline trials and one modafinil trial gave no usable data on the review's outcomes. No pooled medication other than amineptine differed from placebo on any pooled outcome: discontinuation with any medication RR 0.70 (95% CI 0.40–1.23); with mirtazapine RR 0.96 (0.48–1.92); withdrawal-symptom scores SMD 0.17 (−0.43 to 0.77); global state (overall severity ratings, three trials), no significant difference. Amineptine, tested in two small trials by the same three investigators, may have reduced discontinuation (RR 0.22, 0.07–0.72; very low certainty; the authors write that it 'may reduce' discontinuation) and improved global state (two trials, 72 participants; low certainty by the review's rating), although the review prints its global-state figures in two inconsistent versions; according to the review it was withdrawn from the market in 1999 after reports of liver toxicity and non-medical use, and the two case reports cited for this predate the stated year. Outside the pooled outcomes, single small trials reported less fatigue on amantadine, faster visual reaction time but no other cognitive benefit on varenicline, and better scores on 2 of 12 measures of a sustained-attention test on ibudilast, while two mirtazapine trials found no benefit for sleep, one reporting more night awakenings than placebo. Only one trial reported adverse events by arm. The two mirtazapine trials here treated the withdrawal period, over two weeks; they are different from the longer trials of mirtazapine for methamphetamine dependence, reported in a separate claim in this section.
plain: Nine small trials have tested six medicines for meth or amphetamine withdrawal, the low mood, tiredness, sleep changes and craving after stopping. Only six of them, testing four medicines, could be combined. Of those medicines, none clearly helped compared with a placebo, apart from one drug that is no longer sold. Single trials reported a few narrower effects, such as less tiredness on amantadine, and one found more waking at night on mirtazapine. The trials were so few, small and flawed that a benefit cannot be ruled out either, and the medicines' side effects were rarely reported. These short mirtazapine trials are separate from the longer trials of mirtazapine for meth use described elsewhere in this section.
population: People with a DSM or ICD diagnosis of methamphetamine or amphetamine use disorder or withdrawal, in inpatient, residential, laboratory, outpatient and one probation-centre setting (USA, Thailand, Australia, Iran); in four trials both arms also received an adjunctive treatment (low-dose lorazepam with supportive care in the two amineptine trials, counselling or symptomatic therapy in two others)
exposure: Mirtazapine, modafinil, amineptine, amantadine, ibudilast or varenicline
comparator: Placebo
outcome: Discontinuation; global state; withdrawal symptoms; craving; adverse events
magnitude: Discontinuation, any medication RR 0.70 (0.40–1.23), 6 trials, 186 participants; mirtazapine 0.96 (0.48–1.92); modafinil 0.67 (0.22–2.03); amantadine 1.33 (0.34–5.24); amineptine 0.22 (0.07–0.72), 2 trials by the same three investigators, I² 58%; per-arm discontinuation counts appear only in the supplementary forest plots (not read), so no absolute effect can be given. Global state, 3 trials, 103 participants: any medication −0.24 (−0.73 to 0.25) and amineptine −0.49 (−0.80 to −0.17), labelled mean differences in the review's table and abstract; its text gives standardised mean differences of −0.34 (−1.06 to 0.25) and −0.70 (−1.18 to −0.22) instead, and the table's single-trial mirtazapine value lies outside its own interval. Withdrawal symptoms SMD 0.17 (−0.43 to 0.77), 3 trials, 93 participants. Craving SMD 0.34 (−0.77 to 1.45), 2 trials, 48 participants.

grade.reasoning: Randomized trials, but six of nine at high risk of bias (selective reporting in six, randomization concerns in five), and very serious imprecision: one or two trials of 19 to 74 participants per medication, with intervals compatible with large benefit and harm. Publication bias was not assessed by the review and cannot be excluded. The amineptine result rests on two small trials from one group, and its global-state estimate is printed as a mean difference in the abstract and table and as a different standardised mean difference in the text, beside a table value that lies outside its own interval, so its size is uncertain. Status mixed: the two mirtazapine trials point different ways (one of them, pooled for discontinuation, reported lower withdrawal scores in data the review could not pool), and amineptine differs from the other drugs.

statement: In three placebo-controlled trials in people with methamphetamine dependence or moderate to severe methamphetamine use disorder, mirtazapine was followed by somewhat less methamphetamine use than placebo on each trial's primary measure, although most participants kept using. Two trials from one San Francisco team, in men who have sex with men without current major depression (mean baseline CES-D depression scores about 17 and 20) with methamphetamine dependence who all received weekly counselling (60 men treated for 12 weeks; 120 cisgender men and transgender women treated for 24 weeks and followed 12 weeks after stopping), found a lower modelled weekly probability of a methamphetamine-positive urine: relative risk 0.57 (95% CI 0.35–0.93) at 12 weeks in the first trial and 0.67 (0.51–0.87) at 12 weeks in the second, with net relative risks of 0.75 (0.56–1.00) at 24 weeks and 0.73 (0.57–0.96) 12 weeks after medication stopped. Most urine samples stayed positive in both arms (66% vs 78% of samples provided at week 12 of the second trial), end-of-treatment abstinence did not differ significantly (18% vs 8%; OR 2.50, 0.80–7.61), adherence measured by electronic pill containers was below 50% in both arms, and drowsiness was more common on mirtazapine. These two trials share investigators, site, population and analysis model, so they are not independent replications of each other. A larger trial from a different team, one of whose authors is also an author of the first trial (344 adults randomized and 339 treated at six Australian public clinics; 37% women and 49% with a PHQ-9 depression score of 10 or more; given referral information and free to use other services, with no trial counselling described; treated for 12 weeks), found a 2.2-day larger fall in self-reported days of use in the past 28 days from baseline to week 12 than with placebo (7.0 against 4.8 days; 95% CI for the difference 0.2–4.2; rate ratio 0.89, 0.80–0.98); because the mirtazapine arm started about 1 day higher (baseline means 23.1 and 22.0 days), the arms differed by only about 1 day at week 12, both using on about 16 to 17 of 28 days (editors' calculation). It found no difference in methamphetamine-negative oral-fluid tests averaged over weeks 4, 8 and 12 (13.2% vs 12.0% of samples; difference 1.3 points, −4.7 to 7.2) or in depression, sleep, HIV risk behaviour or quality of life; drowsiness (47% vs 33%) and weight gain (10% vs 3%) were more common on mirtazapine, 23% vs 15% stopped the medication for reasons related to it (printed P = .19, about .05 by the editors' recalculation), and no outcome after the 12 weeks of treatment is reported. These trials treated methamphetamine dependence over months; the short trials of mirtazapine for the withdrawal period itself, reported in the claim on medicines for withdrawal, are different trials: pooled, they showed no difference from placebo in discontinuation, and one of them reported lower withdrawal scores, a result the review could not pool.
plain: Three trials have compared the antidepressant mirtazapine with a placebo in people with meth dependence. Two small trials by one San Francisco team, in gay, bisexual and other men who have sex with men (and a few transgender women) who also had weekly counselling, found that mirtazapine may lower the chance of a meth-positive urine test by roughly a quarter to two-fifths. In the larger of those two trials, the share of people who stopped using did not clearly differ between the groups. A larger trial by a different team (one of its researchers also worked on the first San Francisco trial), at six clinics in Australia, also included women and people with symptoms of depression. People given mirtazapine reported cutting down their use by about 2 more days in 4 weeks than people given placebo, but both groups still used on most days, and saliva drug tests showed no difference. In all three trials most people kept using and drowsiness was more common on mirtazapine; in the Australian trial weight gain was too, and somewhat more people stopped taking it, a difference that could be due to chance. Two other, short trials of mirtazapine for withdrawal symptoms are a separate question, described elsewhere in this section.
population: People with DSM-IV methamphetamine dependence (two San Francisco trials: cisgender men and transgender women who have sex with men, without current major depression, with a methamphetamine-positive urine at entry, receiving weekly counselling) or DSM-5 moderate to severe methamphetamine use disorder (one trial of adults at six Australian public outpatient clinics, using at least twice a week, with a positive amphetamine screen, not taking prescribed antidepressants)
exposure: Mirtazapine daily for 12 weeks (first San Francisco trial and the Australian trial) or 24 weeks (second San Francisco trial)
comparator: Matched placebo, with the same weekly counselling in the San Francisco trials and the same referral information and access to other services in the Australian trial
outcome: Methamphetamine-positive weekly urine (qualitative test) and end-of-treatment urine-defined abstinence (San Francisco trials); self-reported days of methamphetamine use in the past 28 days and methamphetamine-negative oral fluid (Australian trial)
magnitude: First trial (n=60): RR 0.57 (0.35–0.93) at 12 weeks; raw final-visit positivity 44% vs 63% (editors' RR 0.71, 0.42–1.18). Second trial (n=120): RR 0.67 (0.51–0.87) at 12 weeks; net RR 0.75 (0.56–1.00) at 24 weeks and 0.73 (0.57–0.96) at 36 weeks; raw positivity 66% vs 78%, 63% vs 74% and 71% vs 88%; end-of-treatment abstinence 18% vs 8% (OR 2.50, 0.80–7.61). Editors' crude week-12 risk ratio in the second trial, from the samples provided (25 of 38 vs 32 of 41): 0.84 (0.64–1.12). The modelled risk ratios measure how far the two arms' fitted trends diverged after allowing for the fitted baseline difference; the mirtazapine arm began with more positive urines (85% vs 75%), one reason the modelled ratios lie further from 1 than the crude contrasts (editors' reading). Australian trial (344 randomized, 339 analysed): days of use in the past 28 days fell by 7.0 vs 4.8 from baseline means of 23.1 vs 22.0; difference in the fall −2.2 days (−4.2 to −0.2), rate ratio 0.89 (0.80–0.98) at week 12; −1.3 (−3.3 to 0.6) at week 4 and −1.9 (−3.9 to 0.1) at week 8; editors' estimate of days used at week 12, about 16.1 vs 17.2, a level difference of about 1.1 days. Methamphetamine-negative oral fluid averaged over weeks 4, 8 and 12, 13.2% vs 12.0% (difference 1.3 points, −4.7 to 7.2). Drowsiness 47% vs 33% and weight gain 10% vs 3% (editors' risk differences 13.6, 3.3 to 23.9, and 6.9, 1.7 to 12.0 percentage points); medication stopped for reasons related to it 23% vs 15% (printed P = .19; editors' recalculation from the counts, P = .053); all discontinuations 28% vs 22% (P = .14).

grade.reasoning: Three double-blind placebo-controlled trials (519 participants analysed: 60, 120 and 339). Risk of bias, one level: in the first trial the registered primary outcome was changed from feasibility to efficacy during recruitment; in the second, 34–41% of urine results were missing at each assessment, with more dropout on mirtazapine, and the analysis assumes data missing completely at random; in the third, the only significant result is on self-reported use, drowsiness (47% vs 33%) could have revealed allocation, no blinding check is reported, the article does not describe allocation concealment, and 14% of week-12 data are missing, handled only under missing-at-random assumptions. Inconsistency, one level: on drug tests the two San Francisco trials found lower modelled urine positivity, while the larger Australian trial found no difference in negative oral-fluid samples (13.2% vs 12.0%), and its effect on self-reported use (rate ratio 0.89) is smaller than the San Francisco estimates (0.57 to 0.75); population, counselling, outcome and type of test may explain part of this, but no analysis shows it. This between-trial difference is a separate problem from the third trial's reliance on self-report, which is counted under risk of bias. Indirectness no longer rated down: the Australian trial adds women, people with depressive symptoms and public clinics without trial counselling, and the outcomes are measures of use; people taking antidepressants, pregnant people and people with a recent suicide attempt remain excluded. Imprecision considered but not rated down: each trial's primary interval excludes no effect, although the Australian interval reaches a trivial 0.2 days and the second trial's 24-week interval reaches 1.00. Rated against a minimal important difference rather than against no effect, imprecision could be rated down one level, which would make the claim very low (the strict reading): the Australian interval ends at 0.2 days and its week-12 level difference is about 1.1 days (editors' calculation); none of the trials states such a threshold. Status replicated (METHODS §6.4): the second San Francisco trial (Coffin et al., 2020) and the Australian trial share no author (reference records), site, sample or analysis model, and both found less use on mirtazapine on their primary outcomes, so two independent trials agree in direction. The first San Francisco trial shares one investigator with the Australian trial (Steven Shoptaw, listed there for concept and design) and its team with the second, so neither of those pairs counts as independent; outside these trials, Coffin and Shoptaw are both authors of a bupropion trial (Trivedi et al., 2021), a link the rule does not count. The second San Francisco trial reports that its effect stayed significant when missing urine samples were counted as positive, when week-1 results were included and when baseline correlates of missingness were adjusted for, with the estimates only in a supplement the editors have not read; the analysis stratified by intensity of use showed no significant effect, and a blinding check at week 24 found 46% vs 49% guessing their arm correctly (P = .83). The Australian trial's primary estimate is reported as robust to multiple imputation and to adjustment for baseline covariates (supplement not read).

statement: In controlled-administration studies in adults, a large part of a methamphetamine dose reaches the circulation by non-injection routes, but the published figures depend on what they are measured against. Absolute bioavailability after a single intranasal dose was 79.4% (SD 13.1) in 8 men, measured against a simultaneous intravenous dose of deuterium-labelled drug (Harris et al., 2003). For the smoked route the same study reported 37.4% (SD 14.2) of the amount placed in the device and about 67% of the amount estimated to have left it, while an earlier study in 6 men reported 90.3% of the amount taken up from the device (Cook et al., 1993); the two sets of figures use different denominators and different equipment, so no single bioavailability can be stated for the smoked route. Time to peak plasma concentration was about 2.7 hours (SD 1.2) after the intranasal and 2.5 hours (SD 3.9) after the smoked condition (Harris et al., 2003), and 5.4 to 7.5 hours after a sustained-release oral formulation (Schepers et al., 2003), so it depends on route and on formulation. It is not the time to peak effects: subjective and cardiovascular effects peaked within about 12 to 18 minutes after smoked and intravenous dosing (Cook et al., 1993, who cite their earlier report for the smoked subjective peak).
plain: Most of a snorted dose reaches the bloodstream: about four fifths in one study of eight men. For smoking, published figures run from about a third to about nine tenths, because they are measured against different starting amounts and with different equipment, so there is no single number. The amount in the blood peaks a couple of hours after snorting or smoking, and later with a slow-release pill, while the felt and heart-rate effects peak within about a quarter of an hour.
population: Adults given single doses of methamphetamine in controlled-administration studies (8 men in one study, 6 men in another, 8 volunteers in the oral study)
exposure: Single methamphetamine dose by a named route (study conditions: 50 mg intranasal and 40 mg placed in the device for the smoked condition, with a 10 mg intravenous reference; about 30 mg placed in the device with a 15.4–15.5 mg intravenous dose in the earlier study; 10 or 20 mg oral sustained-release)
comparator: An intravenous dose in the same person, given simultaneously or separately, as the reference for absolute bioavailability
outcome: Absolute bioavailability and time to peak plasma concentration by route
magnitude: Intranasal F 79.4% (SD 13.1), n=8. Smoked F 37.4% (SD 14.2) of the dose placed in the device and about 67% of the estimated delivered dose (n=8), against f 0.903 (SE 0.104) of the dose taken up from the device (n=6). tmax 2.66 h (SD 1.16) intranasal and 2.47 h (SD 3.91) smoked; 5.4 h (SD 2.5) and 7.5 h (SD 3.4) after 10 mg and 20 mg oral sustained-release. Peak subjective and cardiovascular effects at about 12–18 minutes after smoked and intravenous dosing (the smoked subjective peak as Cook et al. cite it from their earlier report).

risk_of_bias.note: Both bioavailability studies were unblinded, without placebo and without a described randomization of condition order; the smoked estimate depends on a recovery measurement from the delivery device.

inconsistency.note: The two smoked figures differ mainly because they use different denominators and equipment, which is an explained difference; the statement carries both.

imprecision.note: 8 and 6 participants; the amount leaving the device ranged from 11.3 to 36.4 mg, and the smoked time to peak has an SD larger than its mean.

grade.reasoning: Controlled-administration studies with a within-person intravenous reference start high (METHODS §6.3). Risk of bias −1: neither bioavailability study was blinded or placebo-controlled, order was balanced but not described as randomized, and in Harris et al. (2003) an intravenous dose was infused during each session. Imprecision −1: 8 and 6 participants, and the smoked estimate rests on how much material left the device, which varied by a factor of three between people. Not downgraded for indirectness, because bioavailability by route is measured directly. Not downgraded for inconsistency, because the smoked figures are computed on different denominators; the claim therefore refuses to state a single smoked figure. Strict reading: if the two smoked estimates are treated as inconsistent rather than as explained by their denominators, the smoked part of this claim is very low.

statement: In a double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover in 12 men who used methamphetamine intravenously and were not dependent, the two methamphetamine enantiomers differed in disposition and in effect. l-Methamphetamine was eliminated more slowly than d-methamphetamine (half-life 13.3 to 15.0 hours against 10.2 to 10.7) and was converted to amphetamine four to seven times less (amphetamine-to-methamphetamine AUC ratio 0.029 to 0.038 against 0.162 to 0.173), while the volume of distribution was the same. Given separately the isomers produced nearly equal exposure (d/l AUC ratio 0.910 and 0.894 at the two doses), but after the 1:1 racemate exposure to the l-isomer exceeded exposure to the d-isomer (ratio 0.679, 90% CI 0.622 to 0.736). Acutely, the conditions containing d-methamphetamine raised blood pressure and positive subjective ratings more, and for longer (about 6 hours against 2 to 4), than l-methamphetamine at the same dose, and the racemate resembled d-methamphetamine on most measures; l-methamphetamine at the larger dose was not inert, and participants put the same money value on it as on the d-isomer. This is one study of single intravenous doses in men, so it does not describe repeated dosing, other routes, or women (Mendelson et al., 2006).
plain: Methamphetamine exists in two mirror-image forms, and which one is in a batch depends on how it was made. In a lab study, 12 men were given each form by injection on separate days without knowing which was which. The 'l' form stayed in the blood longer but raised blood pressure less and felt weaker and shorter; the 50:50 mixture behaved much like the ordinary 'd' form. One small study, single injected doses, men only.
population: Men who used methamphetamine intravenously, not dependent and not seeking treatment (12 laboratory volunteers)
exposure: Single intravenous doses of d-, l- or racemic methamphetamine (study conditions: 0.25 and 0.5 mg/kg of each enantiomer and 0.5 mg/kg of the racemate)
comparator: Placebo (saline) and the other isomer, in the same participants
outcome: Plasma pharmacokinetics (half-life, clearance, amphetamine formation, relative exposure) and acute cardiovascular and subjective effects
magnitude: Half-life: d 10.2 h (SD 2.3), 10.3 (SD 2.6) and 10.7 (SD 2.6); l 13.6 (SD 3.8), 13.3 (SD 3.5) and 15.0 (SD 4.6) (P<.0001). Amphetamine/methamphetamine AUC ratio: d 0.162–0.173; l 0.029–0.038. Relative exposure d/l: 0.910 (90% CI 0.837–0.983) and 0.894 (0.821–0.967) given separately; 0.679 (0.622–0.736) after the racemate. Peak systolic pressure change: +34.5 mm Hg (SD 18.9) after 0.5 mg/kg d-methamphetamine and +33.4 (SD 17.8) after the racemate, against +19.5 (SD 11.3) after 0.5 mg/kg l-methamphetamine and +4.3 (SD 9.9) after placebo. Peak visual-analogue intoxication 46.0 (SD 35.3), 24.7 (SD 27.4), 30.3 (SD 24.9) and 1.7 (SD 4.7) in the same conditions.

risk_of_bias.note: RoB 2 some concerns: blinding integrity untested, about forty outcomes with uncorrected pairwise tests, and an abstract that contradicts its own table on the subjective comparison.

inconsistency.note: Single study; no inconsistency can be assessed.

indirectness.note: The claim is restricted to single intravenous doses in men, which is what was studied.

imprecision.note: 12 participants; the subjective measures have standard deviations close to their means.

grade.reasoning: A placebo-controlled, double-blind, Latin-square crossover starts high (METHODS §6.3). Risk of bias −1 for the untested blind, the uncorrected multiplicity and the abstract-table mismatch; the pharmacokinetic outcomes alone would merit less, but the claim also covers subjective effects. Imprecision −1: 12 men, one study, wide dispersion on the subjective measures. Not downgraded for indirectness because the claim states the route, the doses and the sample. The finding that exposure to the l-isomer exceeds exposure to the d-isomer after the racemate, and the authors' inference that the l-isomer may accumulate with repeated dosing, rest on single doses and are reported as untested.

statement: In laboratory studies of healthy adults given low doses of methamphetamine, tolerance appears within a single dose and, for some effects but not others, across days of repeated dosing. Within one dose, subjective and cardiovascular effects peaked within about 12 to 18 minutes and had largely subsided while plasma concentrations were still high, which the authors read as acute tolerance (Cook et al., 1993; consistent with Mendelson et al., 2006, where effects peaked at 5-15 minutes and ended within about 6 hours against a half-life of about 10 hours). Across days, in a 15-day residential study of 7 volunteers given 5 mg and 10 mg of oral methamphetamine twice a day, each for 3 days (days 4-6 and 10-12), ratings of 'good drug effect' and 'high' rose above the matched placebo baseline on the first day only and were back to baseline by day 3, and most measures of sleep disruption appeared on the first night only (self-estimated sleep also fell on the second night); over the same three days the fall in food intake, about 1450 kcal a day by the authors' estimate, was sustained, ratings of 'heart pounding' and 'trouble sleeping' stayed raised every day, and unpleasant effects (dizziness, flu-like symptoms, confusion, nausea, 'bad drug effect') appeared or grew by day 3 (Comer et al., 2001). The heart-rate response also fades: it was smaller after 13 days of 10 mg a day in 6 men (F=8.26, P=0.035; Perez-Reyes et al., 1991) and smaller by the third administration within about 36 hours in 9 men given 10 mg with alcohol (Kirkpatrick, Gunderson, Levin, et al., 2012), while blood-pressure effects in that study were unchanged. The fading is not explained by the body handling the drug differently: absorption, clearance and half-life were unchanged after the same 13-day course, and a 20% change in peak concentration or exposure would have been detected (Cook et al., 1992). All of this comes from laboratory studies of oral doses of 5 to 10 mg, or single smoked or intravenous doses, in 6 to 9 people at a time; nothing here tests the doses, the smoked or injected routes, or the binge patterns of non-medical use, and one study using a single daily slow-release 10 mg dose found no loss of ratings of 'high', in a setting where the rating never rose above a fifth of its scale (Perez-Reyes et al., 1991).
plain: Two things happen. Within one dose, the effects people feel and the rise in heart rate come within about a quarter of an hour and then fade while the drug is still in the blood. Over days of repeated low oral doses, the pleasant effects faded by the third day and sleep was disturbed mainly on the first night, but eating stayed suppressed, a pounding heart and trouble sleeping stayed, and unpleasant effects such as dizziness, sickness and feeling confused grew. The heart-rate rise got smaller with repeated doses too. This is not because the body clears the drug faster: that was measured and did not change. Every study here used small oral doses in a laboratory, in six to nine people, so none of it tells you what happens in a binge or with smoking or injecting.
population: Healthy adults with previous stimulant experience in laboratory and residential-laboratory studies (6 to 9 people per study; one study of 7 included 4 women, the others were men only)
exposure: Repeated low doses of methamphetamine (study conditions: 5 or 10 mg orally twice a day for 3 days; 10 mg a day of a slow-release preparation for 13 days; 10 mg orally three times over about 36 hours, alone or with alcohol) or a single smoked or intravenous dose (study conditions: a mean of 21.8 mg taken up from the device and 15.4-15.5 mg intravenous in one study; 0.25 and 0.5 mg/kg intravenous in another)
comparator: The same participants' earlier doses or days, their own matched placebo baseline days, and their own plasma concentration-time course
outcome: Change across doses and days in subjective effects, heart rate and blood pressure, sleep, food intake and unwanted effects, and whether the drug's pharmacokinetics change
magnitude: Within a dose: peak subjective effect at about 18 min (SE 2.1) smoked and 17.4 min (SE 1.1) intravenous, maximum heart-rate change at 11.8 min (SE 1.6) and 12.6 min (SE 2.8), with effects subsiding while plasma concentrations remained high (Cook et al., 1993); peaks at 5-15 min lasting up to about 6 h against a half-life of 10.2-10.7 h (Mendelson et al., 2006). Across days at 10 mg twice daily: 'good drug effect' and 'high' significant against baseline on day 1 (F(1,48)=8.0 and 15.0) and not on day 3; total sleep time, non-REM sleep and sleep efficiency reduced on night 1 only (F=12.5, 8.2, 8.1); food intake down by about 1150 kcal (5 mg twice daily) and 1450 kcal (10 mg twice daily) over the three days, as the authors' approximate figures (F=19.2 to 62.7, all P<0.0001); 'heart pounding' and 'trouble sleeping' raised on all three days (Comer et al., 2001). Heart rate: smaller rise after 13 days (F=8.26, P=0.035; Perez-Reyes et al., 1991); heart-rate area under the curve significantly smaller at the third than the first administration for both methamphetamine-alcohol conditions (F(3,24)=15.4-26.5, p<0.0001), with 'good drug effect' area also smaller (F=12.1-14.9, p<0.005) and blood pressure unchanged (Kirkpatrick, Gunderson, Levin, et al., 2012). Pharmacokinetics unchanged after 13 days, with detectable differences of 14.8-21.2% for the elimination rate constant, 6.1-18.3% for peak concentration and 15.6-20.1% for exposure (Cook et al., 1992).

evidence.locator: Results, 1st–2nd paragraphs (left column); Figure 3; Figure 4 (p. 721)
evidence.extracted: Peak subjective effect came at about 18 min (SE 2.1) from the start of the smoked condition and 17.4 min (SE 1.1) after the intravenous dose, and the maximum heart-rate change at 11.8 min (SE 1.6) and 12.6 min (SE 2.8); the figure plotting effect against concentration shows the effects subsiding while plasma concentrations were still high, and cardiovascular measures returned to baseline within a short period after both routes.

evidence.locator: Results > Subjective effects, 1st paragraph (p. 399, right column, continuing p. 400); Figure 1 (p. 400)
evidence.extracted: In a 15-day residential study of 7 volunteers given oral methamphetamine 5 mg twice a day for three days and 10 mg twice a day for three days (blocks on days 4-6 and 10-12; four took the lower dose first, three the higher), ratings of 'good drug effect' (F(1,48)=8.0) and 'high' (F(1,48)=15.0) were raised above the matched placebo baseline day only on the first day of the larger dose and had returned to baseline by day 3; the smaller dose did not differ from baseline on either rating. The two printed P values are transposed relative to their F values (editors' calculation).

evidence.locator: Results > Subjective effects, 2nd paragraph and Table 1 (p. 400); Results > Sleep (p. 401, right column)
evidence.extracted: Over the same three days the unwanted effects went the other way: dizziness (F=9.8) and flu-like symptoms (F=13.2) rose on day 3 but not day 1, and being unable to concentrate, chills, confusion, depression, nausea and 'bad drug effect' (F=17.4) became significant only on day 3, while 'heart pounding' and 'trouble sleeping' were raised on all three days. Sleep was disrupted mainly on the first night (total sleep time F=12.5, non-REM F=8.2, sleep efficiency F=8.1 and movements F=15.4 on that night only; self-estimated hours slept also fell on night 2, F=7.4), which the authors also read as tolerance; there was no rebound on the placebo days after.

evidence.locator: Results > Food intake, 1st paragraph (p. 401, left column); Figure 3 (p. 401)
evidence.extracted: The fall in food intake was sustained across the three days: total daily intake was lower than the placebo baseline by approximately 1150 kcal at 5 mg twice daily and 1450 kcal at 10 mg twice daily (the authors' round figures; the day-by-day gaps in Figure 3 vary around them), significantly on each of days 1, 2 and 3 (F(1,48)=19.2, 44.4 and 29.9; 62.7, 43.9 and 39.6; all P<0.0001), and intake was still below baseline on the first placebo day after each block.

evidence.locator: Results > Cardiovascular effects, continuing on p. 357 above the Discussion; Figure 3 (p. 357)
evidence.extracted: In 6 men who took 10 mg of slow-release oral methamphetamine daily for 13 days, the rise in heart rate over baseline after a fixed oral challenge dose (0.125 mg/kg) was significantly smaller on day 15 than on day 1 (F=8.26, P<0.03 in the Results and P<=0.035 in the summary, which is the value the F statistic gives). The day-1 and day-15 rises themselves are shown only as bars in Figure 3 and are not printed. There was no placebo challenge and no blinding, so habituation to a repeated procedure is not excluded.

evidence.locator: Results > Subjective effects (p. 355); Discussion, 3rd paragraph (p. 357)
evidence.extracted: In the same men, peak ratings of 'high' after the challenge did not differ significantly between day 1 and day 15 (16.8, SEM 6.5, against 10.0, SEM 3.9, out of 100), and the authors state that this small response, under a fifth of the scale, limited the chance of observing tolerance to the subjective effect; peak blood-pressure rises were likewise too small (under 15 mm Hg systolic and 6 mm Hg diastolic) for tolerance to those effects to be tested.

evidence.locator: Results > Pharmacokinetic Analysis, last paragraph (p. 859, continuing p. 860); Discussion, 3rd paragraph (p. 860, into the right column); Table 2 (p. 861)
evidence.extracted: In the pharmacokinetic arm of the same 13-day regimen (8 men in all: 6 at each challenge dose of 0.125 and 0.250 mg/kg, four of them in both studies about 3 months apart), absorption, apparent clearance, renal clearance, the elimination rate constant and the half-life were unchanged between day 1 and day 15; the only significant changes were upward (peak concentration about 12.5% higher at the larger challenge dose). The printed power analysis gives detectable differences of 21.2% and 14.8% for the elimination rate constant, 18.3% and 6.1% for peak concentration and 20.1% and 15.6% for exposure (lower and higher challenge dose), which the authors describe as a 20% difference being detectable, so the fading response is not explained by faster clearance.

evidence.locator: Results > Tolerance > Cardiovascular and BAL effects; Figure 4 (left panel); Discussion, 3rd paragraph; Methods and materials > Design, Table 2 (timing of administrations)
evidence.extracted: In 9 men given oral methamphetamine 10 mg three times over about 36 hours in a residential laboratory, alone or with alcohol, the heart-rate area under the curve was significantly smaller at the third administration than at the first for both methamphetamine-alcohol conditions (F(3,24)=15.4-26.5, p<0.0001, d=0.8-1.6), and only the larger-alcohol combination still exceeded either drug alone. Blood-pressure effects were unchanged across administrations. The first administration was in the morning of day 2 and the third in the evening of day 3, after one night of drug-disturbed sleep, which the authors name as alternatives to tolerance.

evidence.locator: Results > Tolerance > Subjective effects; Table 4
evidence.extracted: In the same study the wanted subjective effects also fell between the first and third administration: 'good drug effect' area under the curve was significantly smaller at administration 3 for both methamphetamine-alcohol conditions (F(3,24)=12.1-14.9, p<0.005, d=0.7-0.8), and for the larger-alcohol combination ratings of 'content' fell from 122.6 (SEM 40.3) to 72.6 (SEM 26.1), 'energetic' from 118.2 (SEM 31.5) to 70.1 (SEM 23.0), 'high' from 96.6 (SEM 27.0) to 56.0 (SEM 18.3) and drug liking from 3.1 (SEM 1.7) to 1.1 (SEM 1.5).

risk_of_bias.note: The within-dose part rests on a study with no placebo, no randomization and no blinding, whose dissociation was never tested statistically. The across-days part rests on a residential study whose main table marks several entries at thresholds their F values do not reach and whose order of dose blocks was not randomized (Comer et al., 2001), on an open before-and-after study with no placebo challenge in 6 men (Perez-Reyes et al., 1991), and on a study whose alcohol conditions cannot have been blind (Kirkpatrick, Gunderson, Levin, et al., 2012). Every reader's card on these four studies rates the overall risk of bias high.

inconsistency.note: The one divergent result, no loss of ratings of 'high' after 13 days of a single daily slow-release dose, comes from a study whose subjective response never exceeded a fifth of the rating scale, which its authors say left no room to observe tolerance; the claim reports that divergence rather than averaging over it.

imprecision.note: Six to nine participants in every study; the size of the decline across days is not printed in any of them, and the key comparisons are reported as F values without effect sizes or intervals.

grade.reasoning: Placebo-controlled within-person laboratory studies start high (METHODS 6.3). Risk of bias -2: the four supporting studies are small within-person designs with no randomization of condition order (Comer, Perez-Reyes), no placebo condition at all in one (Perez-Reyes), blinding that cannot hold for the alcohol conditions (Kirkpatrick), and significance markings in the main table that do not match the stated thresholds (Comer). Imprecision -1: 6 to 9 people per study and no printed effect sizes for the changes across days. Inconsistency 0: the one null result for subjective effects is explained by its dosing schedule and floor response, and is stated in the claim. Certainty very-low. Status replicated-same-team: the fading of the wanted subjective effects across days comes from one laboratory (Comer et al., 2001 and Kirkpatrick, Gunderson, Levin, et al., 2012 share site and grant), while the fading heart-rate response is supported by two independent groups; a strict reading would call the subjective component single-laboratory and the cardiovascular component replicated.
