statement: In a 20-day residential laboratory study of 8 volunteers with stimulant experience, measured total daily food intake fell by about 43% after a sampled 5 mg oral dose of methamphetamine and by about 37% after a 10 mg dose, relative to the matched placebo conditions (both P<0.01), with no selective effect on fat, carbohydrate or protein; the authors give an average reduction of about 1415 kcal. Intake fell through fewer eating occasions and longer gaps between them at the smaller dose and through smaller meals at the larger one, and ratings of hunger were lower after the 10 mg dose (11.46 against 26.50 on a 0–100 scale). The absolute intakes appear only in a figure, the smaller dose produced the larger percentage reduction, and this is a single study of 8 people (Hart et al., 2001).
plain: In a study where people lived in a laboratory and every item they ate was recorded, a single oral dose of meth cut what they ate that day by roughly a third to a half compared with a dummy capsule, and they said they felt less hungry. It is one small study of eight people, and the actual calorie figures are only shown in a graph.
population: Adults with stimulant experience living in a residential laboratory, not seeking treatment (8 volunteers: 1 woman, 7 men)
exposure: A single sampled oral dose of methamphetamine (study conditions: 5 mg and 10 mg capsules)
comparator: Placebo capsules in the same participants, double-blind, with the order of the two active doses counterbalanced
outcome: Total daily caloric intake measured by continuous food recording; number of eating occasions and intake per occasion; hunger ratings
magnitude: About −43% of total daily calories at 5 mg and −37% at 10 mg against the matched placebo conditions (both P<0.01); an average reduction of about 1415 kcal is given in the discussion. Hunger rating 11.46 (SEM 3.94) against 26.50 (SEM 7.18) after the 10 mg dose. Absolute intakes are shown only in Figure 4.

evidence.locator: Results › Food intake; Figure 4
evidence.extracted: Relative to the matched placebo conditions, total daily caloric intake fell by about 43% after the 5 mg and about 37% after the 10 mg sample dose (P<0.01), with fat, carbohydrate and protein falling in parallel; the smaller dose worked through fewer eating occasions and longer gaps between them, the larger through a smaller mean intake per occasion (both P<0.01). Absolute intakes appear only in the figure.

risk_of_bias.note: RoB 2 high overall, mainly for reporting: only significant items of a 50-item scale tabulated, F values without degrees of freedom, an unexplained P<0.03 threshold and no protocol. The food measure itself is objective and validated against the daily trash.

inconsistency.note: Single study; the two doses agree in direction, although the smaller produced the larger percentage reduction.

imprecision.note: 8 participants; no confidence intervals, and the absolute intakes are only in a figure.

grade.reasoning: A double-blind within-person comparison with counterbalanced dose order starts high (METHODS §6.3). Risk of bias −1 for the reporting problems recorded on the card, although the outcome itself is measured rather than self-estimated. Imprecision −1: eight participants, no intervals, values only in a figure. The causal verb is used because the comparison is within person, double-blind and placebo-controlled; the size of the reduction is much less certain than its direction, and the absence of a dose ordering is stated. Strict reading: the magnitude of the reduction is very low certainty: it rests on percentages whose baselines are shown only in a figure.

statement: In a 20-day residential laboratory study of 9 men who all drank alcohol and used cocaine currently (only one used methamphetamine currently), oral methamphetamine 10 mg combined with alcohol (0.375 or 0.75 g/kg) raised heart rate and ratings of 'good drug effect' more than either drug alone, while methamphetamine reduced the feelings of being drunk and sedated and the divided-attention and vigilance decrements that alcohol alone produced, at breath alcohol concentrations that did not differ between the alcohol-alone and combination conditions; alcohol in turn reduced methamphetamine's disruption of sleep (sleep-onset latency 53.4 minutes, SEM 13.1, after methamphetamine alone against 20.6, SEM 3.9, after alcohol alone). By the third administration of the same combination, about 36 hours later, the extra heart-rate and 'good drug effect' responses were significantly smaller and, with the larger amount of alcohol, no longer differed from alcohol alone, while blood-pressure effects were unchanged. The authors raise the concern that people who feel less drunk may drink more, and that people may underestimate their impairment, but neither was measured: the study had no alcohol self-administration or choice procedure, and no condition tested whether a course of one drug produces tolerance to the other, so this is an acute interaction and not cross-tolerance (Kirkpatrick, Gunderson, Levin, et al., 2012).
plain: Taken together with alcohol, a small oral dose of meth raised the heart rate and the pleasant effects more than either drug on its own, and people felt less drunk and did better on attention tests than with alcohol alone, even though their breath alcohol was the same. Alcohol, for its part, took the edge off the sleep that meth was ruining. By the third time the pair were given, within about a day and a half, those extra effects had largely gone. Whether feeling less drunk makes people drink more was not tested here. This is one study of nine men, with small oral doses in a laboratory; only one of them used meth regularly.
population: Nine men aged about 41 years living in a residential laboratory for 20 days, all drinking alcohol 1-5 days a week and using cocaine currently, three of them meeting criteria for cocaine dependence; only one reported current methamphetamine use
exposure: Oral methamphetamine combined with alcohol (study conditions: methamphetamine 10 mg with a placebo drink; methamphetamine 10 mg with alcohol 0.375 g/kg or 0.75 g/kg of estimated total body water; a placebo capsule with alcohol 0.75 g/kg), given three times over about 36 hours
comparator: The same men under each drug alone and against each block's placebo baseline day; there was no placebo-plus-placebo condition
outcome: Heart rate and blood pressure, breath alcohol, ratings of drug effect, drunkenness and sedation, performance on divided attention, vigilance and learning tasks, and sleep measured by actigraphy and questionnaire; and how these changed from the first to the third administration
magnitude: First administration: both combinations raised heart rate more than either drug alone and the larger alcohol dose more than the smaller (F(21,168)=10.9-30.2, p<0.005); 'good drug effect' was higher under both combinations than under either drug alone (F=12.5-52.0, p<0.05), with peak visual-analogue values of 45.2 (SEM 14.2) and 62.9 (SEM 13.5) for the combinations against 6.0 (SEM 5.8) for methamphetamine alone and 33.9 (SEM 12.8) for alcohol alone; peak 'drunk' 44.2 (SEM 13.5) under alcohol alone against 13.9 (SEM 8.7) under the larger-alcohol combination and 1.1 (SEM 0.8) under methamphetamine alone; peak 'sedated' 34.3 (SEM 11.1) against 10.6 (SEM 7.0) and 3.3 (SEM 3.2). Breath alcohol did not differ between alcohol alone and the larger-alcohol combination. Alcohol alone reduced maximum tracking speed on the divided-attention task compared with every other condition (F(18,144)=6.3-12.9, p<0.05) and hits on the rapid information task compared with methamphetamine alone (F=6.7, p<0.05), while the combinations did not. Sleep on night 2: all methamphetamine conditions reduced hours slept and sleep efficiency compared with alcohol alone (F(12,96)=11.6-30.7, p<0.005), and methamphetamine alone reduced them more than the larger-alcohol combination (F=4.6, p<0.05); awakenings per hour 6.9 (SEM 0.9) against 3.5 (SEM 0.6). Third administration: heart-rate area under the curve significantly smaller than at the first for both combinations (F(3,24)=15.4-26.5, p<0.0001), 'good drug effect' area smaller (F=12.1-14.9, p<0.005), and no remaining difference between the larger-alcohol combination and alcohol alone on either measure; blood pressure unchanged across administrations.

evidence.locator: Results > Acute effects (day 2) > Breath alcohol levels, Cardiovascular effects and Subjective effects; Table 3
evidence.extracted: At the first administration both methamphetamine-alcohol combinations raised heart rate more than either drug alone, and the larger alcohol dose more than the smaller (F(21,168)=10.9-30.2, p<0.005); ratings of 'good drug effect' were higher under both combinations than under either drug alone (F=12.5-52.0, p<0.05), while alcohol alone produced the highest ratings of 'drunk' (peak 44.2, SEM 13.5) and 'sedated' (34.3, SEM 11.1) against 13.9 and 10.6 for the larger-alcohol combination. Breath alcohol did not differ between alcohol alone and that combination.

evidence.locator: Results > Acute effects (day 2) > Cognitive/psychomotor performance effects; Figure 3
evidence.extracted: Alcohol alone reduced maximum tracking speed on the divided-attention task compared with all other conditions (F(18,144)=6.3-12.9, p<0.05) and hits on the rapid information task compared with methamphetamine alone (F=6.7, p<0.05), while neither combination produced these decrements; the combination with the larger alcohol dose did raise errors on the repeated-acquisition task compared with methamphetamine alone and with the smaller-alcohol combination (F=14.4-18.2, p<0.001).

evidence.locator: Results > Sleep effects; Table 5, Actiwatch measures
evidence.extracted: All methamphetamine conditions reduced hours slept and sleep efficiency on the night of day 2 compared with alcohol alone (F(12,96)=11.6-30.7, p<0.005), and methamphetamine alone reduced both more than the combination with the larger alcohol dose (F=4.6, p<0.05); sleep-onset latency was 53.4 minutes (SEM 13.1) after methamphetamine alone against 20.6 (SEM 3.9) after alcohol alone, with 6.9 (SEM 0.9) against 3.5 (SEM 0.6) awakenings an hour.

evidence.locator: Results > Tolerance > Cardiovascular and BAL effects and > Subjective effects; Figure 4; Methods and materials > Design, Table 2 (timing of administrations)
evidence.extracted: By the third administration, about 36 hours after the first, the heart-rate area under the curve was significantly smaller than at the first administration for both combinations (F(3,24)=15.4-26.5, p<0.0001) and only the larger-alcohol combination still exceeded either drug alone; 'good drug effect' area was likewise smaller (F=12.1-14.9, p<0.005) and, for the larger-alcohol combination, no longer differed from alcohol alone, while blood-pressure effects were unchanged across administrations.

evidence.locator: Methods and materials > Participants, 2nd paragraph; Discussion, 2nd-3rd paragraphs
evidence.extracted: Qualifications stated by the authors: only one of the nine men used methamphetamine currently while all nine used cocaine; the concern that people might drink more or misjudge their impairment is called speculative, with no self-administration or choice measure taken; and the smaller third response could reflect the time of day (morning first, evening third) or the previous night's drug-disturbed sleep rather than tolerance. No condition tested tolerance to one drug after a course of the other.

risk_of_bias.note: A within-person crossover with counterbalanced order; the capsule was double-blind but the alcohol conditions cannot have been blind in men drinking 3-7 drinks a day, and about sixty outcomes were tested with uncorrected planned comparisons. Downgraded one level rather than two because the findings cited here rest largely on measured outcomes (breath alcohol, heart rate, task performance, actigraphy) that the broken blind does not affect.

inconsistency.note: The acute interaction agrees with the one earlier human study of this pair and with studies of alcohol combined with cocaine, caffeine and d-amphetamine; the repeated-administration part has not been tested elsewhere.

indirectness.note: The claim is worded for the doses, route and sample studied.

imprecision.note: Nine men, no confidence intervals, and effect sizes printed as d values up to 33.3 that cannot be read as standardized mean differences.

grade.reasoning: A placebo-controlled within-person laboratory study with counterbalanced order starts high (METHODS 6.3). Risk of bias -1: the alcohol conditions were effectively unblinded and the analysis is uncorrected across many outcomes, but the central findings here are objective measures. Imprecision -1: nine men. Certainty low, single study. The claim is worded as an observed interaction, not as cross-tolerance: no condition in this study gave one drug after a course of the other, and the authors' concern that people may drink more was not measured.

verification.flag_note: Staged by the first reader; anchors are ai-located and await a second reader. The senior author may wish to decide whether the interaction belongs in section 6 (interactions) or section 5 (effects); it is filed in section 6 because its importance is the risk of misjudging intoxication.

statement: In 11 adults who used methamphetamine regularly, mainly by snorting it, and were not seeking treatment (one double-blind, placebo-controlled inpatient laboratory study in which each person had placebo and three single doses on separate days in counterbalanced order), a single intranasal dose taken earlier the same day, compared with placebo, is associated with shorter and worse sleep that night. After the highest dose, wrist activity monitors (worn by 6 of the 11) recorded about 2 hours less sleep (4.4 against 6.4 hours) and more awakenings; the two lower doses did not significantly change measured sleep. People's own estimates (all 11) were about 2.9 and 4.9 hours less sleep after the two higher doses, with worse ratings of falling asleep, sleeping well and waking often; the authors read the gap between reported and measured sleep as self-reports overstating the loss, a comparison that mixes 11 people's reports with 6 people's monitors. Single laboratory doses differ from the repeated doses and binges of everyday use, which the study did not test. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: In a small hospital study, people slept less and worse on the night after a single dose of methamphetamine taken earlier that day than after a dummy dose. With the highest dose, a wrist monitor showed about two hours less sleep and more waking. People felt they had lost even more sleep than the monitor showed. Only 11 people took part, the monitor worked for 6 of them, and repeated doses or binges were not tested.
population: Adults aged 22 to 45 (2 women, 9 men) with DSM-IV methamphetamine abuse or dependence who used it mainly intranasally, were not seeking treatment and had no other psychiatric disorder; studied as inpatients
exposure: A single intranasal dose of methamphetamine given by the researchers earlier the same day (three dose levels; amounts and times are study conditions in the study card)
comparator: The same people's placebo day
outcome: Sleep that night: total sleep and awakenings by wrist actigraphy (6 people); estimated hours slept and sleep-quality ratings the next morning (11 people)
magnitude: Actigraphy, highest dose against placebo: 4.4 against 6.4 hours of sleep (an average 2 hours less, p < .01) and more awakenings than after any other condition (p < .01); lower doses not significant. Self-estimated sleep: 7.70 (SEM 0.31) hours after placebo, 6.77 (0.56), 4.83 (0.85) and 2.84 (0.89) after the three active doses, about 2.9 and 4.9 hours less after the two higher doses (p < .001); 'slept well' 85.2 after placebo against 49.6 and 21.4, and 'woke often' 16.5 against 64.8 and 67.6 (100-point scales). No confidence intervals are reported.

evidence.locator: Results › 3.1 Sleep, 1st paragraph; Figure 1 legend (left panels, n = 6)
evidence.extracted: Actigraphy in 6 participants: total sleep after the highest dose 4.4 hours against 6.4 hours after placebo, an average reduction of 2 hours (p < .01); awakenings more frequent after the highest dose than after any other condition (p < .01).

evidence.locator: Results › 3.1 Sleep, 2nd paragraph; Table 1, sleep questionnaire rows
evidence.extracted: All 11 participants: estimated hours slept 7.70 (SEM 0.31) after placebo against 4.83 (0.85) and 2.84 (0.89) after the two higher doses, about 2.9 and 4.9 hours less (p < .001); 'fell asleep easily' 57.50 against 27.40 and 10.22; 'slept well' 85.20 against 49.60 and 21.44; 'woke often' 16.50 against 64.80 and 67.56; 'satisfied with sleep' 80.30 against 42.40 and 25.33 (df 1 and 30).

evidence.locator: 2.3 Sleep Monitoring; Discussion, 2nd and 4th paragraphs
evidence.extracted: Actigraphy data were lost for the first five participants through equipment malfunction, so objective sleep comes from 6 of 11. The authors contrast nearly 5 fewer self-reported hours with 2 fewer measured hours and note that only single doses were studied, while illicit use, anecdotally, comes in multiple dose cycles that may continue over several consecutive days.

risk_of_bias.note: Counterbalanced order (scheme not described); blinding of a noticeable drug not checked, which matters for the self-rated sleep; actigraphy lost in 5 of 11 through equipment failure.

indirectness.note: Worded for the doses, route and setting studied.

imprecision.note: Eleven people (6 with actigraphy), one study, no confidence intervals.

grade.reasoning: A placebo-controlled within-person laboratory study with counterbalanced order starts high. Risk of bias -1 (order scheme not described; blinding not checked for self-rated outcomes; objective sleep missing in 5 of 11). Imprecision -2 (one study of 11 people, objective sleep in 6, no intervals). Very low. Not downgraded for indirectness because the claim is worded for single laboratory doses in experienced people and says that binges were not tested. Single study; the same participants appear in the acute-effects report of the same group, which is not independent evidence.

statement: In the same 11 adults who used methamphetamine regularly and were not seeking treatment (one double-blind, placebo-controlled inpatient laboratory study), the morning after the highest of three single intranasal doses, compared with the morning after placebo, is associated with lower self-ratings of feeling alert, content, friendly, social and talkative, a faster heart rate (90 against 78 beats per minute) and higher blood pressure (diastolic 79 against 69 mm Hg), with methamphetamine still measurable in the blood after every dose. Ratings of feeling depressed, feeling anxious and wanting methamphetamine did not change, and no effect was detected on tests of attention, memory and reaction speed; the paper gives no numbers for those tests and tested only once in the morning, so only a large impairment could have been detected. After the two lower doses, only one of the tabulated mood ratings changed. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: The morning after the highest dose in a small hospital study, people felt less alert, content and friendly than after a dummy dose, and their heart rate and blood pressure were still higher. They did not feel sadder or more worried and did not want methamphetamine more. Memory and attention tests showed no change, but the study was small, tested only once that morning and did not print the test results. Lower doses changed little the next morning.
population: Adults aged 22 to 45 (2 women, 9 men) with DSM-IV methamphetamine abuse or dependence who used it mainly intranasally, were not seeking treatment and had no other psychiatric disorder; studied as inpatients
exposure: A single intranasal dose of methamphetamine the previous day (three dose levels; amounts and times are study conditions in the study card)
comparator: The same people's morning after placebo
outcome: Next-morning mood and drug-effect ratings, craving, cognitive and psychomotor performance, heart rate, blood pressure and plasma methamphetamine
magnitude: Highest dose against placebo (100-point scales): alert 38.1 against 55.6; content 37.4 against 53.9; friendly 43.0 against 65.0; social 40.8 against 67.1; talkative 37.4 against 58.5 (each marked p < .05); heart rate 90.5 against 78.4 bpm; systolic 124 against 118 and diastolic 78.6 against 69.0 mm Hg (p < .05). After the lowest dose, 'social' 50.4 against 67.1 (p < .05); no other tabulated mood rating, heart rate or blood pressure changed significantly after the two lower doses. Depressed, anxious and craving ratings unchanged and no significant performance effect (no values reported).

evidence.locator: Results › 3.2 Subjective effects; Table 1, subjective-effect rows
evidence.extracted: Next morning after the highest dose, against placebo: alert 38.09 against 55.55, content 37.36 against 53.91, friendly 43.00 against 65.00, social 40.82 against 67.09, talkative 37.36 against 58.46 (marked p < .05); energetic 22.80 against 35.20 marked only as different from the lowest dose; 'social' also lower after the lowest dose (50.36; F = 4.46).

evidence.locator: Results › 3.4 Physiological measures; Table 1, physiological rows
evidence.extracted: Next morning after the highest dose: heart rate 90.46 against 78.36 bpm, systolic pressure 124.00 against 118.00 and diastolic 78.55 against 69.00 mm Hg (all p < .05 against placebo); plasma methamphetamine still measurable after all three active doses.

evidence.locator: Results › 3.3 Cognitive/Psychomotor effects; Discussion, 3rd paragraph
evidence.extracted: No significant residual effect on the digit-symbol, repeated-acquisition, divided-attention, rapid-information and digit-recall tasks (no means or statistics given); ratings of 'depressed', 'anxious' and 'I want meth' were not altered by the previous day's dose (no values given).

evidence.locator: Discussion, 4th paragraph
evidence.extracted: The authors note that mood and performance were measured at only one morning time point, that subtle performance effects might need repeated testing through the day, that only single doses were studied, and that the persisting cardiovascular elevation may matter for toxicity with repeated use.

risk_of_bias.note: Selective reporting (no numbers for performance or for the unchanged mood items) and possible unblinding for self-ratings.

indirectness.note: Worded for single laboratory doses in experienced people.

imprecision.note: Eleven people; the absence of a performance effect is not precise.

grade.reasoning: A placebo-controlled within-person laboratory study with counterbalanced order starts high. Risk of bias -1 (self-rated mood by participants who may have recognised the dose; performance and several mood results reported without numbers). Imprecision -2 (11 people, one morning test, no intervals; the null performance result cannot exclude moderate effects). Very low. Single study.

statement: In adults with methamphetamine dependence newly admitted to residential treatment in California (one open-label randomized trial, 135 people), a supervised programme of treadmill and weight training, compared with an equal number of health-education sessions, is associated with larger falls in self-rated depression and anxiety over the programme: at its end, Beck Depression Inventory scores averaged 2.4 against 4.8 and Beck Anxiety Inventory scores 2.2 against 5.1 (on the depression scale, 0 to 13 counts as minimal). Both groups improved steeply from mild or minimal levels; the exercise group started with more anxiety (16.5 against 11.9 points, a gap the paper reports as non-significant but the editors calculate as clearly significant), which by itself would produce part of a larger fall; the end-of-programme differences of 2.4 and 2.9 points were smaller than the 3.5 points the trial was designed to detect; participants knew their group and rated their own symptoms; and these outcomes were secondary in the trial's registration, whose post-discharge follow-up is not reported. A 2024 systematic review lists two other studies from China whose authors also reported less depression and anxiety with exercise (one of them a single dance session), but it gives no numbers and did not appraise them. No harms were recorded in the trial. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: In one trial in a live-in treatment centre, people with methamphetamine dependence who were given supervised exercise ended up with slightly lower depression and anxiety scores than people given health-education classes. Both groups improved a lot. The exercise group started out more anxious, people knew which group they were in and rated themselves, and the difference was smaller than the trial hoped to find. Other studies reporting the same direction are known only from a review without numbers. Nobody was harmed.
population: Adults aged 18 to 47 with DSM-IV methamphetamine dependence newly admitted to a publicly funded residential treatment programme in Southern California (2010 to 2013); 30% women, 48% Latino; people with major depression excluded by the trial registration
exposure: A supervised, progressive aerobic and resistance exercise programme during residential treatment (study conditions in the study card)
comparator: An equal number of group health-education sessions in the same treatment programme
outcome: Self-rated depression (Beck Depression Inventory) and anxiety (Beck Anxiety Inventory), weekly, over the programme
magnitude: Treatment by time: depression beta -0.63 (P = 0.001); anxiety beta -0.95 (P = 0.001). End of programme: BDI 2.43 (SD 4.22) against 4.82 (SD 5.71); BAI 2.18 (SD 4.94) against 5.11 (SD 7.79); differences 2.4 and 2.9 points, standardized about 0.48 and 0.45 (editors' calculation assuming everyone randomized contributed; the number analysed is not reported). Baseline: BDI 13.7 (SD 5.3) against 12.0 (SD 6.3); BAI 16.5 (SD 6.0) against 11.9 (SD 5.1), reported P = 0.08 (editors' calculation p < 0.0001). No confidence intervals for the main effects.

evidence.page: Results › Changes in depression and anxiety symptoms
evidence.locator: Results › Changes in depression and anxiety symptoms, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: Treatment by time effects: depression beta -0.63, P = 0.001, end-of-programme BDI 2.43 (SD 4.22) with exercise against 4.82 (SD 5.71) with health education; anxiety beta -0.95, P = 0.001, BAI 2.18 (SD 4.94) against 5.11 (SD 7.79); adjusted for demographics.

evidence.page: Results › Changes in depression and anxiety symptoms
evidence.locator: Results › Changes in depression and anxiety symptoms, 1st paragraph; Results › Participant characteristics
evidence.extracted: Baseline BDI 13.7 (SD 5.3) against 12.0 (SD 6.3), reported P = 0.21; baseline BAI 16.5 (SD 6.0) against 11.9 (SD 5.1), reported P = 0.08, with 69 and 66 randomized (editors' calculation: anxiety t about 4.8, p < 0.0001; depression p about 0.09). No harms or unintended effects in either group.

evidence.locator: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01103531, Study Plan › Design Details; Primary and Secondary Outcome Measures
evidence.extracted: Registered primary outcome: self-reported days of methamphetamine use over the 12 weeks after discharge; psychiatric symptoms registered as a secondary outcome measured to discharge and at 12 and 26 weeks after discharge; masking: none (open label). The paper calls depression and anxiety its primary outcomes and reports only the programme period.

evidence.locator: Methods › Statistical Analyses; Discussion, 5th paragraph
evidence.extracted: The trial was powered to detect a 3.5-point difference (SD 5) between groups; the authors' limitations are a residential treatment sample, self-reported measures only, stress topics in the health-education sessions and a 70% male sample.

evidence.locator: Results › 3.1 Negative emotions, 3rd paragraph; Table 1, rows (16), (22), (23), (24); Discussion, 4th paragraph
evidence.extracted: A systematic review (17 entries) reports improved depression and anxiety with exercise in four entries: a 60-person trial (ref 16), two reports of the trial above (refs 22, 23) and a single dance session in women (ref 24); no numbers, no appraisal results, and the trial above is counted three times across the review.

risk_of_bias.note: Open label and self-reported outcomes (high risk for measurement); baseline anxiety imbalance; registered secondary outcomes reported as primary.

inconsistency.note: Not downgraded: the review's second-hand reports point the same way.

indirectness.note: Worded for people in residential treatment in early abstinence; not for the comedown after occasional use.

imprecision.note: One trial, 135 people, end-of-programme differences smaller than the planned minimum, no confidence intervals.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable; the review did not examine it.

grade.reasoning: Randomized evidence starts high. Risk of bias -2 (open-label allocation with self-rated outcomes; a large baseline imbalance in anxiety; outcomes switched from registered secondary to reported primary, with follow-up unreported). Imprecision -1 (one trial of 135; differences below the trial's own target; no intervals). Very low. Not downgraded for indirectness because the claim is worded for residential treatment in early abstinence. The review's other studies are known only as directions without numbers and one of its 'supporting' entries is this same trial, so the status stays single study.

statement: In people with methamphetamine use disorder, mostly in compulsory drug rehabilitation centres in China, the evidence is insufficient to say how much exercise reduces craving. One systematic review (2024; critically low confidence under AMSTAR 2) lists five studies whose authors reported lower craving with exercise than in control conditions, during and shortly after single sessions of dancing, cycling or treadmill exercise and after programmes of combined aerobic and resistance exercise or Tai Chi, and a sixth in which methamphetamine use after treatment fell among people with less severe use. The review gives no numbers, did not appraise the studies, and misreports some of their details; none of the studies was read for this claim. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated (directions as reported by the review).
plain: Several studies, mostly from treatment centres in China, say people had less craving for methamphetamine during and after exercise than without it. We know them only through one weak review that gives no numbers and did not check how well the studies were done, so nobody can say how big the effect is or how long it lasts.
population: People with methamphetamine use disorder (DSM-5) in rehabilitation or residential treatment, mostly in compulsory drug rehabilitation institutions in China; studies in men only, women only or both
exposure: Single exercise sessions or exercise programmes (aerobic, resistance, dance, Tai Chi; study conditions in the study card)
comparator: The control conditions of the included studies (not tabulated by the review; often health education or no exercise)
outcome: Self-rated craving (visual analogue scales, Desires for Drug Questionnaire, cue-induced craving) and, in one study, methamphetamine use after treatment
magnitude: Not quantifiable: the review reports only directions, with lower craving with exercise in refs 25, 30, 34, 35 and 36 and less methamphetamine use among people with lower-severity use in ref 37, and gives no effect sizes, intervals or appraisal results.

evidence.locator: Results › 3.3 Drug cravings, 3rd paragraph; Table 1, rows (25), (30), (34), (35), (36), (37); Discussion, 4th paragraph
evidence.extracted: Lower craving reported with single sessions of dance or aerobic exercise in women (ref 34), acute cycling (ref 30), acute exercise compared across intensities (ref 25), a programme of aerobic and resistance exercise with lower inflammatory markers (ref 35) and Tai Chi in women (ref 36); less methamphetamine use after the programme among people with lower-severity use (ref 37). No numbers given.

evidence.locator: 2. Methodology, 2nd and 4th paragraphs; Table 1, rows (22), (23), (29), (37)
evidence.extracted: Search of two databases, English only, 2014 to 2023; risk of bias said to be assessed with AMSTAR 2 (a tool for reviews) with no results reported; no additional data requested and no analysis beyond the articles. One 135-person trial appears three times and one entry is a protocol without results.

risk_of_bias.note: Not appraisable: the review reports no risk-of-bias results; outcomes are self-rated craving in unblinded participants.

inconsistency.note: Not downgraded: all reported directions agree.

indirectness.note: Second-hand through a review that misdescribes some studies; settings mostly compulsory rehabilitation in China.

imprecision.note: No effect sizes, intervals or sample sizes per outcome.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable; small positive studies may be over-represented.

grade.reasoning: Seen only through a review, the claim starts from the design of the studies described (mostly randomized or controlled experiments): high. Risk of bias -2 (the studies were not appraised; craving was self-rated by unblinded participants). Indirectness -1 (second-hand, with errors in the review's descriptions). Imprecision -2 (no numbers at all). Very low. Status replicated because the review reports the same direction for studies from several groups, but none was read here and the size of any effect is unknown.
